items.text: Opening Mishnah: Four New Years
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Four New Years
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates four New Year dates: Nisan for kings and festivals, Elul for animal tithes (with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon saying Tishrei), Tishrei for years, Sabbatical years, Jubilees, planting, and vegetables, and Shevat for trees (Beit Shammai says the first, Beit Hillel says the fifteenth).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating there are four New Year dates, beginning with Nisan as the New Year for kings and festivals.
The Mishnah states that Elul is the New Year for animal tithes, with Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon dissenting and saying it is Tishrei.
The Mishnah states that Tishrei is the New Year for years, Sabbatical years, Jubilees, planting, and vegetables.
The Mishnah states that Shevat is the New Year for trees according to Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel says it is the fifteenth of Shevat.

items.text: Gemara's Question and Answer: Purpose of the New Year for Kings
items.text_en: Gemara's Question and Answer: Purpose of the New Year for Kings
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halakhic purpose the New Year for kings serves. Rav Chisda answers that it is for dating documents, citing a Mishnah that early-dated promissory notes are invalid while late-dated ones are valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halakhic purpose the New Year for kings serves.
Rav Chisda answers that the New Year for kings is used for dating documents (שטרות).
The Gemara cites a Mishnah that early-dated promissory notes are invalid while late-dated ones are valid, supporting Rav Chisda's answer.

items.text: Baraita: Rule for Counting a King's Regnal Year
items.text_en: Baraita: Rule for Counting a King's Regnal Year
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a king ascends on the twenty-ninth of Adar, once the first of Nisan arrives, it counts as his first year. But if he ascends on the first of Nisan itself, his year is not counted until the next Nisan. The Gemara then begins analyzing this ruling.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, teaching that a king who ascends on the twenty-ninth of Adar has his first year counted from the following first of Nisan, but if he ascends on the first of Nisan itself, his year is not counted until the next Nisan.

The Gemara quotes the master's statement about the king who ascended on the twenty-ninth of Adar and then begins to raise a question, implied by the word 'הא' (behold), about the implication of the ruling.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's implication
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that Nisan is the new year for kings and that one day in the year counts as a year. It then addresses a case where a king was appointed in Adar, lest one think he should be credited with two years, teaching that he only gets one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah teaches that Nisan is the New Year for kings and that one day in a year counts as a year, then asks why the next clause is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the clause is necessary for a case where the king was appointed in Adar, lest one think he should be credited with two years, so it teaches that he only gets one.

items.text: Baraita on regnal years for successive kings
items.text_en: Baraita on regnal years for successive kings
items.desc_en: A baraita is presented detailing three cases: a king dies in Adar and his successor ascends in Adar, both get a year; dies in Nisan and successor ascends in Nisan, both get a year; dies in Adar and successor ascends in Nisan, the first gets a year and the second gets a second year. The Gemara explains why each case is necessary, addressing potential concerns about counting a year for two kings, counting a year at the beginning of the year, and counting two years for a king appointed in Adar.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents three cases of king succession and how to count regnal years.
The Gemara asks why the first case of the baraita is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that one year can be counted for two kings, countering a possible assumption.
The Gemara asks why the second case of the baraita is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that one day at the beginning of the year is also considered a year, countering a possible distinction.
The Gemara asks why the third case of the baraita is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is needed for a case where the king was appointed in Adar and is a king's son, countering the assumption that two years should be counted.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's scriptural derivation for Nisan
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's scriptural derivation for Nisan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from a verse that kings' years are counted from Nisan, by comparing Solomon's reign to the Exodus, which is known to be in Nisan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן) derives from a verse that kings' years are counted only from Nisan, by juxtaposing Solomon's reign to the Exodus from Egypt.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the Exodus date
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the Exodus date
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how we know the Exodus is counted from Nisan, suggesting it might be from Tishrei. It proves from verses that the fortieth year is called the same in Av and Shevat, implying the new year is not Tishrei. A further challenge about the verse referring to the Tabernacle's erection is resolved by a gezerah shavah from Rav Pappa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how we know that the Exodus itself is counted from Nisan, suggesting it might be counted from Tishrei.

The Gemara rejects the possibility, citing verses that call both the fifth month (Av) and the eleventh month (Shevat) in the fortieth year 'the fortieth year', proving that the new year is not Tishrei.
The Gemara objects that the second verse (in Shevat) might refer to the erection of the Tabernacle rather than the Exodus.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's resolution via גזירה שווה
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution via גזירה שווה
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the objection by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the phrase 'שנת עשרים' (twentieth year) to 'שנת ארבעים' (fortieth year), establishing that both refer to the Exodus.

items.text: Gemara's challenge about the order of events
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge about the order of events
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the event in Av precedes the event in Shevat, and proves from a verse that Sihon was still alive when Aaron died, establishing the chronological order.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the proof: perhaps the event in Shevat (the later month) actually precedes the event in Av chronologically, undermining the inference about the new year.
The Gemara rejects the challenge, citing a verse that Sihon was still alive when Aaron died, proving the Av event is earlier.

items.text: Opening question: What did the Canaanite king hear?
items.text_en: Opening question: What did the Canaanite king hear?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Canaanite king heard of Aaron's death and the departure of the clouds of glory, which he mistakenly thought gave him permission to fight Israel. Rabbi Abahu then offers a homiletic reading of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Canaanite king heard, and answers that he heard of Aaron's death and the departure of the clouds of glory, mistakenly thinking permission was given to fight Israel.
Rabbi Abahu offers a homiletic reading of the verse, interpreting 'וַיִּרְאוּ' as 'וַיִּירָאוּ' (they feared), citing Resh Lakish's principle that 'כִּי' has four meanings.

items.text: Reconciliation: Sihon is Arad is Canaan
items.text_en: Reconciliation: Sihon is Arad is Canaan
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the apparent contradiction between the Canaanite king and Sihon, and resolves it by stating that Sihon, Arad, and Canaan are the same person, with different names.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the apparent contradiction between the Canaanite king and Sihon.
The Tanna resolves the contradiction by stating that Sihon, Arad, and Canaan are the same person with different names.

items.text: Rejecting Iyar as the new year for kings
items.text_en: Rejecting Iyar as the new year for kings
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that perhaps the new year for kings is Iyar, but rejects this based on verses that call both Nisan and Iyar the 'second year', implying that the new year is not Iyar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that perhaps the new year for kings is Iyar.
The Gemara rejects Iyar by citing verses that call both Nisan and Iyar the 'second year', proving that the new year is not Iyar.

items.text: Rejecting Sivan as the new year for kings
items.text_en: Rejecting Sivan as the new year for kings
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Sivan as the new year, but rejects it because the verse would then need to say 'in the third month of the second year', which it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes Sivan as the new year for kings.
The Gemara rejects Sivan because the verse would then need to say 'in the third month of the second year', which it does not.

items.text: Rejecting Tammuz, Av, and Adar
items.text_en: Rejecting Tammuz, Av, and Adar
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly suggests and dismisses Tammuz, Av, and Adar as possible new years for kings, without detailed argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara briefly suggests and dismisses Tammuz, Av, and Adar as possible new years for kings, without detailed argument.

items.text: Proof from Solomon's building: second month is Nisan
items.text_en: Proof from Solomon's building: second month is Nisan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar brings a proof from the verse about Solomon building the Temple, interpreting 'second' as the second month of the year for kings. Ravina objects that it might mean the second day of the month, but the Gemara rejects this and also rejects the possibility of the second day of the week, concluding that it must be the month.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar brings a proof from the verse about Solomon building the Temple, interpreting 'second' as the second month of the year for kings.
Ravina objects that 'second' might mean the second day of the month, but the Gemara rejects this because the verse would have explicitly said 'second of the month'.

The Gemara rejects the possibility of 'second' meaning the second day of the week, because such a phrase is not found in Scripture, and it compares the second 'second' to the first 'second' — just as the first is a month, so too the second is a month.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan: kings counted from Nisan
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan: kings counted from Nisan
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's view, listing multiple verses that show the year count for kings begins from Nisan, including the exodus, Aaron's death, and the conquest of Sihon.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rabbi Yochanan, beginning with verses showing the exodus count from Nisan and linking to Aaron's death.
The baraita continues citing verses about Sihon's defeat, the Canaanite king's hearing, Aaron's death, and the Tabernacle's establishment in the first month.
The baraita concludes by citing verses about the second year, the third month, and Solomon's building in the second month, reinforcing the Nisan-based count.

items.text: Distinction: Jewish kings from Nisan, non-Jewish from Tishrei
items.text_en: Distinction: Jewish kings from Nisan, non-Jewish from Tishrei
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the rule of counting from Nisan applies only to Jewish kings, but for non-Jewish kings, the year begins from Tishrei, as proven from the book of Nehemiah where both Kislev and Nisan are called the twentieth year.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the rule of counting from Nisan applies only to Jewish kings, but for non-Jewish kings, the year begins from Tishrei.
Rav Chisda cites verses from Nehemiah where both Kislev and Nisan are called the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, proving that the non-Jewish regnal year begins from Tishrei.
The Gemara concludes that since the same regnal year is used for both Kislev and Nisan, the new year for non-Jewish kings cannot be Nisan, confirming Rav Chisda's distinction.

items.text: Question: Is the reference definitely to Artaxerxes?
items.text_en: Question: Is the reference definitely to Artaxerxes?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the 'twentieth year' in the verses refers to Artaxerxes, or perhaps to another king, leaving the matter unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the 'twentieth year' in the verses refers to Artaxerxes, or perhaps to another king, leaving the matter unresolved.

items.text: Rav Pappa's gezeirah shavah
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's gezeirah shavah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that the phrase "year twenty" in Nehemiah refers to Artaxerxes, using a gezeirah shavah from another instance of "year twenty" in the same book.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the 'year twenty' in Nehemiah refers to a different counting system.
Rav Pappa answers by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the phrase 'שנת עשרים' in Nehemiah to prove it refers to Artaxerxes.

items.text: Proof that the Kislev event preceded Nisan
items.text_en: Proof that the Kislev event preceded Nisan
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that the event in Kislev preceded the one in Nisan by citing a baraita and the verses from Nehemiah chapters 1 and 2.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how we know that the Kislev event preceded the Nisan event, suggesting the opposite might be true.
The Gemara rejects the possibility, citing a baraita that establishes the chronological order: Hanani spoke to Nehemiah in Kislev, and Nehemiah spoke to the king in Nisan.
The baraita cites the verse from Nehemiah chapter 1, showing Hanani's report to Nehemiah occurred in Kislev of the twentieth year.
The baraita cites the verses from Nehemiah chapter 2, showing Nehemiah's request to the king occurred in Nisan of the same year, confirming the Kislev event preceded Nisan.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection from Haggai
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection from Haggai
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects by citing verses from Haggai that seem to show a different counting of years for Darius, implying a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects by citing verses from Haggai that show a sixth-month date in year two of Darius and a seventh-month date also in year two, arguing that if the counting were by Jewish kings' reckoning, the seventh-month date should be in year three.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's answer: Cyrus counted like Jewish kings
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's answer: Cyrus counted like Jewish kings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu answers that Cyrus was a righteous king, so they counted his years from Nisan like Jewish kings, resolving the discrepancy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu answers that Cyrus was a righteous king (מלך כשר), so they counted his regnal years from Nisan like Jewish kings, resolving the discrepancy in the verses.

items.text: Rav Yosef's counter-objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's counter-objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef raises two difficulties: the verses still contradict, and the case of Darius is different from Cyrus. The baraita resolves that Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes are the same person.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that if Cyrus's reign is counted like Jewish kings, the verses contradict: the Temple was finished in year 6 of Darius, but Ezra arrived in year 7, which should have been year 8.
Rav Yosef further objects that the case of Cyrus is different from Darius, and the baraita resolves that Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes are the same person.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's resolution: before and after souring
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's resolution: before and after souring
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak resolves the remaining difficulty by distinguishing between before and after the decree 'soured' (i.e., the permission to build was revoked and renewed).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: despite the previous resolution, the chronological inconsistency remains unresolved.
Rabbi Yitzchak resolves the difficulty by distinguishing between the period before the decree 'soured' (i.e., the permission was revoked and then renewed) and after it soured.

items.text: Rav Kahana's objection
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects to Rabbi Yitzchak's answer by questioning whether the decree actually soured, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects to Rabbi Yitzchak's answer by questioning whether the decree actually soured, citing a verse.

items.text: Debate on the king's motive for the decree
items.text_en: Debate on the king's motive for the decree
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak questions whether the king's decree to provide offerings was praiseworthy, given that it was conditional on prayers for the king's life. The Gemara cites a baraita that one who gives charity for the sake of his children's life is a complete righteous person, but resolves that the distinction lies between Israel and Gentiles.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak questions whether the king's decree to provide offerings was praiseworthy, given that it was conditional on prayers for the king's life.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that one who gives charity for the sake of his children's life is a complete righteous person.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Israel and Gentiles.

items.text: Proof that the king acted with ulterior motive
items.text_en: Proof that the king acted with ulterior motive
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: the king's decree was motivated by fear of rebellion, as he built the Temple with alternating layers of stone and wood so it could be burned. The Gemara distinguishes his construction from King Solomon's, noting differences in placement and materials.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the proof that the king acted with ulterior motive is from the verse describing the Temple's construction with alternating layers of stone and wood, showing he built it to be burned if the Jews rebelled.
The Gemara objects: Did not King Solomon also build the Temple with alternating layers of stone and wood, as the verse states?

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing Solomon's construction from the king's: Solomon placed the wood above, sunk it into the building, and sealed it with plaster, whereas the king did none of these, revealing his ulterior motive.

items.text: Interpretation of 'shegal' as a dog
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'shegal' as a dog
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef or Rabbi Yitzchak cites a verse to prove the king's ulterior motive, interpreting 'shegal' as a dog. The Gemara raises difficulties from other verses where 'shegal' appears, resolving that the dog was trained to drink wine, and that in a prophetic context, 'shegal' refers to the Torah's preciousness to Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef or Rabbi Yitzchak cites the verse 'וַיֹּאמֶר לִי הַמֶּלֶךְ וְהַשֵּׁגַל יוֹשֶׁבֶת אֶצְלוֹ' to prove that the king's intent was malicious.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Limah in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Limah in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Limah in the name of Rav explains that 'שֵׁגַל' means a female dog, implying the king's debased behavior.
The Gemara objects from another verse where 'שֵׁגַל' appears alongside drinking wine, questioning how a dog could drink wine.
The Gemara resolves that the dog was trained to drink wine, so the objection is not difficult.
The Gemara objects from a prophetic verse where 'שֵׁגַל' appears in a positive context, questioning what good news the prophet would be conveying if it meant a dog.
The Gemara resolves that the prophet is telling Israel that because the Torah is as precious to them as a 'שֵׁגַל' is to the nations, they merited the gold of Ophir.
The Gemara offers an alternative: 'שֵׁגַל' actually means queen, and Rabbah bar Limah received this as a tradition.
The Gemara explains that the king called her 'שֵׁגַל' either because she was as beloved to him as a 'שֵׁגַל' or because he seated her in the place of a 'שֵׁגַל'.

items.text: Alternative proof from the fixed quantities
items.text_en: Alternative proof from the fixed quantities
items.desc_en: Another alternative proof is offered: the king initially gave without fixed measure but later specified amounts, indicating a change of heart. The Gemara counters that perhaps he was initially unaware of the costs, but concludes that the very specification shows a change.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative proof that the king changed his mind, citing the verse where fixed quantities of silver, wheat, wine, oil, and salt were specified.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the king was initially unaware of the costs, so the fixed quantities do not necessarily indicate a change of heart.
The Gemara resolves that the very specification of fixed quantities shows a change from the original practice, proving the king's change of heart.

items.text: The New Year for pilgrimage festivals and bal t'acher
items.text_en: The New Year for pilgrimage festivals and bal t'acher
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the first of Nisan is the New Year for pilgrimage festivals, meaning that one who vows to bring an offering must bring it by the first festival. Rav Chisda explains this relates to the prohibition of bal t'acher, and cites Rabbi Shimon's opinion that three festivals in order are required, with variations depending on when the vow was made.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the first of Nisan can be the New Year for pilgrimage festivals, since the first festival (Pesach) is on the fifteenth of Nisan.

Rav Chisda explains that the first of Nisan is the New Year for the festival that falls in that month, i.e., Pesach, serving as the starting point for counting the three pilgrimage festivals regarding the prohibition of bal t'acher.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation with Rabbi Shimon's baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation with Rabbi Shimon's baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the practical difference is for one who vows, regarding the prohibition of bal t'acher, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that three festivals in order are required, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai elaborates that the number of festivals varies depending on when the vow was made.

items.text: Baraita listing obligations subject to bal t'acher
items.text_en: Baraita listing obligations subject to bal t'acher
items.desc_en: A baraita enumerates various types of offerings and obligations that are subject to the prohibition of delaying, including blood-offerings, valuations, dedications, consecrations, sin-offerings, guilt-offerings, burnt-offerings, peace-offerings, charity, tithes, firstborn, ma'aser, and the paschal lamb.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists all offerings and obligations subject to the prohibition of delaying (בל תאחר), including blood-offerings, valuations, dedications, consecrations, sin-offerings, guilt-offerings, burnt-offerings, peace-offerings, charity, tithes, firstborn, ma'aser, and the paschal lamb.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: dispute on number of festivals for 'bal t'acher'
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: dispute on number of festivals for 'bal t'acher'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the Tanna Kamma's view that three festivals trigger 'bal t'acher', then records dissenting opinions: Rabbi Shimon requires three in order starting with Passover, Rabbi Meir says one festival suffices, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says two, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says Sukkot alone triggers it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the Tanna Kamma's ruling that for gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and corner produce, once three festivals have passed one transgresses 'bal t'acher' (the prohibition against delaying).
Rabbi Shimon adds that the three festivals must be in their proper order, with Passover first.
Rabbi Meir rules that even one festival passing is sufficient to transgress 'bal t'acher'.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that two festivals passing trigger the prohibition.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says that once Sukkot has passed, one transgresses 'bal t'acher'.

items.text: Gemara's question: Tanna Kamma's source
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Tanna Kamma's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna Kamma requires three festivals, and answers that the verse lists three festivals to teach the law of 'bal t'acher'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the rationale of the first tanna, noting that since the chapter already discussed the three pilgrimage Festivals, why does the verse need to list them again.
The Gemara concludes that the repetition of the three festivals comes to teach the halakha of 'bal t'acher' (you shall not delay).

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon argues that the verse need not mention Sukkot explicitly, since it is the last festival; its mention teaches that it is the final deadline.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon explains that the verse need not mention Sukkot explicitly since it is already the subject; its mention teaches that it is the final festival, making it the deadline.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's source and the Rabbis' objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's source and the Rabbis' objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir derives his view from the verse 'וּבָאתָ שָּׁמָּה ... וַהֲבֵאתֶם שָּׁמָּה', implying immediate obligation. The Rabbis counter that this verse teaches only a positive command, not 'bal t'acher'. Rabbi Meir retorts that once the Torah commands 'bring' and he fails to bring, he automatically violates 'bal t'acher'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Meir's rationale, and answers that he derives it from the verse 'וּבָאתָ שָּׁמָּה ... וַהֲבֵאתֶם שָׁמָּה' (and you shall come there... and you shall bring there).
The Rabbis counter that this verse teaches only a positive command (עשה), not the prohibition of 'bal t'acher'.
Rabbi Meir retorts that since the Merciful One commanded 'bring' and he did not bring, he automatically stands in violation of 'bal t'acher'.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's source and the Rabbis' alternative
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's source and the Rabbis' alternative
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives his two-festival requirement from the verse 'אֵלֶּה תַּעֲשׂוּ לַה׳ בְּמוֹעֲדֵיכֶם', interpreting 'מוֹעֲדֵיכֶם' as a minimum of two. The Rabbis reject this and apply the verse to Rabbi Yonah's teaching that all festivals are equated for atonement of Temple impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the rationale for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion that two festivals trigger the prohibition of בל תאחר.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives his opinion from the verse 'אֵלֶּה תַּעֲשׂוּ לַה׳ בְּמוֹעֲדֵיכֶם', interpreting the plural 'מוֹעֲדֵיכֶם' as a minimum of two festivals.
The Rabbis reject this derivation, explaining that the verse is needed for Rabbi Yonah's teaching.
Rabbi Yonah teaches that all festivals are equated with each other, as they all atone for impurity of the Temple and its sacred objects.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds that Sukkot alone triggers 'bal t'acher' because the verse mentions it to indicate that this festival causes the obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the rationale for Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon explains that the verse mentions Sukkot to indicate that this festival causes the obligation.

items.text: Derashah on the festival sequence: Shavuot's make-up days
items.text_en: Derashah on the festival sequence: Shavuot's make-up days
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov interpret the verse listing three festivals. It answers that they use it for Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya's teaching that Shavuot has make-up days all seven days, by analogy to Passover. The Gemara then addresses a potential analogy to Sukkot (eight days), but rejects it because the eighth day is a separate festival. It concludes that Sukkot is written to be equated with Passover for the law of make-up days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov interpret the verse listing the three festivals.
They use it for the teaching that Shavuot has make-up days all seven days, by analogy to Passover.
The Gemara objects that one could analogize Shavuot to Sukkot, which has eight days.
The objection is rejected because the eighth day of Sukkot is a separate festival.
The Gemara objects that the eighth day is separate only for certain matters, but for make-up days it is part of Sukkot.
A mishna is cited showing that the last day of the festival is a make-up day for the first day.
The Gemara resolves the objection by preferring the analogy to Passover, since grasping the smaller number is more certain.
The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote Sukkot in the verse if it is not used for the analogy.
It is written to equate Sukkot with Passover for the law of make-up days.

items.text: Inference from Passover to Sukkot
items.text_en: Inference from Passover to Sukkot
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that just as the festival of Matzot (Passover) requires an overnight stay (linah), so too the festival of Sukkot requires an overnight stay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Passover (חג המצות) to Sukkot (חג הסוכות) that both require an overnight stay (לינה).

items.text: Source for Passover's linah
items.text_en: Source for Passover's linah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: And there (regarding Passover), from where do we derive this? It is written: 'And you shall turn in the morning and go to your tents.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: And there (regarding Passover), from where do we derive this? It is written: 'And you shall turn in the morning and go to your tents.'

items.text: Source for tashlumin of Shavuot
items.text_en: Source for tashlumin of Shavuot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: And for the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, from where do they derive the supplementary offerings (tashlumin) for Shavuot? They derive it from what Rabba bar Shmuel taught: The Torah said 'Count days and sanctify the month, count days and sanctify Shavuot.' Just as the month has its count, so too Shavuot has its count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar derive the supplementary offerings (תשלומין) for Shavuot (עצרת)?

The Gemara answers: They derive it from what Rabba bar Shmuel taught, that the Torah said 'Count days and sanctify the month, count days and sanctify Shavuot' — just as the month has its count, so too Shavuot has its count.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding Shavuot's count
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding Shavuot's count
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: But say that Shavuot is only one day? Rava answers: Do we count only days for Shavuot, and not weeks? But the Master said: It is a mitzvah to count days and a mitzvah to count weeks. Moreover, it is written 'Festival of Weeks.'

sub.desc_en: An anonymous objection is raised: But say that Shavuot (עצרת) is only one day, so the analogy to Pesach (which has multiple days requiring לינה) fails.

Rava answers: Do we count only days for Shavuot, and not weeks? The Master said it is a mitzvah to count days and a mitzvah to count weeks; moreover, the Torah calls it 'Festival of Weeks,' indicating it is a multi-day festival requiring לינה.

items.text: Question about Passover's suitability for pilgrimage
items.text_en: Question about Passover's suitability for pilgrimage
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Is Passover subject to being brought on the pilgrimage festivals? Passover has a fixed time; if one brings it, he brings it, and if not, it is deferred!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Passover is subject to being brought on the pilgrimage festivals, noting that since Passover has a fixed time, if one brings it he brings it, and if not it is deferred.

items.text: Two answers: Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Two answers: Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: 'Passover' means when one takes it (the offering). Rav Sheshet says: What is 'Passover'? It refers to the peace-offerings of Passover. The Gemara then objects: If so, this is the same as regular peace-offerings! The answer is: It teaches about peace-offerings that come due to Passover, and it teaches about peace-offerings that come on their own accord.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that 'Passover' in the Mishnah means when one takes the Passover offering.
Rav Sheshet explains that 'Passover' refers to the peace-offerings brought on Passover.
The Gemara objects that if so, these peace-offerings are identical to regular peace-offerings.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches both peace-offerings that come due to Passover and those that come on their own, distinguishing them.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya: the comparison to Pesach
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya: the comparison to Pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches that the prohibition of bal t'acher applies to all offerings, not just those similar to Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches that the prohibition of בל תאחר (delaying fulfillment) applies to all offerings, not just those similar to Pesach.

items.text: Derivation of the prohibition from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the prohibition from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the prohibition of bal t'acher from the verse 'כי תדור נדר', extending it to nedavah, damim, arachin, charamin, hekdeshot, chatat, asham, olah, shelamim, tzedakah, ma'aser, bechor, leket, shikchah, and pe'ah. It also derives that the prohibition applies to the animal itself, not its substitute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the prohibition of bal t'acher) derived?
The baraita derives that nedavah (freewill offering) is included alongside neder (vow) through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of the word 'neder'.
The baraita expounds the verse to include damim, arachin, charamin, hekdeshot, chatat, asham, olah, and shelamim under the prohibition.
The baraita further includes tzedakah, ma'aser, bechor, leket, shikchah, and pe'ah, and teaches that the sin is on the person, not on the offering.

items.text: Clarification of 'חילופיו' – what substitute is excluded?
items.text_en: Clarification of 'חילופיו' – what substitute is excluded?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's exclusion of substitutes (חילופיו). It considers whether the substitute of an olah or shelamim is excluded, but notes that those are themselves offered. It then suggests the substitute of a chatat, but that goes to death. Finally, it concludes that the substitute of a todah is meant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what substitute (חילופיו) is excluded by the verse 'לֹא תְאַחֵר לְשַׁלְּמוֹ'.
The Gemara considers and rejects the possibility that the substitute of an olah or shelamim is excluded, because those substitutes themselves are offered.
The Gemara considers and rejects the substitute of a chatat, because that substitute goes to death and is not offered.
The Gemara concludes that the excluded substitute is that of a todah (thanksgiving offering), which cannot be offered if its substitute is mixed in.

items.text: Support from Rabbi Chiya's baraita about a todah mixed with its substitute
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Chiya's baraita about a todah mixed with its substitute
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita of Rabbi Chiya about a todah that was mixed with its substitute and one died, leaving the other without remedy. This illustrates the problem of a substitute that cannot be offered. The Gemara then questions why a verse is needed to exclude such a case, since it is inherently unfit for sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya's baraita is cited: a todah that was mixed with its substitute and one died leaves the other without remedy.
The Gemara analyzes the dilemma: if one tries to offer it with bread it might be the substitute (which does not require bread), and if without bread it might be the todah (which does require bread).
The Gemara objects: since this substitute is inherently unfit for sacrifice, why would a verse be needed to exclude it from the prohibition of בל תאחר (delaying fulfillment)?

items.text: Rav Sheshet's and Rava's alternative explanations
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's and Rava's alternative explanations
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the verse excludes substitutes of olah and shelamim in a case where the original animal was blemished after two festivals, was redeemed, and then a festival passed for the substitute. Rava explains for Rabbi Meir's view that the case is where the animal was blemished during the festival and redeemed, and then the festival passed. In both cases, one might think the substitute is subject to bal t'acher, but the verse teaches it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the verse excludes substitutes of olah and shelamim in a case where the original animal was blemished after two festivals, redeemed, and then a festival passed for the substitute.

Rava explains for Rabbi Meir's view that the case is where the animal was blemished during the festival and redeemed, and then the festival passed, so one might think the substitute is subject to בל תאחר (the prohibition of delaying), but the verse teaches it is not.

items.text: Derivation that a blemish does not disqualify a bechor from the previous year
items.text_en: Derivation that a blemish does not disqualify a bechor from the previous year
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the derivation that a bechor that passed its year is not disqualified, citing the opinion of Acherim who compare bechor to ma'aser. It then explains why this derivation is necessary: one might think that only bechor, which is not subject to the rite of waving, is not disqualified, but other sacrifices that are subject to waving might be disqualified; the verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation of the rule that a blemish does not disqualify a bechor from the previous year, noting that it already comes from Acherim.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Acherim derive from a verse that a bechor (בכור) is compared to ma'aser (מעשר), so just as ma'aser is not disqualified from one year to the next, so too a bechor is not disqualified.

The Gemara explains that the derivation is necessary: one might have thought that only a bechor (בכור), which is not subject to the rite of waving (הרצאה), is not disqualified, but other sacrifices (קדשים) that are subject to waving might be disqualified; the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Further question: 'וְאַכַּתִּי'
items.text_en: Further question: 'וְאַכַּתִּי'
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further difficulty with the previous derivation, setting up the next stage of the argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further difficulty with the previous derivation, setting up the next stage of the argument.

items.text: Ben Azzai's derivation about the one who delays his vow
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's derivation about the one who delays his vow
items.desc_en: Ben Azzai derives from the word 'אותו' that only the animal itself is subject to 'בל ירצה' (disqualification), but the one who delays his vow is not. Instead, the verse 'בך חטא' teaches that the sin is on him, not on his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Ben Azzai's teaching that the word 'אותו' limits the disqualification of 'בל ירצה' to the animal itself, not the one who delays his vow.
Ben Azzai derives that only the animal itself is subject to 'בל ירצה', not the one who delays his vow.
Ben Azzai concludes that the sin is on the man himself, not on his wife.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the need for the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the need for the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without the verse, one might have thought that the sin of delaying causes a man's wife to die, based on Rabbi Yochanan's statement that a man's wife dies only if he lacks money to pay. The verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one might have thought that the sin of delaying a vow causes a man's wife to die, based on Rabbi Yochanan's statement, but the verse teaches otherwise.
The Gemara concludes that the verse teaches otherwise — the sin of delaying does not cause the wife's death.

items.text: Baraita expounding the verses about vows
items.text_en: Baraita expounding the verses about vows
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds each phrase of the verse 'מוצא שפתיך תשמור ועשית' to derive various obligations: positive commandment, negative commandment, court enforcement, types of offerings, and charity.

sub.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'מוצא שפתיך' to include various obligations: a positive commandment, a negative commandment, court enforcement, vows, sacrifices, and charity.

items.text: Gemara questions the need for each derivation
items.text_en: Gemara questions the need for each derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why each derivation is necessary, suggesting that some are already derived from other verses. For the positive and negative commandments, they are derived from other sources. For court enforcement, it is derived from 'יקריב אותו' which teaches coercion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to derive the positive and negative commandments from 'מוצא שפתיך' and 'תשמור', since they are already derived from other verses.
The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to derive court enforcement from 'ועשית', since it is already derived from 'יקריב אותו' which teaches coercion.

items.text: Gemara explains the need for two cases: one who vowed but did not separate, and one who separated but did not offer
items.text_en: Gemara explains the need for two cases: one who vowed but did not separate, and one who separated but did not offer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: one who vowed but did not separate (the animal) and one who separated but did not offer it. Each case has a unique reason why one might think there is no violation, so both are taught.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah's two cases are: one who vowed but did not separate the animal, and one who separated but did not offer it.
The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: if only the first case were taught, one might think the second case is exempt because the animal is already in God's treasury.
The Gemara completes the explanation: if only the second case were taught, one might think the first case is exempt because mere speech is nothing, so both are necessary.

items.text: Gemara questions the case of 'said and did not separate'
items.text_en: Gemara questions the case of 'said and did not separate'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of 'said and did not separate' seems impossible because a vow (נדר) is defined as saying 'upon me' an offering, while a freewill offering (נדבה) is saying 'this is' an offering. Rava resolves that it refers to one who says 'upon me an offering on condition that I am not responsible for it.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of 'said and did not separate' is impossible because a vow (נדר) is defined as saying 'upon me' an offering, while a freewill offering (נדבה) is saying 'this is' an offering, and the latter carries no liability for loss.

Rava resolves that the case refers to one who says 'upon me an offering on condition that I am not responsible for it,' thereby combining the verbal commitment of a vow (נדר) with the limited liability of a freewill offering (נדבה).

items.text: Rava's statement about charity being immediate
items.text_en: Rava's statement about charity being immediate
items.desc_en: Rava states that charity must be given immediately because the poor are present. The Gemara questions if this is obvious, and explains that without the verse, one might think it is like offerings which have three festivals, but here the poor are always present.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that charity (צדקה) must be given immediately because the poor are present.
The Gemara objects that Rava's statement is obvious.
The Gemara explains that without the verse, one might think charity follows the rule of offerings requiring three festivals, but here the poor are always present, so it is immediate.

items.text: Rava's statement about passing one festival and the objection from the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Pappeyas
items.text_en: Rava's statement about passing one festival and the objection from the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Pappeyas
items.desc_en: Rava says that after one festival passes, one violates a positive commandment. The Gemara objects from a testimony about a peace-offering's offspring that was eaten on the holiday, implying it was delayed. Rav Zevid in the name of Rava resolves the objection.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that once one festival has passed without bringing the offering, one violates a positive commandment (עשה).

The Gemara raises an objection from the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Pappeyas, who ate the offspring of a peace-offering on the festival of Sukkot (חג), implying it was delayed beyond Passover.
The Gemara questions how the offspring could have been delayed until the festival of Shavuot (עצרת) without violating the positive commandment, since one festival (Passover) had already passed.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava begins to resolve the objection, explaining that the case is one where the offspring was born after Passover, so no festival had yet passed for it.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's reference to Shavuot
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's reference to Shavuot
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the phrase 'we will eat its young as peace-offerings on the festival' in the Mishnah refers to Shavuot. The Gemara notes that wherever the Mishnah mentions Pesach, it also mentions Atzeret (Shavuot).

items.text: Rava's statement and the objection regarding daily violation
items.text_en: Rava's statement and the objection regarding daily violation
items.desc_en: Rava states that once three festivals have passed, one violates bal t'acher every day. An objection is raised from a baraita that says violation occurs after a year without festivals or festivals without a year. Rav Kahana defends the objection, noting that the tanna focuses on establishing a prohibition, not additional prohibitions.

items.text: Analysis of the baraita: year without festivals
items.text_en: Analysis of the baraita: year without festivals
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the baraita's phrase 'a year without festivals' and questions how such a scenario is possible. It distinguishes between the opinion that festivals have a fixed order and the opinion that they do not.

items.text: Resolution for Rabbi and the Sages regarding a leap year
items.text_en: Resolution for Rabbi and the Sages regarding a leap year
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi, who counts a year as 365 days, a year without festivals can occur if the animal was consecrated after Passover and the year is intercalated. For the Sages, who count twelve months, a similar scenario is possible with a leap year.

items.text: Rav Shmaya's teaching and the dispute with Acherim
items.text_en: Rav Shmaya's teaching and the dispute with Acherim
items.desc_en: Rav Shmaya teaches that Shavuot can occur five, six, or seven days apart depending on the months. The Gemara identifies the disputant as Acherim, who holds that the difference between Shavuot and the next Shavuot is only four days, or five in a leap year.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry: Is an heir obligated in bal t'acher?
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry: Is an heir obligated in bal t'acher?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether an heir is subject to bal t'acher, considering the verse 'When you vow a vow' implies the vower, but the verse 'and you shall come there and bring there' might obligate the heir. The Gemara cites a baraita from Rabbi Chiya that excludes an heir, interpreting 'from with you' as excluding an heir, though the phrase also applies to gleanings.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry: Is a woman obligated in bal t'acher?
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry: Is a woman obligated in bal t'acher?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether a woman is obligated in bal t'acher, given she is not obligated in the pilgrimage but is obligated in rejoicing. Abaye responds that she is obligated because she is included in rejoicing, but clarifies that he was speaking according to Rabbi Zeira's reasoning, as Abaye himself holds that a woman's husband causes her rejoicing.

items.text: Dispute: When does the year begin for a firstborn animal?
items.text_en: Dispute: When does the year begin for a firstborn animal?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks from when the year is counted for a firstborn animal regarding bal t'acher. Abaye says from birth, Rav Acha bar Yaakov says from when it is fit for presentation. The Gemara concludes they do not disagree: one refers to a blemished animal (תם) and the other to an unblemished one.

items.text: Clarification of the previous Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Clarification of the previous Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the previous Mishnah's ruling about a blemished animal refers to one whose months have been completed, allowing it to be eaten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the previous Mishnah's ruling about a blemished animal refers to one whose months have been completed, allowing it to be eaten.

items.text: Baraita: Nisan as the new year for months
items.text_en: Baraita: Nisan as the new year for months
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the first of Nisan is the new year for months, intercalation, and the shekel offering, with some adding for house rentals.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the functions for which Nisan is the new year: months, intercalation, and shekel offerings, with an additional opinion adding house rentals.

items.text: Derivation of Nisan as the first month
items.text_en: Derivation of Nisan as the first month
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive that Nisan is the first month from the verse 'Guard the month of spring,' but faces objections that it could be Iyar or Adar. Rav Chisda then derives it from the verse about the seventh month, which is Tishrei, but again objections arise about Marcheshvan or Elul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that Nisan is the first month for counting months, citing the verse 'Guard the month of spring' and identifying Nisan as the month with spring.

An objection is raised that the verse could refer to Iyar or Adar, but the requirement of 'spring' eliminates Iyar and the requirement of 'most spring' (רוב אביב) is not written, so the objection is rejected.
Rav Chisda derives that Nisan is the first month from the verse about the seventh month (Tishrei), which has the harvest (אסיפה), showing that Tishrei is seventh, so Nisan is first.

An objection is raised that the verse could refer to Marcheshvan or Elul, but the requirement of 'harvest' eliminates Marcheshvan and the requirement of 'most harvest' (רוב אסיף) is not written, so the objection is rejected.

items.text: Amoraic proofs from biblical verses
items.text_en: Amoraic proofs from biblical verses
items.desc_en: Ravina, Rabbah bar Ulla, Rav Kahana, Rav Acha bar Yaakov, Rav Ashi, and an alternative source each bring a verse from the Prophets or Writings that explicitly names a month and its number, proving the order of months from Nisan.

sub.desc_en: Ravina opens by stating that the order of months from Nisan is not learned from the Torah but from the Prophets, citing the verse 'on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month of Shevat'.
Rabbah bar Ulla brings a supporting verse from Esther: 'in the tenth month, which is the month of Tevet'.
Rav Kahana cites a verse from Zechariah: 'on the fourth day of the ninth month, in Kislev'.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov cites a verse from Esther: 'in the third month, which is the month of Sivan'.
Rav Ashi cites a verse from Esther: 'the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar'.
An alternative source offers a verse from Esther: 'in the first month, which is the month of Nisan'.

items.text: Why earlier proofs were rejected
items.text_en: Why earlier proofs were rejected
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the earlier amoraim did not use the verse from the Torah: 'first' might mean first in context, not the calendar. The Tanna of our Mishnah deals with years, not months.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all the earlier amoraim did not cite the verse from the Torah (the one used by the Tanna of the Mishnah).
The Gemara answers that the verse might mean 'first' in the context of its own narrative, not as a calendar designation.
The Gemara adds that the Tanna of our Mishnah deals with years, not months, so the verse about months is irrelevant.

items.text: Intercalation: counted from Nisan?
items.text_en: Intercalation: counted from Nisan?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether intercalation is counted from Nisan, citing a baraita that intercalation is only done in Adar. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'intercalation' here means the cessation of intercalation, as per a Mishnah. The dispute about until when one can intercalate (until Purim or later) is discussed, and the Tanna of our Mishnah only deals with the beginning of the year, not the cessation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the counting for intercalation (עיבור) begins from Nisan.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that intercalation is only done in Adar, not from Nisan.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'intercalation' here refers to the cessation of intercalation (הפסקת עיבורין), citing a Mishnah about the dispute until when one can intercalate.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the first opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the first opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason of the first opinion (until Purim): because people start asking about Passover laws 30 days before, and delaying intercalation might lead to treating חמץ (leaven) lightly.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the second opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the second opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the second opinion (after Purim): people know that intercalation depends on calculation, and the sages' calculation was not completed until then.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna of our Mishnah only deals with the beginning of the year (התחלה), not the cessation of intercalation (הפסקה).

items.text: Derivation of the shekel offering from new produce
items.text_en: Derivation of the shekel offering from new produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the shekel offering for the new year must come from new produce, using a verbal analogy from 'year' in the context of Nisan. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that communal offerings on Nisan 1 should ideally be from new produce, but if from old, one fulfills the obligation. A baraita supports this, adding that an individual who donates may do so as long as they give it to the community.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is the law of the shekel offering (תרומת שקלים) derived?

Rabbi Yoshiya answers by citing a verse (Numbers 28:14) and deriving a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'שנה' (year) in the context of Nisan, teaching that the offering must come from new produce.
The Gemara objects: why not derive the verbal analogy from Tishrei (the year of years), where the verse says 'מראשית השנה' (from the beginning of the year)?

The Gemara rejects the objection: one derives a year that has months (Nisan, which is called 'ראשון לחדשי השנה') from another year that has months, not from a year that has no months (Tishrei, which is called 'ראש השנה' without reference to months).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that communal offerings brought on Nisan 1 should ideally (לכתחילה) be from new produce, but if brought from old produce, one fulfills the obligation (בדיעבד), though he has diminished the mitzvah.
A baraita supports Shmuel's ruling, adding that an individual who donates from his own property may do so, provided he gives the offerings to the community.

items.text: Concern about mixing old and new
items.text_en: Concern about mixing old and new
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to address a potential concern that one might mix old and new produce, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that one might mix old and new produce, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Clarification of the Tanna's ruling on rental
items.text_en: Clarification of the Tanna's ruling on rental
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna of our Mishnah teaches that if one brought the animal after the first of Nisan, he has fulfilled his obligation, implying that the year is not counted from day to day. This is contrasted with the baraita that counts twelve months from day to day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna's phrase 'יפה יפה' (very well) teaches that one should not hand over the animals to the community in a negligent manner.

The Gemara answers that the Tanna of our Mishnah, by stating 'אם הביא יצא' (if he brought it he has fulfilled his obligation), implies that the year is not counted from day to day, so the ruling is not absolute.

items.text: Baraita on rental and the principle of thirty days
items.text_en: Baraita on rental and the principle of thirty days
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited about renting a house for a year, counting twelve months from day to day, but if one says 'this year,' even if he moved in on the first of Adar, the year ends on the first of Nisan. The Gemara explains that even according to the opinion that a single day counts as a year, here one does not rent for less than thirty days. It then questions why the rental doesn't begin in Tishrei, and answers that people typically rent for the entire rainy season.

sub.desc_en: The Yesh Omrim opinion is introduced, citing a baraita about renting a house for a year: if one says 'this year,' even if he moved in on the first of Adar, the year ends on the first of Nisan.
The Gemara explains that even according to the opinion that a single day counts as a year, here one does not rent for less than thirty days.
The Gemara questions why the rental year does not begin in Tishrei.
The Gemara answers that people typically rent for the entire rainy season.
The Gemara adds that even the first Tanna of the baraita and our Tanna agree that in Nisan, rental contracts are also commonly found.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna for the New Year for animal tithes
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna for the New Year for animal tithes
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the author of the Mishnah's ruling that the first of Elul is the New Year for animal tithes as Rabbi Meir. It then notes that the ruling about festivals is from Rabbi Shimon, leading to a contradiction. Rav Yosef resolves this by saying the Mishnah is from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who adopts Rabbi Shimon's view for festivals and Rabbi Meir's view for animal tithes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that the first of Elul is the New Year for animal tithes and identifies its author as Rabbi Meir, supported by a baraita.
The Gemara notes that the ruling about festivals is attributed to Rabbi Shimon, creating a contradiction within the Mishnah between its beginning and end (Rabbi Shimon) and its middle (Rabbi Meir).
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by stating that the Mishnah is from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who adopts Rabbi Shimon's view for festivals and Rabbi Meir's view for animal tithes.

items.text: Resolving the count of four New Years
items.text_en: Resolving the count of four New Years
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah lists four New Years according to all opinions: for Rabbi Meir, exclude festivals; for Rabbi Shimon, exclude animal tithes. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the Mishnah means four months that contain several New Years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the Mishnah's list is a composite of different opinions, then there are five New Years, not four.
Rava answers: the Mishnah lists four New Years according to all opinions — for Rabbi Meir, exclude festivals; for Rabbi Shimon, exclude animal tithes.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative resolution: the Mishnah means four months that contain several New Years.

items.text: Objection from the Omer and Two Loaves
items.text_en: Objection from the Omer and Two Loaves
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited listing the sixteenth of Nisan and the sixth of Sivan as New Years, which would add to the count. Rav Papa answers that the Mishnah only counts items that take effect from the night before; the Omer and Two Loaves do not take effect from the night before. The Gemara objects that festivals also do not take effect from the night before, but are counted; the answer is that since one must bring the offering from the outset, it is considered obligatory.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the sixteenth of Nisan and the sixth of Sivan as New Years, objecting that this would add to the Mishnah's count of four New Years.
Rav Papa answers that the Mishnah only counts items that take effect from the night before; the Omer and Two Loaves do not take effect from the night before.
The Gemara objects that festivals also do not take effect from the night before, yet they are counted in the Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that since one must bring the festival offering from the outset, it is considered obligatory and thus counted.

items.text: Alternative resolution and the case of Jubilee
items.text_en: Alternative resolution and the case of Jubilee
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Jubilee years also do not take effect from the night before, yet are counted. It answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that Jubilee takes effect from Rosh Hashanah. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi offers another answer: the Mishnah counts only items not dependent on a human action; festivals depend on human action but the prohibition of delaying vows applies automatically.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Jubilee years also do not take effect from the night before, yet the Mishnah counts them as a Rosh Hashanah.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that Jubilee takes effect from Rosh Hashanah.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi offers an alternative answer: the Mishnah counts only items not dependent on human action; festivals depend on human action but the prohibition of delaying vows applies automatically.

items.text: Introduction of the dispute about Jubilee years
items.text_en: Introduction of the dispute about Jubilee years
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier mention of Jubilee years refers to the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, distinguishing it from the current discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the mention of Jubilee years in the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that the reference is to the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

items.text: Clarification of the four New Years and the dispute in Shevat
items.text_en: Clarification of the four New Years and the dispute in Shevat
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the four New Years correspond to four new moons, and the Gemara clarifies that the first of Shevat is a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, while three other dates are agreed upon.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the four New Years correspond to four new moons.
The Gemara clarifies that the first of Shevat is a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, while three other dates are agreed upon.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's derivations from the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's derivations from the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that both opinions derive from the same verse. Rabbi Meir holds that the New Year for animal tithes is Elul, based on the timing of lambing and grain harvest, while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold it is Tishrei, based on the singing of stalks.

sub.text: Mishnah citation (Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon)
sub.text_en: Mishnah citation (Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon state that the New Year for animal tithes is the first of Tishrei.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon derive their positions from the same verse (Psalms 65:14).
Rabbi Meir reasons that the sheep conceive in Adar and give birth in Av, making the New Year for animal tithes Elul.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon reason that the sheep conceive in Nisan and give birth in Elul, making the New Year for animal tithes Tishrei.

items.text: Objections and counter-explanations to the derivations
items.text_en: Objections and counter-explanations to the derivations
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises objections: the other opinion also has the verse's other clause. It explains that the 'singing' clause refers to early stalks in Nisan, and the 'grain' clause refers to late stalks from Adar. The Gemara then questions the consistency of each opinion's reading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the other opinion (Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon) also has the verse's clause 'יִתְרוֹעֲעוּ אַף יָשִׁירוּ' (they will shout, even sing), which seems to contradict their position.
The Gemara answers that the 'singing' clause refers to early stalks (אפלתא) that are already in Nisan, not to the main grain harvest.
The Gemara objects that the other opinion (Rabbi Meir) also has the verse's clause 'וַעֲמָקִים יַעַטְפוּ בָר' (and valleys are covered with grain), which seems to contradict his position.
The Gemara answers that the 'grain' clause refers to late stalks (חרפיית) that come from Adar, not to the main grain harvest.

The Gemara questions the consistency of each opinion's reading: for Rabbi Meir, the verse aligns with his position, but for Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, the verse should be read in the opposite order.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the dispute is about the analogy of tithes
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the dispute is about the analogy of tithes
items.desc_en: Rava explains that both agree on the verse's plain meaning, but they dispute the analogy between animal tithe and grain tithe: Rabbi Meir compares them regarding the timing of tithing (close to completion), while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon compare them regarding the New Year (Tishrei).

sub.desc_en: Rava rejects the previous analysis and establishes that both sides agree on the plain meaning of the verse, but they dispute the analogy between animal tithe and grain tithe.

sub.text: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Meir's position
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Meir's position
sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Meir compares animal tithe to grain tithe regarding the timing of tithing close to completion, leading to Elul as the New Year for animal tithe.

sub.text: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon compare animal tithe to grain tithe regarding the New Year being Tishrei, leading to Tishrei as the New Year for animal tithe.

items.text: The halakhic significance of the first of Tishrei for years
items.text_en: The halakhic significance of the first of Tishrei for years
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the first of Tishrei as the New Year for years is relevant for dating documents. The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction with the first of Nisan being the New Year for kings: Nisan is for Jewish kings, Tishrei for gentile kings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that the first of Tishrei is the New Year for years and asks what halakhic application this has.
Rav Pappa answers that the halakhic relevance is for dating documents, citing the Mishnah that early-dated promissory notes are invalid but late-dated ones are valid.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah also states the first of Nisan is the New Year for kings, and Rav Chisda already explained that this is for dating documents, creating an apparent contradiction.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing that Nisan is the New Year for Jewish kings, while Tishrei is the New Year for gentile kings.

items.text: Further explanations of Rav Chisda's statement and alternative interpretations
items.text_en: Further explanations of Rav Chisda's statement and alternative interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Chisda merely teaches a Mishnah, and explains he derives from verses. Alternatively, Rav Chisda follows Rabbi Zeira's teaching that the first of Tishrei is for the tekufah (season), according to Rabbi Eliezer. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is for judgment, as the verse indicates the year's judgment begins in Tishrei.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Chisda's statement merely teaches a Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that Rav Chisda derives his ruling from verses, not from the Mishnah.
Alternatively, Rav Chisda follows Rabbi Zeira's teaching that the first of Tishrei is for the tekufah (season), according to Rabbi Eliezer who holds the world was created in Tishrei.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the first of Tishrei is for judgment, as the verse indicates the year's judgment begins in Tishrei.

items.text: Heavenly court enters judgment only after earthly court sanctifies the month
items.text_en: Heavenly court enters judgment only after earthly court sanctifies the month
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'For it is a statute for Israel, a judgment for the God of Jacob' teaches that the heavenly court only enters judgment on Rosh Hashanah after the earthly court has sanctified the new month.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the new moon that is covered as Rosh Hashanah and cites the verse 'For it is a statute for Israel, a judgment for the God of Jacob'.
A baraita teaches that the heavenly court only enters judgment after the earthly court has sanctified the new month.

items.text: Israel enters judgment first, like a king before the public
items.text_en: Israel enters judgment first, like a king before the public
items.desc_en: A second baraita teaches that Israel enters judgment first, based on the same verse. Rav Chisda explains that a king enters judgment before the public, either because it is improper for the king to wait outside, or to prevent the intensification of divine wrath.

sub.desc_en: A second baraita teaches that Israel enters judgment first, based on the verse 'כי חק לישראל הוא' (For a statute for Israel it is).
Rav Chisda explains that a king enters judgment before the public, citing the verse 'משפט עבדו ומשפט עמו' (the judgment of his servant and the judgment of his people).
The Gemara offers a first reason: it is improper for the king to wait outside while the public enters first.
The Gemara offers a second reason: the king enters first to prevent the intensification of divine wrath.

items.text: Source for sabbatical years starting in Tishrei
items.text_en: Source for sabbatical years starting in Tishrei
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for sabbatical years beginning in Tishrei. It derives from a verbal analogy between 'year' in the sabbatical verse and 'year' in the verse about Tishrei, since both are years without months, unlike Nisan which has months.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that sabbatical years begin in Tishrei, and cites the verse about the seventh year.
The Gemara derives a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the word 'year' in the sabbatical verse and 'year' in the Tishrei verse.
The Gemara objects: Why not derive the verbal analogy from Nisan, which is also called the first of the months of the year?

The Gemara resolves: We derive a year without months (the sabbatical year, which has no named months) from another year without months (Tishrei, which is called 'the beginning of the year' without specifying months), and not from a year with months (Nisan, which is explicitly tied to months).

items.text: Jubilee year begins in Tishrei according to Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Jubilee year begins in Tishrei according to Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the jubilee year can start on the first of Tishrei when the verse says it begins on Yom Kippur (the tenth). It answers that this follows Rabbi Yishmael, who teaches that the year is sanctified from its beginning, and slaves are freed only on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the jubilee year can begin on the first of Tishrei when the verse explicitly states it begins on Yom Kippur, the tenth of Tishrei.

The Gemara answers that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who derives from the verse 'וְקִדַּשְׁתֶּם אֵת שְׁנַת הַחֲמִשִּׁים' that the jubilee year is sanctified from its beginning (Rosh Hashanah), not only from Yom Kippur.

Rabbi Yishmael explains the practical halacha: from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur, slaves are not freed to their homes nor subjugated to their masters, but eat, drink, and rejoice; only on Yom Kippur, after the shofar is blown, are slaves freed and fields returned.

items.text: Rabbis: You sanctify years, not months; and only the fiftieth year
items.text_en: Rabbis: You sanctify years, not months; and only the fiftieth year
items.desc_en: The Rabbis hold that you sanctify years (the jubilee year) but not months. A baraita further clarifies that the fiftieth year is sanctified, but not the fifty-first, even though we add from the profane to the holy.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis rule that you sanctify years (the jubilee year) but not months.
A baraita clarifies that the fiftieth year is sanctified, but not the fifty-first, even though we add from the profane to the holy.

items.text: Rejection of Rabbi Yehuda's view on the Jubilee year
items.text_en: Rejection of Rabbi Yehuda's view on the Jubilee year
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis count the fiftieth year as separate, excluding Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the fiftieth year counts for both the Jubilee and the next cycle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis count the fiftieth year as separate, excluding Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the fiftieth year counts for both the Jubilee and the next cycle.

items.text: Question: Source for adding from non-sacred to sacred
items.text_en: Question: Source for adding from non-sacred to sacred
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that we add from non-sacred time onto sacred time?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the principle of adding from the profane onto the sacred (תוספת מחול על הקודש)?

items.text: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael on the verse 'In plowing and in harvest you shall rest'
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael on the verse 'In plowing and in harvest you shall rest'
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse to refer to plowing in the year before the Sabbatical year that enters the Sabbatical, and harvesting of the Sabbatical year that goes out. Rabbi Yishmael interprets it to exclude the harvesting of the omer, which is a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse 'In plowing and in harvest you shall rest' to refer to plowing in the year before the Sabbatical year that enters the Sabbatical, and harvesting of the Sabbatical year that goes out.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the verse to exclude the harvesting of the omer, which is a mitzvah, by analogy to plowing which is a permitted act.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's source for adding from non-sacred to sacred
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's source for adding from non-sacred to sacred
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael derives the principle of adding from non-sacred to sacred from the verse 'And you shall afflict your souls on the ninth' regarding Yom Kippur, and extends it to all days of rest through a series of derivations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Yishmael derive the principle of adding from non-sacred to sacred (מוסיפין מחול על קודש)?

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael derives it from a baraita on the verse 'וְעִנִּיתֶם אֶת נַפְשׁוֹתֵיכֶם בְּתִשְׁעָה' (and you shall afflict your souls on the ninth), which teaches that one begins fasting while it is still day, showing addition from non-sacred to sacred.
The baraita extends the addition to the exit of Yom Kippur, deriving from 'מֵעֶרֶב עַד עֶרֶב' (from evening to evening) that one adds at both ends.

The baraita generalizes the principle to all days of rest (שבתות and ימים טובים) by deriving from 'תִּשְׁבְּתוּ' and 'שַׁבַּתְּכֶם', concluding that wherever there is a rest day, one adds from non-sacred to sacred.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's interpretation of the verse 'on the ninth'
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's interpretation of the verse 'on the ninth'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva does with the verse 'And you shall afflict your souls on the ninth', and answers that he uses it to teach that one who eats and drinks on the ninth is credited as if he fasted on the ninth and tenth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does Rabbi Akiva do with this verse 'וְעִנִּיתֶם אֶת נַפְשׁוֹתֵיכֶם בְּתִשְׁעָה' (and you shall afflict your souls on the ninth)?

The Gemara answers: Rabbi Akiva uses it for the teaching of Chiya bar Rav Midifti, who taught that the verse 'בְּתִשְׁעָה' (on the ninth) implies that one who eats and drinks on the ninth is credited by Scripture as if he fasted on the ninth and tenth.
Chiyya bar Rav Midifti teaches that the verse 'on the ninth' is interpreted to mean that one who eats and drinks on the ninth is credited by Scripture as if he fasted on both the ninth and the tenth.

items.text: Conclusion of previous sugya: fasting on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous sugya: fasting on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that one who fasts on both the ninth and tenth of Tishrei is credited as if he fasted on both days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that one who fasts on both the ninth and tenth of Tishrei is credited as if he fasted on both days.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on Jubilee requirements
