items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on Jubilee requirements
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the Jubilee year is valid even without releasing slaves, but requires shofar blasts; Rabbi Yosei holds it is valid even without shofar blasts, but requires releasing slaves. The Gemara explains the reasoning: the world can exist without releasing slaves but not without shofar blasts, and the mitzvah of releasing slaves is entrusted to the court, while shofar blasts are not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yehuda's position: the Jubilee year is valid even without releasing slaves or shofar blasts, but the word 'הִיא' excludes the possibility of validity without releasing slaves.
Rabbi Yosei states his position: the Jubilee year is valid even without releasing slaves or shofar blasts, but the word 'הִיא' excludes the possibility of validity without shofar blasts.
The Gemara asks: since both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei derive their positions from the same word 'הִיא', why does Rabbi Yosei prioritize shofar blasts over releasing slaves?
The Gemara answers: the world can exist without releasing slaves but cannot exist without shofar blasts, so shofar blasts are more essential.
The Gemara offers an alternative reason: releasing slaves is entrusted to the court (בית דין), while shofar blasts are not, so the court's failure to act does not invalidate the year.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and the meaning of 'deror'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and the meaning of 'deror'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda prioritizes shofar over releasing slaves, and explains that he interprets the verse 'proclaim liberty throughout the land' as referring to the shofar blast, based on the principle that a verse is interpreted by what precedes it, not by what precedes that. It then explains the meaning of 'deror' as freedom, citing Rabbi Yehuda's analogy of a dweller who trades freely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted that Rabbi Yosei has his stated reason, but what is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning for prioritizing shofar over releasing slaves?

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda interprets the verse 'וּקְרָאתֶם דְּרוֹר בָּאָרֶץ' (proclaim liberty throughout the land) as referring to the shofar blast, based on the principle that a verse is interpreted by what precedes it (לפניו) and not by what precedes that (לפני פניו).
The Gemara cites a baraita explaining that 'דְּרוֹר' (deror) means freedom, and Rabbi Yehuda illustrates it with the analogy of a dweller who trades freely throughout the land.

items.text: Sages' view: all three elements are essential
items.text_en: Sages' view: all three elements are essential
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the Sages disagree with both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei, holding that all three elements (shofar, releasing slaves, and letting fields lie fallow) are essential. They interpret the verse as applying to what precedes it, what precedes that, and what follows it. The Gemara clarifies that the word 'yovel' teaches that the Jubilee applies even outside the land, and 'ba'aretz' teaches that it applies outside the land only when it applies in the land.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan reports that the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei, holding that all three elements (shofar, releasing slaves, and letting fields lie fallow) are essential.

The Gemara explains that the Sages interpret the verse as applying to what precedes it, what precedes that, and what follows it, and clarifies that the word 'יובל' teaches that the Jubilee applies even outside the land, while 'בארץ' teaches that it applies outside the land only when it applies in the land.

items.text: Deriving the year for orlah from Tishrei
items.text_en: Deriving the year for orlah from Tishrei
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for counting the years of orlah from Tishrei, deriving it from a verbal analogy between 'year' in the context of orlah and 'year' in the context of Tishrei (the beginning of the year). It rejects a derivation from Nisan because Tishrei is a year without months (i.e., a solar year), while Nisan is a year with months (lunar).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the years of orlah (ערלה, the prohibition of fruit from a tree's first three years) are counted from Tishrei?

The Gemara answers: It is derived via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שנה' (year) in the orlah verses to the word 'שנה' in the verse about Tishrei, 'מראשית השנה' (from the beginning of the year).
The Gemara objects: Why not derive the verbal analogy from Nisan, about which it is written 'ראשון הוא לכם לחדשי השנה' (it is the first of the months of the year)?

The Gemara resolves: We derive a year that has no months (Tishrei, a solar year) from a year that has no months, and we do not derive a year that has no months from a year that has months (Nisan, a lunar year).

items.text: Baraita: planting 30 days before Rosh Hashanah counts as a year
items.text_en: Baraita: planting 30 days before Rosh Hashanah counts as a year
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who plants, bends, or grafts a tree 30 days before Rosh Hashanah of the Sabbatical year has that count as a full year, allowing the tree to be kept during the Sabbatical year; less than 30 days does not count, and the tree must be removed.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that planting, bending, or grafting thirty days before Rosh Hashanah of the Sabbatical year counts as a full year, allowing the plant to be kept in the seventh year; less than thirty days does not count and is forbidden.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the produce of a tree planted for orlah or revai is forbidden until the 15th of Shevat, which is the New Year for trees.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the produce of a tree planted for orlah or revai is forbidden until the 15th of Shevat, which is the New Year for trees.

items.text: Biblical derivation for the date
items.text_en: Biblical derivation for the date
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yannai, derives from the verse 'in the fourth year and in the fifth year' that sometimes the fourth year is still orlah and sometimes the fifth year is still revai, establishing the 15th of Shevat as the cutoff.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the date of the 15th of Shevat) derived?

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yannai, answers by citing the verse 'in the fourth year and in the fifth year' (Leviticus 19:24-25).

Rabbi Yannai explains the derivation: sometimes the fourth year is still forbidden as ערלה (orlah) and sometimes the fifth year is still forbidden as רבעי (revai), establishing the 15th of Shevat as the cutoff.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Meir's view
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Meir's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that this position contradicts Rabbi Meir, who holds that a single day in the year counts as a year, as seen in his ruling about a bull being 24 months and one day old. Rabbi Elazar's dissenting view is also cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the position (that the new year for trees is the fifteenth of Shevat) contradicts Rabbi Meir, who holds that a single day in the year counts as a year, as seen in his ruling about a bull being 24 months and one day old.
The baraita cites Rabbi Elazar's dissenting view that the bull is 24 months and 30 days, and elaborates Rabbi Meir's general rule about the ages of sacrificial animals.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Meir's principle applies only at year's end
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Meir's principle applies only at year's end
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Meir, his principle that one day counts as a year applies only at the end of the year, not at the beginning, so the 15th of Shevat as the start of the year is consistent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Meir, his principle of one day counting as a year applies only at the end of the year, not at the beginning.

items.text: Rava's a fortiori argument
items.text_en: Rava's a fortiori argument
items.desc_en: Rava supports this with a kal vachomer from niddah: if the end of the day counts for the beginning, then certainly one day at the end of the year counts for the entire year, implying the 15th of Shevat is the start.

sub.desc_en: Rava supports this with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from niddah: if the end of the day counts for the beginning of niddah, then one day at the end of the year should count for the beginning of the year.

items.text: Gemara's inference from Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Meir holds that thirty days count as a year, then a single day should also count at the beginning of the year, based on the principle of kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if thirty days count as a year, should not a single day at the beginning of the year also count, by קל וחומר (a fortiori reasoning)?

items.text: Rejection of Rabbi Elazar's position and Rav Nachman's statement
items.text_en: Rejection of Rabbi Elazar's position and Rav Nachman's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the possibility that the mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar, because he requires thirty days before Rosh Hashanah for planting, plus another thirty for the year to count, totaling sixty days. Rav Nachman bar Abba cites a tradition that each opinion requires its own period plus thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar, he requires thirty days for planting plus another thirty for the year to count, totaling sixty days.

The Gemara cites a baraita listing the opinions of Rabbi Elazar (thirty days), Rabbi Yehuda (three days), and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon (two weeks) regarding the minimum time for planting before the Sabbatical year.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Abba citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Abba citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Abba in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha states that each opinion requires its own period plus an additional thirty days for the year to count.
The Gemara offers an alternative: if the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, it would require three plus thirty days.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Meir's thirty days are for absorption
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Meir's thirty days are for absorption
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the mishnah indeed follows Rabbi Meir, and the thirty days he requires are for the tree to absorb the planting, not for the year to count. The Gemara then questions why thirty-one days are not needed, and answers that the thirtieth day counts for both the absorption and the year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, and his thirty days are for the tree to absorb the planting (קליטה), not for the year to count.
The Gemara questions why thirty-one days are not needed, since the thirtieth day should count for the year separately.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Meir holds the thirtieth day counts for both the absorption and the year.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement: both derive from the same verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement: both derive from the same verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that both Rabbi Meir and the Sages derive their positions from the same verse about Noah's flood. Rabbi Meir learns that one day in the year counts as a year, while the Sages interpret the verse differently, arguing that 'one' refers to the beginning of the six-hundredth year.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by stating that Rabbi Meir and the Sages both derive their positions from the same verse about Noah's flood, and explains Rabbi Meir's interpretation that one day in the year counts as a year.
Rabbi Yochanan explains the Sages' alternative interpretation of the same verse, arguing that 'one' refers to the beginning of the six-hundredth year, not a full year.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's derivation from the same verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's derivation from the same verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Elazar's reasoning: from the phrase 'on the first day of the month' he learns that one day in the month counts as a month, and therefore thirty days in the year count as a year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Elazar's reasoning for his position.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse 'בָּרִאשׁוֹן בְּאֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ' (on the first day of the month) that one day in the month counts as a month, and therefore thirty days in the year count as a year.

items.text: Inference that both hold the world was created in Nisan
items.text_en: Inference that both hold the world was created in Nisan
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous discussion that both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar hold that the world was created in Nisan, since they use the flood narrative which began in the second month (Marcheshvan).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar hold that the world was created in Nisan, based on their use of the flood narrative which began in the second month (Marcheshvan).

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that the world was created in Tishrei
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that the world was created in Tishrei
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer states that the world was created in Tishrei, and lists several events that occurred in Tishrei, including the birth of the patriarchs, the conception of Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah, and Joseph's release from prison.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer states that the world was created in Tishrei, and lists several events that occurred in Tishrei, including the birth of the patriarchs, the conception of Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah, and Joseph's release from prison.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Rosh Hashanah the servitude of our ancestors in Egypt ceased, in Nisan they were redeemed, and in Tishrei they will be redeemed in the future.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Rosh Hashanah the servitude of our ancestors in Egypt ceased, in Nisan they were redeemed, and in Tishrei they will be redeemed in the future.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's expanded list
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's expanded list
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua adds that the world was created in Nisan, the patriarchs were born and died in Nisan, Isaac was born on Passover, and Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah were remembered on Rosh Hashanah, among other events.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that the world was created in Nisan, the patriarchs were born and died in Nisan, Isaac was born on Passover, Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah were remembered on Rosh Hashanah, Joseph left prison on Rosh Hashanah, servitude ceased in Nisan, and redemption will be in Nisan.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate creation month
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate creation month
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues from the verse 'Let the earth sprout vegetation' that Tishrei is the month when the earth produces grass and trees are full of fruit, indicating creation in Tishrei. Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the verse 'And the earth brought forth vegetation' shows Nisan is the month of full grass and fruit-bearing trees, indicating creation in Nisan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues from the verse 'Let the earth sprout vegetation' that Tishrei is the month of creation, because it is when the earth produces grass and trees are full of fruit.
Rabbi Yehoshua counters that Nisan is the month of creation, citing the verse 'And the earth brought forth vegetation' and noting that in Nisan the earth is full of grass and trees produce fruit.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the verses
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Eliezer, the verse says 'tree making fruit' (עֵץ עוֹשֶׂה פְּרִי), which implies fruit already present, but it is explained as a blessing for future generations. For Rabbi Yehoshua, the verse says 'tree of fruit' (עֵץ פְּרִי), which is explained by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that all creation was created fully grown, according to their will.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rabbi Eliezer: but the verse says 'tree making fruit' (עֵץ עוֹשֶׂה פְּרִי), implying fruit already present, contradicting your proof from the verse 'tree of fruit' (עֵץ פְּרִי).
The Gemara answers: that verse is written as a blessing for future generations, not describing the original creation.
The Gemara asks Rabbi Yehoshua: but the verse says 'tree of fruit' (עֵץ פְּרִי), not 'tree making fruit' (עֵץ עוֹשֶׂה פְּרִי), which seems to support Rabbi Eliezer.

The Gemara answers: that verse is explained by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who taught that all creation was created fully grown (לְקוֹמָתָן), according to their will (לְצִבְיוֹנָן), as derived from the verse 'וַיְכֻלּוּ...צְבָאָם' read as 'צִבְיוֹנָם'.

items.text: Debate on the birth month of the patriarchs
items.text_en: Debate on the birth month of the patriarchs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the patriarchs were born in Tishrei, citing the verse 'in the month of Eitanim' (the strong ones). Rabbi Yehoshua argues they were born in Nisan, citing 'in the month of Ziv' (the radiant ones). The Gemara resolves that 'Eitanim' refers to strength in mitzvot, and 'Ziv' refers to the radiance of trees, as explained by Rav Yehuda regarding the blessing on blossoming trees in Nisan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the patriarchs were born in Tishrei, citing the verse 'in the month of Eitanim' (the strong ones).
The Gemara supports Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation by citing verses where 'Eitan' means strength, and connects the verses to the merit of the patriarchs and matriarchs.
Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the patriarchs were born in Nisan, citing the verse 'in the month of Ziv' (the radiant ones).
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehoshua must address the verse 'in the month of Eitanim', and resolves that it refers to strength in mitzvot.
The Gemara resolves that 'Ziv' refers to the radiance of trees, citing Rav Yehuda's teaching about the blessing on blossoming trees in Nisan.

items.text: Death of the patriarchs in the same month as birth
items.text_en: Death of the patriarchs in the same month as birth
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that according to each opinion, the patriarchs died in the same month they were born, as derived from Moses' statement 'I am today one hundred and twenty years old', teaching that God completes the years of the righteous from day to day and month to month.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that according to each opinion, the patriarchs died in the same month they were born, citing the verse 'בן מאה ועשרים שנה אנכי היום' (I am one hundred and twenty years old today) to show that God fills the years of the righteous precisely.

items.text: Isaac's birth on Passover
items.text_en: Isaac's birth on Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that Isaac was born on Passover from the verse 'At the appointed time I will return to you'. It calculates that the angel spoke to Abraham at Sukkot, and Isaac was born the following Nisan. The difficulty of a six-month pregnancy is resolved by the Tanna that the year was intercalated, and Mar Zutra explains that for a seven-month pregnancy, birth can occur at the end of truncated months, as derived from the verse 'at the revolutions of the days'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that Isaac was born on Passover?

The Gemara answers from the verse 'At the appointed time I will return to you', and deduces that the angel spoke to Abraham at Sukkot (the festival of Tishrei) and Isaac was born the following Nisan (Passover).
The Gemara objects: But a six-month pregnancy is not viable; even if the year was intercalated, subtracting days of impurity shortens the term.

Mar Zutra resolves: Even according to the opinion that a full-term pregnancy is nine months, a seven-month pregnancy can occur at the end of truncated months, as derived from the verse 'at the revolutions of the days' (תקופות הימים).

items.text: Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah remembered on Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah remembered on Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives that Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah were remembered on Rosh Hashanah through a verbal analogy of 'remembrance' (זְכִירָה) and 'visitation' (פְּקִידָה) from the verses about Rachel, Hannah, and Sarah, linking to Rosh Hashanah as a day of remembrance.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah were remembered (visited) on Rosh Hashanah.
The gemara asks: from where do we derive this?
Rabbi Elazar derives the connection through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'remembrance' (זְכִירָה) and 'visitation' (פְּקִידָה) linking Rachel, Hannah, and Sarah to Rosh Hashanah.
The gemara cites the verses: 'for the Lord had visited Hannah' and 'the Lord visited Sarah' to complete the verbal analogy of visitation.

items.text: Joseph's release from prison on Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Joseph's release from prison on Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that Joseph left prison on Rosh Hashanah from the verse 'Blow the shofar at the new moon, at the covered day for our festival', which is interpreted as Rosh Hashanah, and the following verse 'For it is a statute for Israel' connects to Joseph's release.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that Joseph left prison on Rosh Hashanah, and cites the verse 'תקעו בחדש שופר בכסה ליום חגנו' (blow the shofar at the new moon, at the covering for our festival day), which is interpreted as referring to Rosh Hashanah.

The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'Blow the shofar at the new moon, at the covered day for our festival, for it is a statute for Israel,' which is interpreted as referring to Rosh Hashanah and Joseph's release.

items.text: Opening citation
items.text_en: Opening citation
items.desc_en: The daf begins by citing a verse from Psalms about testimony in Joseph.

sub.desc_en: The daf opens by citing a verse from Psalms (עֵדוּת בִּיהוֹסֵף שָׂמוֹ בְּצֵאתוֹ וְגוֹ׳) as a starting point for the discussion.

items.text: First opinion: redemption in Nisan, future redemption in Tishrei
items.text_en: First opinion: redemption in Nisan, future redemption in Tishrei
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that on Rosh Hashanah the servitude of the forefathers in Egypt ceased, citing verses. It then asserts that in Nisan they were redeemed, and in Tishrei they will be redeemed in the future, using a verbal analogy on 'shofar'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that on Rosh Hashanah the servitude of the forefathers in Egypt ceased, citing a verse from Psalms to support the verbal analogy.
The Gemara concludes that in Nisan they were redeemed, and in Tishrei they will be redeemed in the future, using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'שופר' (shofar) from Psalms and Isaiah.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion: both redemptions in Nisan
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion: both redemptions in Nisan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua argues that both the past and future redemption occur in Nisan, deriving this from the phrase 'leil shimmurim' (a night of protection). The Gemara then offers an alternative interpretation of that phrase.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that both the past and future redemption occurred in Nisan, deriving this from the phrase 'לֵיל שִׁמּוּרִים' (a night of protection), which he interprets as a night protected from harmful forces since the six days of creation.

The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation of 'לֵיל שִׁמּוּרִים' (a night of protection), explaining it as a night protected from harmful forces (מזיקין), rather than from the six days of creation.

items.text: Support from the flood narrative
items.text_en: Support from the flood narrative
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer follow their respective positions regarding the flood. Rabbi Yehoshua holds the flood began on the 17th of Iyar, while Rabbi Eliezer holds it was on the 17th of Marcheshvan, each providing astronomical reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer follow their respective positions, citing a supporting baraita.

The baraita cites the verse about the flood's start and presents Rabbi Yehoshua's position that it was the 17th of Iyar, when the constellation כימה (Pleiades) sets by day and springs diminish, but due to the generation's sins God reversed nature and brought the flood.
Rabbi Eliezer states that the flood began on the 17th of Marcheshvan, when the constellation כימה (Pleiades) rises by day and springs are naturally strong.

items.text: Explanation of the change in creation
items.text_en: Explanation of the change in creation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that because the generation of the Flood changed their behavior, God changed the order of creation, causing the constellation Kimah to rise during the day and bringing the Flood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that because the generation of the Flood changed their behavior, God changed the order of creation, causing the constellation Kimah to rise during the day and bringing the Flood.

items.text: Question on the word 'second'
items.text_en: Question on the word 'second'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Yehoshua, the word 'second' in the verse refers to the second year of the Flood, but according to Rabbi Eliezer, what does 'second' mean? It answers: second to judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Yehoshua, the word 'second' in the verse fits, but according to Rabbi Eliezer, what does 'second' mean?
The Gemara answers: 'Second' means second to judgment, i.e., the Flood was a judgment following the earlier judgment of the generation of Enosh.

items.text: Question on the word 'changed' and Rav Chisda's explanation
items.text_en: Question on the word 'changed' and Rav Chisda's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Yehoshua, the word 'changed' refers to the change in the order of creation, but according to Rabbi Eliezer, what does 'changed' mean? It answers with Rav Chisda's statement: they sinned with hot water and were punished with hot water, as derived from the verse 'and the waters subsided' and the verse 'and the king's anger subsided'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Yehoshua, the word 'changed' fits the narrative, but according to Rabbi Eliezer, what does 'changed' mean?
Rav Chisda explains: they sinned with hot water and were punished with hot water, as derived from the verse 'and the waters subsided' and the verse 'and the king's anger subsided'.

items.text: Dispute between Jewish and gentile sages on counting the Flood
items.text_en: Dispute between Jewish and gentile sages on counting the Flood
items.desc_en: The Tanna taught: The Jewish sages count the years of the Flood according to Rabbi Eliezer, and the tekufah (seasons) according to Rabbi Yehoshua. The gentile sages count even the Flood according to Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches a baraita: Jewish sages count the years of the Flood according to Rabbi Eliezer and the seasons according to Rabbi Yehoshua, while gentile sages count even the Flood according to Rabbi Yehoshua.

items.text: Discussion on counting for vegetables, tithes, and vows
items.text_en: Discussion on counting for vegetables, tithes, and vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the counting for vegetables, tithes, and vows. It questions why the Tanna lists 'vegetables' separately from 'tithes', and explains that the Tanna is referring to rabbinic tithes (ma'aser yerakot) while the Torah tithes are different. It further explains the two types of vegetables that determine when tithing begins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's list of items counted from Rosh Hashanah and asks what 'vegetables' refers to, answering that it means the tithe of vegetables (מעשר ירק).
The Gemara objects: 'Vegetables' is already included in 'tithes' (מעשרות); it explains that the Tanna lists rabbinic tithes (מעשר ירק) alongside Torah tithes.

The Gemara asks why the Tanna lists rabbinic tithes before Torah tithes; it answers that the rabbinic tithe is more beloved to the Tanna, so it is placed first, and our Tanna lists only rabbinic tithes, implying Torah tithes all the more so.

The Gemara asks why the Tanna uses the plural 'vegetables' (ירקות) rather than 'tithe' (מעשר); it answers that there are two types of vegetables — those that are bound and those that are not — each with its own rule for when tithing begins, as taught in a Mishnah.

items.text: Beginning of a baraita on vegetable tithing before Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraita on vegetable tithing before Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a baraita about one who gathered vegetables on the eve of Rosh Hashanah before sunset, and then gathered again after sunset, setting up a case for the laws of tithing across the new year.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a case of one who gathered vegetables on the eve of Rosh Hashanah before sunset and then gathered again after sunset, setting up the tithing question across the new year.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Tithing from old to new produce
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Tithing from old to new produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that once the sun sets on Rosh Hashanah, one may not tithe from new produce for old or vice versa. It also specifies the tithes due in the second and third years of the Sabbatical cycle.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that after sunset on Rosh Hashanah, one may not tithe from new produce for old or vice versa, and specifies which tithes apply in the second and third years of the Sabbatical cycle.

items.text: Gemara's derivation: First tithe is never suspended
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation: First tithe is never suspended
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from the verse "כִּי תְכַלֶּה לַעְשֵׂר" that the third year has only one tithe (ma'aser ani), but first tithe is never suspended. The Gemara supports this by comparing first tithe to an inheritance, which has no cessation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where in the Torah are these rules derived?

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites the verse 'כי תכלה לעשר' (When you have finished tithing) to prove that the third year has only one tithe — מעשר ראשון (first tithe) and מעשר עני (poor man's tithe), while מעשר שני (second tithe) is suspended.

The Gemara objects: Perhaps even מעשר ראשון (first tithe) should be suspended? It then answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the verse 'ואל הלוים תדבר' (Speak to the Levites), comparing מעשר ראשון to an inheritance (נחלה) which has no cessation.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing the verse 'וְאֶל הַלְוִיִּם תְּדַבֵּר', which compares first tithe to an inheritance (נחלה) that has no cessation, so first tithe is never suspended.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov on first tithe
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov on first tithe
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's view that the verse "וּבָא הַלֵּוִי" teaches that first tithe is always given. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov argues that no additional verse is needed, as the comparison to inheritance already proves first tithe has no cessation.

sub.desc_en: A supporting baraita (תניא אידך) cites the same verse and derives the same rule, adding that Rabbi Yehuda learns from 'ובא הלוי' (the Levite shall come) that as long as the Levite comes, you must give him the tithe, thus מעשר ראשון is never suspended.

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the derivation is unnecessary, as the same verbal analogy from 'ואל הלוים תדבר' (Speak to the Levites) already teaches that מעשר ראשון is like an inheritance with no cessation.

items.text: Vows: Defining a year for a vow of prohibition
items.text_en: Vows: Defining a year for a vow of prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a vow of prohibition for a year: if one says "for this year," even if he vowed on the 29th of Elul, the year ends on the first of Tishrei. The Gemara explains that this follows common language, not the month of Nisan.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches: One who vows to forbid benefit from a friend for a year counts twelve months from day to day; but if he says 'this year,' even if he only vowed on the 29th of Elul, once the first of Tishrei arrives, the year is considered complete.

The Gemara resolves: Even according to the opinion that a single day in the year is not considered a year, here the vow is accepted for self-affliction (לצעוריה נפשיה קביל עליה), and he has indeed been afflicted.
The Gemara objects: Why not say the year starts from Nisan? It answers: In vows, we follow common human language (הלך אחר לשון בני אדם), which considers Tishrei as the new year.

items.text: Produce stages: When is produce subject to the Sabbatical year?
items.text_en: Produce stages: When is produce subject to the Sabbatical year?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that fenugreek is subject once it sprouts, and grain and olives once they reach a third of their growth. Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yose HaGelili derives from the verse that produce which reached a third before Rosh Hashanah in the seventh year is treated with Sabbatical-year sanctity in the eighth year.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that fenugreek is subject to tithes from the time it sprouts, and grain and olives from the time they reach a third of their growth.
The Gemara clarifies that 'when it sprouts' means when it sprouts for seeds (i.e., when the seeds are visible).
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for the rule about grain and olives reaching a third of their growth.

sub.text: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yose HaGelili
sub.text_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yose HaGelili
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yose HaGelili derives from the verse 'מקץ שבע שנים' (at the end of seven years) that produce which reached a third of its growth before Rosh Hashanah in the seventh year is treated with Sabbatical-year sanctity in the eighth year.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Asi
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Asi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira begins to question Rav Asi about the derivation, setting up the next stage of the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira addresses Rabbi Asi, initiating a new line of questioning or discussion.

items.text: Gemara's question about the harvest festival
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the harvest festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'the harvest festival at the end of the year' implies that grain that has not yet grown one-third by Rosh Hashanah is not subject to the Sabbatical year. It argues that the term 'Asif' refers to harvest, and the Sages know that any grain harvested by the festival had already reached one-third before Rosh Hashanah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether grain that has not grown at all by Rosh Hashanah is exempt from the Sabbatical year, based on the verse 'the harvest festival at the end of the year'.
The Gemara rejects the question, arguing that the term 'Asif' means harvest, and the Sages know that any grain harvested by the festival had already reached one-third before Rosh Hashanah.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya questions the Sages' knowledge of one-third
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya questions the Sages' knowledge of one-third
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the Sages can distinguish between one-third and less than one-third. Rabbi Zeira rebukes him, saying that all measures of the Sages are precise, giving examples of the mikveh, egg-sized food, and a three-by-three handbreadth cloth.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the Sages can distinguish between one-third and less than one-third.
Rabbi Zeira rebukes Rabbi Yirmeya for stepping outside the halacha (הלכה), asserting that all measures of the Sages are precise.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's examples of precise measures
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's examples of precise measures
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira provides three examples of precise measures: a mikveh (מקוה) of forty se'ah, an egg-sized portion for food impurity, and a three-by-three handbreadth cloth for midras (מדרס) impurity.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya retracts and cites a question about the Omer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya retracts and cites a question about the Omer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya retracts his objection, citing a question from colleagues to Rav Kahana: from where did the Israelites bring the Omer when they entered the land? Rav Kahana answers: from grain that had not yet reached one-third while in gentile hands.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya retracts his previous objection, declaring it invalid.
The colleagues ask Rav Kahana: from where did the Israelites bring the Omer (עומר) when they entered the land, given that grain in gentile hands is excluded by the verse 'קְצִירְכֶם' (your harvest)?
The Gemara objects: how do we know they actually offered the Omer at all?
The Gemara rejects the objection, citing the verse 'וַיֹּאכְלוּ מֵעֲבוּר הָאָרֶץ' (they ate from the produce of the land) which implies they first offered the Omer and then ate.
The colleagues repeat their question: from where did they bring the Omer?
Rav Kahana answers: they brought the Omer from grain that had not yet reached one-third (שליש) while in gentile hands.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution about the Omer
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution about the Omer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the grain had not yet reached one-third, and the Sages did not know? It answers that they did know. Further objections about the possibility of no growth at all are resolved by the verse that the people crossed the Jordan on the tenth of the month, and the land is called 'a desirable land' which grows quickly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the grain had entered (reached one-third growth) but the Sages did not know it.
The Gemara answers: rather, they did know — here too they knew.
The Gemara objects further: perhaps the grain had not entered at all, but where it entered a quarter, between one-third and less than one-third they do not know.

The Gemara resolves: it cannot enter your mind, for it is written 'and the people went up from the Jordan on the tenth of the month' — and if it had not entered at all, could it have filled in five days? Rather, the land is called 'a desirable land' (אֶרֶץ צְבִי) which grows quickly, and here too it is written 'a desirable land'.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's objection and Rabbi Zeira's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's objection and Rabbi Zeira's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina objects that the term 'Asif' cannot mean harvest, as the verse 'when you gather from your threshing floor and your winepress' refers to the waste of the threshing floor and winepress. Rabbi Zeira laments that Rabbi Chanina has thrown an axe into their reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina objects that the term 'אסיף' (Asif) cannot mean harvest, because the verse 'באספך מגרנך ומיקבך' (when you gather from your threshing floor and your winepress) refers to the waste of the threshing floor and winepress, not the harvest.
Rabbi Zeira laments that Rabbi Chanina has thrown an axe into their reasoning, indicating that the objection is devastating.

items.text: Alternative source from a baraita
items.text_en: Alternative source from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks an alternative source, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef says: 'And it shall produce grain for the three years.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive the rule, and cites Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef's teaching from the verse 'and it shall produce grain for three years'.

items.text: Derashah on the verse for the third year tithe
items.text_en: Derashah on the verse for the third year tithe
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the verse 'to the third' (lishlosh) as 'to a third' (lishlish), indicating that produce is tithed based on reaching one-third of its growth. It then cites another verse to support this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the verse 'to the third' (lishlosh) as 'to a third' (lishlish), indicating that produce is tithed based on reaching one-third of its growth.
The Gemara objects that the verse is needed for its plain meaning, then cites another verse to support the reinterpretation.

items.text: Mishnah on rice and similar produce
items.text_en: Mishnah on rice and similar produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that rice, millet, poppy, and sesame that rooted before Rosh Hashanah are tithed for the previous year and permitted in the Sabbatical year; otherwise, they are forbidden in the Sabbatical year and tithed for the next year.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that rice, millet, poppy, and sesame that rooted before Rosh Hashanah are tithed for the previous year and permitted in the Sabbatical year; otherwise, they are forbidden in the Sabbatical year and tithed for the next year.

items.text: Rabba's initial and revised classification
items.text_en: Rabba's initial and revised classification
items.desc_en: Rabba first states the general rule: trees follow budding, grain and olives follow one-third growth, vegetables follow harvesting. He then questions which category the Sages assigned these items to. He concludes that because they grow in separate clusters, the Sages follow rooting.

sub.desc_en: Rabba states the general rule: trees follow budding, grain and olives follow one-third growth, vegetables follow harvesting.
Rabba questions which category the Sages assigned these items (rice, millet, etc.) to.
Rabba revises his position: because these items grow in separate clusters, the Sages follow rooting.

items.text: Abaye's objection: gathering the granary
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: gathering the granary
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that one could gather the granary together and separate terumah from the new produce on the new and from the old on the old, implying that rooting is not the sole determinant.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that one could gather the granary and separate terumah from new on new and old on old, challenging the sole reliance on rooting.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar citing Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar citing Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: for Egyptian beans sown for seed, if some rooted before Rosh Hashanah and some after, one may not separate terumot and ma'aserot from one on the other. Instead, one gathers the granary and separates from new on new and old on old.

items.text: Abaye's response: dispute over bilah
items.text_en: Abaye's response: dispute over bilah
items.desc_en: Abaye responds that Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds that there is bilah (mixture), while the Sages hold there is no bilah, explaining the difference in approach.

sub.desc_en: Abaye responds that the cited baraita reflects Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's view, who holds that there is bilah (mixture), allowing the described procedure.
Abaye concludes that the Sages, by contrast, hold that there is no bilah, explaining why they would not permit the procedure described in the baraita.

items.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani citing Shmuel, and Rabbi Zeira's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani citing Shmuel, and Rabbi Zeira's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports that Shmuel ruled the halakhah follows Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar. Rabbi Zeira challenges this, noting that Shmuel elsewhere said there is no bilah except for wine and oil. The Gemara notes that Shmuel's statement that all follows the final ripening of the fruit was overlooked.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports that Shmuel ruled the halakhah follows Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar, who spoke in the name of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri.
Rabbi Zeira challenges the report, noting that Shmuel elsewhere stated that there is no bilah (mixing of old and new produce) except for wine and oil.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement that all follows the final ripening of the fruit (גמר פרי) was overlooked by Rabbi Zeira, reconciling the two positions.

items.text: Necessity of multiple rulings on בילה and גמר פרי
items.text_en: Necessity of multiple rulings on בילה and גמר פרי
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to state both that the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and that there is no בילה for all, and also the principle that everything follows the fruit's ripening stage. Each statement is necessary to prevent a mistaken inference, and the final statement about no בילה teaches that for wine and oil there is בילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah's rulings are all necessary, beginning with the first necessity: if only the law following Rabbi Shimon Shezuri were stated, one might mistakenly think he holds there is בילה (mixing), so the Mishnah teaches that for all other cases there is no בילה.

The Gemara explains the second necessity: if only the statement that there is no בילה for all were stated, one might think the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, so it also teaches that the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri.

The Gemara explains the third necessity: if only those two statements were made, one might think there is a contradiction in Shmuel's own rulings, so the Mishnah also teaches that everything follows the fruit's ripening stage (גמר פרי).

The Gemara explains the fourth necessity: if only the principle of following the fruit's ripening were stated, one might think it applies even to grain and olives, so the Mishnah also teaches that the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri specifically in the matter where he disagrees.
The Gemara resolves the remaining question: the statement 'לכל אין בילה' (for all there is no mixing) is necessary to teach that for wine and oil there is indeed בילה (mixing).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva on tithing produce
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva on tithing produce
items.desc_en: A Tannaitic source presents Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view that only produce that grows from last year's water is tithed for the past year, excluding vegetables that grow on current water. Rabbi Akiva argues that produce that grows on most water is tithed for the past year, excluding vegetables that grow on any water. Rabbi Avahu explains the practical difference between them: certain onions and Egyptian beans that were deprived of water for thirty days before Rosh Hashanah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from the verse 'באספך מגרנך ומיקבך' (when you gather from your threshing floor and winepress) that produce growing on last year's water is tithed for the previous year, excluding vegetables that grow on the coming year's water.
Rabbi Akiva interprets the same verse differently: produce growing on the majority of water (רוב מים) is tithed for the previous year, excluding vegetables that grow on any water.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions.

Rabbi Avahu answers that the difference lies in the case of sterile onions (בצלים הסריסין) and Egyptian beans (פול המצרי), citing a Mishnah that determines their tithe status based on whether they were deprived of water for thirty days before Rosh Hashanah.

items.text: Reason for the New Year for Trees on Shevat 1
items.text_en: Reason for the New Year for Trees on Shevat 1
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the first of Shevat is the New Year for trees. Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya explains the reason: because by then most of the year's rains have fallen, even though most of the winter season is still outside. The Gemara clarifies the phrasing: it means that even though most of the season is still outside, most of the rains have already fallen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the first of Shevat is the New Year for the tree (ראש השנה לאילן).
The Mishnah states that the first of Shevat is the New Year for trees.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this date.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this date.
Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya explains the reason: because most of the year's rains have fallen, even though most of the season (תקופה) is still outside.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Oshaya explains: because most of the year's rains have already fallen, even though most of the winter season is still outside.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Akiva and the etrog
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Akiva and the etrog
items.desc_en: A Baraisa recounts that Rabbi Akiva once picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and treated it with two tithes, demonstrating the practical application of the New Year for Trees.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts a story: Rabbi Akiva gathered an etrog on the first of Shevat and treated it with two tithes (one for the previous year and one for the coming year).
A Baraisa recounts that Rabbi Akiva picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and treated it with two tithes, demonstrating the practical application of the New Year for Trees.

items.text: Opening statement of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening statement of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the New Year for trees is on Shevat 1 according to Beit Shammai and Shevat 15 according to Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the New Year for trees is on Shevat 1 according to Beit Shammai and Shevat 15 according to Beit Hillel.

items.text: Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda's alternative tradition
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda's alternative tradition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda argues that the practice regarding the etrog did not follow Beit Shammai or Beit Hillel, but rather the custom of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda asserts that the practice regarding the etrog was not according to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel but according to Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Supporting Tosefta about the etrog
items.text_en: Supporting Tosefta about the etrog
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabban Gamliel states that the etrog is like a tree in three ways and like a vegetable in one way (tithing at the time of picking), while Rabbi Eliezer says it is like a tree in all respects.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabban Gamliel rules that the etrog is like a tree in three ways (עורלה (orlah), רבעי (neta revai), and שביעית (shemittah)) and like a vegetable in one way (tithing at the time of picking).
Rabbi Eliezer states that the etrog is like a tree in all respects, disagreeing with Rabban Gamliel's distinction.

items.text: Gemara's objection: combining leniencies
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: combining leniencies
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: How could one follow both leniencies of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel? It cites a baraita that one must follow either school entirely, not pick and choose leniencies or stringencies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can adopt the stringencies of both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
A baraita is cited: one must follow Beit Hillel consistently; adopting leniencies from both schools is wicked, and adopting stringencies from both is foolish.
The Gemara resolves: one must follow either Beit Shammai entirely or Beit Hillel entirely, not mix.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's uncertainty
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's uncertainty
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva was uncertain whether Beit Hillel said the New Year for trees is on Shevat 1 or Shevat 15.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva was uncertain whether Beit Hillel said the New Year for trees is on Shevat 1 or Shevat 15.

items.text: Reiteration and challenge to Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda
items.text_en: Reiteration and challenge to Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda's statement and challenges: If the practice followed Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer, then on Shevat 1 it followed Beit Shammai!

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda repeats that the practice was according to Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer, and adds that the etrog was treated as Shevat 1 like Beit Shammai.
The Gemara challenges: If the practice followed Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer, then on Shevat 1 it followed Beit Shammai, creating a contradiction.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina (or Rabbi Chananya) explains that the case involves an etrog whose fruits ripened before Shevat 15, and the incident happened then, but in principle it could be earlier.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina (or Rabbi Chananya) explains that the case involves an etrog whose fruits formed before Shevat 15, and the practice was applied even earlier, as the actual event occurred.

items.text: Ravina's emendation
items.text_en: Ravina's emendation
items.desc_en: Ravina suggests a textual emendation: the date was Shevat 15, not Shevat 1, and the practice followed Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer, not Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: Ravina suggests a textual emendation: the Mishnah should read 'not Shevat 1 but Shevat 15, and not according to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel but according to Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.'

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's deduction
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's deduction
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna deduces that since Rabban Gamliel says the etrog is tithed as a vegetable after picking, its New Year is Tishrei.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna deduces that since Rabban Gamliel treats the etrog's tithing as a vegetable (following the time of picking), its New Year for tithing is Tishrei.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar about tithing etrogim picked before and after sunset on Shevat 15, which implies a different New Year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: if one picked an etrog before sunset on Shevat 15 and another after sunset, they cannot be tithed from one to the other, indicating that Shevat 15 is the New Year for the etrog, not Tishrei.

items.text: Clarifying Rabban Gamliel's position on the etrog's New Year
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabban Gamliel's position on the etrog's New Year
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes Rabban Gamliel follows the time of picking, but the mishna says Shevat. It then cites Rabba bar Rav Huna's version: even though Rabban Gamliel says the etrog follows picking like a vegetable, its New Year is Shevat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: who holds that the etrog follows the time of picking, such that Rabban Gamliel's position in the mishna (which says its New Year is Shevat) is consistent?
Rabba bar Rav Huna resolves the difficulty: even though Rabban Gamliel rules that the etrog follows picking like a vegetable, its New Year is still Shevat.

items.text: Explaining the different phrasing in the mishna
items.text_en: Explaining the different phrasing in the mishna
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishna says 'if the second year enters the third' for other trees but 'if the third enters the fourth' for the etrog. It answers that the mishna teaches incidentally that the etrog is difficult because everyone handles it in the seventh year, so it does not bear fruit for three years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishna uses different phrasing for the etrog (third entering fourth) compared to other trees (second entering third).
The Gemara answers that the mishna incidentally teaches that the etrog is difficult because everyone handles it in the seventh year, so it does not bear fruit for three years.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai about the etrog's New Year
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai about the etrog's New Year
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai when the New Year for the etrog is. Rabbi Yannai answers Shevat. Rabbi Yochanan clarifies whether it is Shevat of the months or Shevat of the tekufa, and Rabbi Yannai says of the months.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai when the New Year for the etrog is, and Rabbi Yannai answers Shevat.
Rabbi Yochanan asks whether the Shevat is the Shevat of the months or the Shevat of the tekufa, and Rabbi Yannai answers of the months.

items.text: Rava asks about a leap year
items.text_en: Rava asks about a leap year
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman, or alternatively Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai, what the rule is in a leap year. The answer is to follow the majority of years.

sub.text: Rava's question (or alternative: Rabbi Yochanan's question)
sub.text_en: Rava's question (or alternative: Rabbi Yochanan's question)
sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman (or alternatively Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Yannai) what the rule is for the New Year of the etrog in a leap year.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's answer (or alternative: Rabbi Yannai's answer)
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer (or alternative: Rabbi Yannai's answer)
sub.desc_en: The answer is to follow the majority of years, i.e., treat the leap year like a regular year and set the New Year for the etrog in Shevat.

items.text: Rabba's ruling on etrog between years and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rabba's ruling on etrog between years and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rabba rules that an etrog from the sixth year that enters the seventh is exempt from tithes and removal, while one from the seventh entering the eighth is exempt from tithes but obligated in removal. Abaye objects: if the first case is exempt from removal because we follow ripening, then it should be obligated in tithes. Rabba responds that since everyone handles it, it is exempt from tithes.

sub.desc_en: Rabba rules that an etrog from the sixth year entering the seventh is exempt from tithes and removal, while one from the seventh entering the eighth is exempt from tithes but obligated in removal.
Abaye objects: if the first case is exempt from removal because we follow ripening, then it should be obligated in tithes.
Rabba responds that since everyone handles the etrog, it is exempt from tithes.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's alternative ruling
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's alternative ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna rules that an etrog from the sixth year entering the seventh is always considered sixth-year, and one from the seventh entering the eighth is always considered seventh-year.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna rules that an etrog from the sixth year entering the seventh is always considered sixth-year, and one from the seventh entering the eighth is always considered seventh-year.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution as a dispute among Tanna'im
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution as a dispute among Tanna'im
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon contradicts both Rabba and Rav Hamnuna. The Gemara notes that the first clause challenges Rav Hamnuna, and the latter clause challenges both Rabba and Rav Hamnuna. It resolves that this is a dispute among Tanna'im.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon, which states that an etrog from the sixth year entering the seventh is exempt from both tithe and removal, and from the seventh entering the eighth is exempt from both tithe and removal, contradicting both Rabba and Rav Hamnuna.
The Gemara notes that the first clause of the baraita challenges Rav Hamnuna, and the latter clause challenges both Rabba and Rav Hamnuna, setting up the need for resolution.

items.text: Supporting baraita and question about Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Supporting baraita and question about Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei reports Avtolmos's testimony in the name of five elders that the etrog follows picking for tithes, and the Sages in Usha ruled it follows picking for both tithes and Sabbatical year. The Gemara then asks: who mentioned the Sabbatical year?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei reports Avtolmos's testimony in the name of five elders that the etrog follows picking for tithes, and the Sages in Usha ruled it follows picking for both tithes and Sabbatical year.
The Gemara asks: who mentioned the Sabbatical year in the earlier discussion, prompting the citation of this baraita?

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah regarding etrog
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah regarding etrog
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause and should read: 'Etrog — after its picking for tithes and after its blossoming for the Sabbatical year.' The Sages in Usha ruled that for both tithes and Sabbatical year, the determining factor is after its picking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the Mishnah's missing clause by stating that the etrog's status for tithes follows its picking and for the Sabbatical year follows its blossoming, while the Sages of Usha ruled that both follow its picking.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's ruling on etrog
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish's ruling on etrog
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish both state that an etrog from the sixth year that enters the seventh year is always considered sixth-year produce. Rabbi Yochanan adds that even if it was the size of an olive and grew to the size of a loaf, it is still liable for tithes.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish both rule that an etrog from the sixth year entering the seventh is always considered sixth-year produce.
Ravin reports in Rabbi Yochanan's name that even if the etrog was olive-sized and grew to a loaf-sized, it remains liable for tithes.

items.text: Baraita on trees and the New Year for trees
items.text_en: Baraita on trees and the New Year for trees
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a tree's fruits blossomed before the fifteenth of Shevat, they are tithed for the previous year; if after, for the coming year. Rabbi Nechemya limits this to trees that produce two brooks (harvests) per year. The Gemara clarifies that this means trees that produce like two brooks, but trees that produce only one brook, such as date palms, olives, and carobs, are always tithed for the coming year even if they blossomed before the fifteenth.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: a tree's fruits are tithed for the previous year if they blossomed before the fifteenth of Shevat, and for the coming year if after.
Rabbi Nechemya limits the rule to trees that produce two brooks (harvests) per year.
The Gemara questions how a tree can literally produce two brooks per year.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Nechemya means trees that produce like two brooks, not literally two.
The Gemara explains that trees producing only one brook per year, such as date palms, olives, and carobs, are always tithed for the coming year even if they blossomed before the fifteenth.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about carob trees
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about carob trees
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that the people practice with carob trees according to Rabbi Nechemya's opinion, meaning they treat them as if they produce like two brooks and are tithed for the coming year only if they blossomed after the fifteenth.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the people practice with carob trees according to Rabbi Nechemya's opinion.

items.text: Resh Lakish's objection from the Mishnah of Bnot Shuach
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's objection from the Mishnah of Bnot Shuach
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish raises an objection to Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah about Bnot Shuach (a type of carob), which states that their Sabbatical year is the second year because they produce fruit over three years. This contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that carobs follow Rabbi Nechemya.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan by citing the Mishnah of Bnot Shuach, which states that their Sabbatical year is the second year because they produce fruit over three years, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that carobs follow Rabbi Nechemya.

items.text: Discussion of Rabbi Yochanan's silence and possible responses
items.text_en: Discussion of Rabbi Yochanan's silence and possible responses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan was silent in response to Resh Lakish's objection. Rabbi Abba the Kohen asks Rabbi Yosef the Kohen why he was silent, suggesting he could have answered that he was stating Rabbi Nechemya's opinion while Resh Lakish cited the Rabbis. The Gemara explores several possible responses: that the people's custom does not override a prohibition, that the tithe of carobs is rabbinic while the Sabbatical year is biblical, and concludes with doubt whether Rabbi Yochanan accepted the objection.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan was silent; Rabbi Abba the Kohen asks Rabbi Yosef the Kohen why he did not answer that he was stating Rabbi Nechemya's opinion while Resh Lakish cited the Rabbis.
The Gemara objects that Resh Lakish could have replied: 'You abandon the Rabbis and act according to Rabbi Nechemya?'

The Gemara suggests Rabbi Yochanan could have answered that he only reported a custom (נָהֲגוּ), not a halachic permission, but the objection is that in a place of prohibition, custom does not override.

The Gemara suggests Rabbi Yochanan could have answered that the tithe of carobs is rabbinic (דְּרַבָּנַן) while the Sabbatical year prohibition is biblical (דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא), so the objection is not parallel.
Rabbi Abba the Kohen expresses doubt whether Resh Lakish's objection was actually answered, and concludes that it is uncertain whether Rabbi Yochanan accepted the objection or not.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the world is judged at four seasons: at Passover concerning crops, at Shavuot concerning fruit trees, at Rosh Hashanah all creatures pass before God, and at Sukkot concerning water.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the world is judged at four seasons: at Passover for crops, at Shavuot for fruit trees, at Rosh Hashanah all creatures pass before God, and at Sukkot for water.

items.text: Gemara's first question: which crop?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: which crop?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which crop is judged at Passover, concluding it is the crop about to be sown. It then questions whether a single judgment applies, citing a baraita that distinguishes between past and future judgments, and Rava infers two judgments. Abaye advises to plant hardy crops early to precede judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which crop is judged at Passover, rejecting the current standing crop and concluding it is the crop about to be sown.
The Gemara objects that a single judgment is insufficient, citing a baraita that distinguishes between past and future judgments for crops and humans.
Rava infers from the baraita that the crop undergoes two judgments.
Abaye advises that if one sees late crops thriving, one should plant early crops first so they are judged before the late ones.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah cannot follow Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, or Rabbi Natan, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir holds all are judged on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur, Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes times for crops and humans, Rabbi Yosei judges daily, and Rabbi Natan judges hourly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, ruling out Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Natan.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir holds all are judged on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur; Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes times for crops and humans.
The baraita continues: Rabbi Yosei says man is judged daily, and Rabbi Natan says man is judged hourly, each citing a verse.

items.text: Resolution: Tanna DeVei Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Resolution: Tanna DeVei Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects identifying the Mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda, because the Mishnah's treatment of humans would contradict his view. Rava concludes that the Mishnah follows Tanna DeVei Rabbi Yishmael, who judges crops at the three festivals and humans on Rosh Hashanah with sealing on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah were Rabbi Yehuda's view, the Mishnah's treatment of humans would contradict his explicit position.

Rava resolves that the Mishnah follows Tanna DeVei Rabbi Yishmael, who judges crops at the three festivals and humans on Rosh Hashanah with sealing on Yom Kippur, and the Mishnah refers to the beginning of judgment.

items.text: Rav Chisda on Rabbi Yosei's rationale
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on Rabbi Yosei's rationale
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that Rabbi Yosei's proof from 'You inspect him each morning' is not like Rabbi Natan's hourly inspection; rather, Rabbi Yosei derives his view from the verse about doing justice 'day by day'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks why Rabbi Yosei does not adopt Rabbi Natan's hourly inspection, and questions whether both 'בחינה' (examination) and 'פקידה' (inspection) are merely general oversight.
Rav Chisda explains that Rabbi Yosei's rationale is derived from the verse 'לעשות משפט עבדו ומשפט עמו ישראל דבר יום ביומו' (to do justice for His servant and His people Israel, day by day).

items.text: Rav Chisda on king and community
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on king and community
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda deduces from the same verse that the king is judged before the community, either because it is improper for the king to wait or to forestall anger.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda adds that a king enters judgment before the community, citing the same verse, and offers two reasons: it is improper for the king to wait outside, or to prevent the intensification of divine anger.

items.text: Rav Yosef on current prayer practice
items.text_en: Rav Yosef on current prayer practice
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef notes that we pray for the sick and suffering nowadays according to Rabbi Yosei, or alternatively according to the Rabbis via Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that a cry is beneficial both before and after the decree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that nowadays we pray for the sick and the afflicted according to Rabbi Yosei's view that judgment is daily.

An alternative explanation is offered: we may always follow the rabbis (who hold judgment on Rosh Hashanah), and rely on Rabbi Yitzchak's statement that crying out is beneficial both before and after the decree.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva on the festivals' offerings
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva on the festivals' offerings
items.desc_en: A baraita explains the reasons for bringing the Omer at Passover, two loaves at Shavuot, water libation at Sukkot, and the recitation of Kingships, Remembrances, and Shofar on Rosh Hashanah, all to bless produce and bring merit. Rabbi Abahu adds the reason for a ram's horn, recalling the Binding of Isaac. Rabbi Yitzchak questions why we blow and sound when seated, since the Torah only commands a memorial of teruah.

sub.text: Baraita citing Rabbi Yehuda from Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Baraita citing Rabbi Yehuda from Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: A baraita explains that the Omer is brought at Passover to bless the grain, and the two loaves at Shavuot to bless the fruit of the tree.
The baraita explains that the water libation at Sukkot blesses the rains, and on Rosh Hashanah one recites Kingships, Remembrances, and Shofar to coronate God and bring merit.
Rabbi Abahu explains that a ram's horn is used to recall the Binding of Isaac, as if the people bound themselves before God.
Rabbi Yitzchak questions why the shofar is blown and sounded while seated, since the Torah only commands a memorial of teruah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Shofar blasts to confuse Satan
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Shofar blasts to confuse Satan
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that they blow the shofar while standing and sitting to confuse Satan.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that they blow the shofar while standing and sitting to confuse Satan.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: Shofar at year's start prevents calamity at end
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak: Shofar at year's start prevents calamity at end
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says that any year in which they do not blow the shofar at its beginning will be afflicted at its end, because Satan was not confused.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that a year without shofar blasts at its start will be afflicted at its end because Satan was not confused.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: A year that begins poor becomes rich
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak: A year that begins poor becomes rich
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says that a year that is poor at its beginning becomes rich at its end, citing the verse 'from the beginning of the year' (written as 'from the poverty').

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that a year which is 'poor' (רש

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: Judgment according to present deeds
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak: Judgment according to present deeds
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says that a person is judged only according to their deeds at that moment, as derived from the verse about God hearing the boy's voice where he is.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that a person is judged only according to their deeds at that moment, citing the verse about God hearing the boy's voice 'where he is'.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: Three things that recall one's sins
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak: Three things that recall one's sins
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak lists three things that cause a person's sins to be recalled: a leaning wall, intense prayer, and one who brings a lawsuit against another. Rabbi Avin adds that the one who brings the lawsuit is punished first, as shown from Sarah and Abraham.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak lists three things that recall a person's sins: a leaning wall, intense prayer, and one who brings a lawsuit against another.
Rabbi Avin adds that the one who brings a lawsuit is punished first, citing the case of Sarah and Abraham.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: Four things that tear up a decree, with an addition
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak: Four things that tear up a decree, with an addition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak lists four things that tear up a person's evil decree: charity, crying out, changing one's name, and changing one's deeds. Some add changing one's place, but the Gemara explains that the merit of the Land of Israel is what helped Abraham.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak lists four things that tear up a person's evil decree: charity, crying out, changing one's name, and changing one's deeds, each supported by a biblical verse.
Some add changing one's place to the list, citing the verse about Abraham leaving his land and being promised greatness.
The Gemara rejects the addition, explaining that Abraham's merit was due to the Land of Israel, not the change of place itself.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: Obligation to greet one's teacher and purify oneself on the festival
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak: Obligation to greet one's teacher and purify oneself on the festival
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that a person must greet their teacher on the festival, and must purify themselves for the festival, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states the obligation to greet one's teacher on the festival, citing the verse about the Shunammite woman.
Rabbi Yitzchak adds the obligation to purify oneself for the festival, citing the verse 'וּבְנִבְלָתָם לֹא תִגָּעוּ' (do not touch their carcasses).

items.text: Baraita: The verse 'do not touch their carcasses' applies only on the festival
items.text_en: Baraita: The verse 'do not touch their carcasses' applies only on the festival
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'do not touch their carcasses' applies to the festival, not to ordinary impurity. A kal vachomer argument shows that if priests are not warned about severe impurity, certainly Israelites are not warned about light impurity, so the verse must refer to the festival.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'וּבִנְבָלָתָם לֹא תִגָּעוּ' and initially suggests it might warn Israelites against touching a carcass, but then limits the warning to priests only, based on the verse 'אֱמוֹר אֶל הַכֹּהֲנִים'.

The gemara presents a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if priests are not warned about severe impurity (tum'ah of a corpse), certainly Israelites are not warned about light impurity (tum'ah of a carcass), so the verse must apply to the festival.
The gemara resolves that the verse 'וּבִנְבָלָתָם לֹא תִגָּעוּ' applies specifically on the festival (בָּרֶגֶל), teaching the obligation to purify oneself for the festival.

items.text: Three books opened on Rosh Hashanah: righteous, wicked, and intermediate
items.text_en: Three books opened on Rosh Hashanah: righteous, wicked, and intermediate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Kruspadai in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah: one for completely righteous, one for completely wicked, and one for intermediates. The righteous are immediately written for life, the wicked for death, and intermediates are suspended until Yom Kippur. Rabbi Avin and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cite verses to support this.

sub.text: Rabbi Kruspadai in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Kruspadai in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Kruspadai in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah: one for the completely righteous, one for the completely wicked, and one for intermediates, with immediate verdicts for the first two and a suspended verdict for the third until Yom Kippur.

Rabbi Avin cites the verse 'יִמָּחוּ מִסֵּפֶר חַיִּים' (Let them be blotted out of the book of life) and interprets its three phrases as referring to the books of the wicked, the righteous, and the intermediates respectively.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a different verse, 'מְחֵנִי נָא מִסִּפְרְךָ' (erase me from Your book), and similarly interprets its three phrases as referring to the three books.
