items.text: Tannaitic dispute: Three categories on the Day of Judgment according to Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: Three categories on the Day of Judgment according to Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: A baraita records Beit Shammai's view: three categories on the Day of Judgment — completely righteous are written for eternal life, completely wicked for Gehinnom, and intermediates descend to Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents Beit Shammai's view that on the Day of Judgment there are three categories: the completely righteous are written for eternal life, the completely wicked for Gehinnom, and the intermediates descend to Gehinnom.

items.text: Opening: The fate of intermediate sinners and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Opening: The fate of intermediate sinners and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The section begins with the description of sinners who are refined like silver and gold, and Hannah's praise. It then presents the dispute: Beit Shammai says the wicked are consumed, while Beit Hillel says God inclines toward mercy, citing David's psalms.

sub.desc_en: The section opens by describing intermediate sinners who are refined like silver and gold, and cites Hannah's praise of God who brings down and raises up.
Beit Hillel states that God inclines toward mercy, citing David's psalm of thanksgiving.

items.text: The judgment of Jewish and Gentile sinners, and the eternal punishment of heretics
items.text_en: The judgment of Jewish and Gentile sinners, and the eternal punishment of heretics
items.desc_en: This section details the punishment of Jewish sinners and Gentile sinners who descend to Gehinnom for twelve months, after which their bodies are consumed and souls scattered. In contrast, heretics, apostates, and those who led others astray are judged for generations, with Gehinnom ending but they do not, as they stretched their hands against the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that Jewish sinners and Gentile sinners descend to Gehinnom for twelve months, after which their bodies are consumed and souls scattered under the feet of the righteous.
The Tanna Kamma contrasts heretics, apostates, and those who led others astray, who are judged for generations and never consumed, because they stretched their hands against the Temple.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin and Rava on the appearance of the wicked
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin and Rava on the appearance of the wicked
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin says their faces are like the bottom of a pot. Rava adds that the handsome men of Mehoza are called 'sons of Gehinnom.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin states that the faces of the wicked are like the bottom of a pot.
Rava adds that the handsome men of Mehoza are called 'sons of Gehinnom,' illustrating the appearance of the wicked.

items.text: Gemara's question: How does Beit Hillel reconcile mercy with the verse about fire?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: How does Beit Hillel reconcile mercy with the verse about fire?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Beit Hillel's position: if God inclines toward mercy, how can the verse 'I will bring the third through fire' apply? The answer distinguishes between Jewish sinners with many sins (no remedy) and those with equal sins and merits, where the verse applies, but otherwise mercy prevails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Beit Hillel's position: if God inclines toward mercy, how can the verse 'I will bring the third through fire' apply?
The answer distinguishes between Jewish sinners with many sins (no remedy) and those with equal sins and merits, where the verse applies, but otherwise mercy prevails.

items.text: Rava's homily on David's psalm
items.text_en: Rava's homily on David's psalm
items.desc_en: Rava expounds on the verse 'Ahavti ki yishma Hashem': the congregation of Israel says, 'When am I beloved before You? When You hear my supplication.' Despite being poor in mitzvot, it is fitting for God to save.

sub.desc_en: Rava expounds on the verse 'אָהַבְתִּי כִּי יִשְׁמַע ה׳' (I love that the Lord hears), interpreting it as the congregation of Israel saying they are beloved when God hears their supplication, and despite being poor in mitzvot, it is fitting for God to save them.

items.text: Definitions of 'sinners of Israel in body' and 'those who cast fear in the land of the living'
items.text_en: Definitions of 'sinners of Israel in body' and 'those who cast fear in the land of the living'
items.desc_en: Rav defines 'sinners of Israel in body' as one who does not put on tefillin. Rav defines 'sinners of the nations in body' as one who commits a transgression. Rav Chisda and Rav Yehuda explain 'those who cast fear in the land of the living' as a leader who imposes excessive fear on the community not for Heaven's sake, and such a leader will not see a Torah scholar as a son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes 'sinners of Israel in body'.
Rav defines 'sinners of Israel in body' as one who does not put on תפילין (phylacteries).
Rav defines 'sinners of the nations in body' as one who commits a transgression.
Rav Chisda explains 'those who cast fear in the land of the living' as a leader who imposes excessive fear on the community not for Heaven's sake.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds that such a leader will not see a Torah scholar as a son, citing the verse 'לֹא יִרְאֶה כׇּל חַכְמֵי לֵב'.

items.text: How does God incline toward mercy? The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
items.text_en: How does God incline toward mercy? The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel says God inclines toward mercy. Rabbi Eliezer says He suppresses sins, citing 'Yashuv yerachameinu yichbosh avonoteinu.' Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says He carries sins, citing 'Nosei avon ve'over al pesha.' The school of Rabbi Yishmael says He passes over sins one by one, but Rava notes the sin itself is not erased; if there is a majority of sins, it is counted with them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how God inclines toward mercy, citing Beit Hillel's statement that He tilts toward mercy.
Rabbi Eliezer answers that God suppresses sins, citing the verse 'יָשׁוּב יְרַחֲמֵנוּ יִכְבּוֹשׁ עֲוֹנוֹתֵינוּ' (He will again have compassion on us, He will suppress our iniquities).
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers that God carries sins, citing the verse 'נוֹשֵׂא עָוֹן וְעוֹבֵר עַל פֶּשַׁע' (He bears iniquity and passes over transgression).
The school of Rabbi Yishmael answers that God passes over sins one by one, and that is the standard measure.
Rava resolves that the sin itself is not erased; if there is a majority of sins, it is counted with them.

items.text: Rava's principle: One who overlooks his own attributes has his sins overlooked
items.text_en: Rava's principle: One who overlooks his own attributes has his sins overlooked
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that whoever overlooks his own attributes (is forgiving) has all his sins overlooked, as per the verse 'Nosei avon ve'over al pesha.' A story is told about Rav Huna bar Yehoshua who was ill; Rav Pappa saw him and thought he was dying, but he recovered. Rav Huna explained that God said, 'Since he did not stand by his word, do not stand with him,' citing the same verse.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that whoever overlooks his own attributes (is forgiving) has all his sins overlooked, citing the verse 'נוֹשֵׂא עָוֹן וְעוֹבֵר עַל פֶּשַׁע' (He bears iniquity and passes over transgression).

sub.text: Story about Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: A story is told: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua fell ill, Rav Pappa visited and thought he was dying, but he recovered; Rav Huna explained that God said, 'Since he did not stand by his word, do not stand with him,' citing the same verse.

items.text: Interpretation of 'lish'eirit nachalato'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'lish'eirit nachalato'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina explains the phrase 'lish'eirit nachalato' as a tail with a thorn: it refers to the remnant of His inheritance, not the entire inheritance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina interprets the phrase 'lish'eirit nachalato' as a tail with a thorn, meaning it refers only to the remnant of His inheritance, not the entire inheritance.

items.text: Three Amoraim resolve contradictions between justice and mercy verses
items.text_en: Three Amoraim resolve contradictions between justice and mercy verses
items.desc_en: Rav Huna, Rabbi Elazar, and Ilfa (or Ilfai) each note apparent contradictions between verses describing God as just and merciful. They resolve them by explaining that initially God acts as a righteous judge, but ultimately shows mercy.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the topic: for one who makes himself like leftovers (humble).
Rav Huna raises a contradiction between verses about God's justice and mercy, resolving that initially God acts as a righteous judge (צדיק) and ultimately as a pious one (חסיד).
Rabbi Elazar raises a contradiction between verses about God's mercy and reward, resolving that initially God repays according to deeds and ultimately shows mercy.
Ilfai (or Ilfa) raises a contradiction between verses about abundant mercy and truth, resolving that initially God acts with truth and ultimately with abundant mercy.

items.text: The Thirteen Attributes and the power of repentance
items.text_en: The Thirteen Attributes and the power of repentance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan describes God wrapping Himself like a prayer leader to teach Moses the order of prayer, including the Thirteen Attributes. Rav Yehuda states that a covenant ensures these attributes never return empty. The section includes the interpretation of 'Hashem Hashem' as God's mercy before and after sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse describing God passing before Moses and proclaiming.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that God wrapped Himself like a prayer leader to teach Moses the order of prayer, promising that when Israel sins they should perform this order and He will forgive them.
Rav Yehuda states that a covenant is established for the Thirteen Attributes that they never return empty, citing the verse 'הנה אנכי כורת ברית'.

items.text: Repentance tears up the decree even after it is sealed
items.text_en: Repentance tears up the decree even after it is sealed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that repentance is great because it tears up a person's decree. Rav Pappa questions whether this applies only before the decree is issued, but Abaye proves from the verse 'and he will heal him' that it refers to a decree that has already been sealed, as healing is needed only for an existing wound.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that repentance is great because it tears up a person's decree, citing the verse 'and he will heal him'.
Rav Pappa questions Abaye whether the repentance tears up the decree only before it is issued, not after it is sealed.
Abaye proves from the verse 'and he will heal him' that the decree has already been sealed, since healing is needed only for an existing wound.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and distinction between individual and community
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and distinction between individual and community
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that if one repents between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur they are forgiven, but if not, even many offerings do not help. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between an individual (whose repentance can annul the decree) and the community (whose decree is not annulled). A further baraita about God's eyes on the land illustrates that for the community, the decree is not changed but only fulfilled in a different manner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that if one repents between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur they are forgiven, but if not, even many offerings do not help.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between an individual (whose repentance can annul the decree) and the community (whose decree is not annulled).
A further baraita about God's eyes on the land illustrates that for the community, the decree is not changed but only fulfilled in a different manner.

items.text: Further challenges and resolution: individuals at sea
items.text_en: Further challenges and resolution: individuals at sea
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the community's decree cannot be torn for good, and answers that it is possible in that case. A second baraita about sailors shows that if they cry out before the decree they are answered, but after the decree they are not. The Gemara explains that these sailors are considered like individuals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, if the decree can be changed for good, the community's decree cannot be torn and increased.
The Gemara answers that the case is different because it is possible to add rain in a beneficial way.
A baraita about sailors at sea is cited, showing that if they cry out before the decree they are answered, but after the decree they are not.
The Gemara resolves that these sailors are considered like individuals, not a community, so the rule about individuals applies.

items.text: Bluriah the convert's question and Rabbi Yosei's parable
items.text_en: Bluriah the convert's question and Rabbi Yosei's parable
items.desc_en: Bluriah the convert asks Rabban Gamliel about the contradiction between 'who does not lift up faces' and 'May God lift up His face to you'. Rabbi Yosei the Kohen answers with a parable: a debtor who offended the king must first appease his fellow before the king forgives him. This distinguishes between sins against God and sins against other people. The section ends with Rabbi Akiva's teaching.

sub.desc_en: Bluriah the convert asks Rabban Gamliel about the apparent contradiction between 'who does not lift up faces' and 'May God lift up His face to you'.

Rabbi Yosei the Kohen answers with a parable: a debtor who offended the king must first appease his fellow before the king forgives him, distinguishing between sins against God and sins against other people.
Rabbi Yosei applies the parable: the verse 'who does not lift up faces' refers to sins between a person and another, while 'May God lift up His face to you' refers to sins between a person and God.
The section ends with a transition noting that Rabbi Akiva came and taught a further lesson.

items.text: Distinction between before and after the decree for an individual
items.text_en: Distinction between before and after the decree for an individual
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially distinguishes between before and after the decree for an individual, but then notes that this is a dispute among Tannaim. Rabbi Meir's baraita is cited, describing two people with identical illnesses or judgments, where one is saved and the other not due to the completeness of their prayer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a distinction: one case is before the decree (גזר דין) and the other after, but notes this applies to an individual.
The Gemara states that the decree for an individual is a dispute among Tannaim, citing Rabbi Meir's baraita about two people with identical illnesses or judgments.
Rabbi Meir explains that one was saved because he prayed a complete prayer (תפילה שלמה), while the other did not and was not answered.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yitzchak on the efficacy of prayer
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yitzchak on the efficacy of prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asserts that the distinction between before and after the decree applies to an individual. Rabbi Yitzchak argues that crying out is beneficial both before and after the decree.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asserts the distinction: one case is before the decree, the other after.
Rabbi Yitzchak states that crying out (צעקה) is beneficial for a person both before and after the decree.

items.text: Can a community's decree be torn?
items.text_en: Can a community's decree be torn?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a community's decree can be torn, citing a contradiction between verses. It resolves that both verses refer to after the decree, but one involves a decree with an oath and the other without.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a decree for the community can be torn, citing contradictory verses about washing away sin and the stain remaining, suggesting a distinction between before and after the decree.
The Gemara rejects the distinction and explains that both verses refer to after the decree, but one is a decree accompanied by an oath (שבועה) and the other is not.

items.text: Proof that a decree with an oath cannot be torn
items.text_en: Proof that a decree with an oath cannot be torn
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Ami (or Rav Yonatan) cites a verse to prove that a decree accompanied by an oath cannot be torn. Rava and Abaye then debate whether Torah study or acts of kindness can atone for such a decree, citing their own longevity as evidence.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Ami / Rav Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Ami / Rav Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Ami (or Rav Yonatan) cites the verse 'לָכֵן נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי לְבֵית עֵלִי אִם יִתְכַּפֵּר עֲוֹן בֵּית עֵלִי בְּזֶבַח וּבְמִנְחָה' to prove that a decree accompanied by an oath cannot be torn.
Rava argues that while the decree cannot be atoned through זֶבַח וּמִנְחָה (sacrifices), it can be atoned through Torah study.
Abaye adds that atonement is achieved through both Torah study and acts of kindness (גמילות חסדים).

The gemara notes that Rabbah and Abaye descended from Eli's house; Rabbah, who engaged only in Torah, lived 40 years, while Abaye, who engaged in both Torah and acts of kindness, lived 60 years, supporting their respective positions.

items.text: The family of Eli and the power of Torah study
items.text_en: The family of Eli and the power of Torah study
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts a family in Jerusalem whose members died at age eighteen. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai told them they might be from the house of Eli, and advised them to engage in Torah study to live. They did so and lived, and the family was named after him.

sub.desc_en: A baraita tells of a family in Jerusalem whose members died at age 18; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai suggested they might be from Eli's house and advised them to engage in Torah to live.
The family followed the advice, engaged in Torah, and lived, and the family was called by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's name.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai advises them to engage in Torah study to live, and they do so and live.
The family is thereafter called the family of Rabban Yochanan after him.

items.text: A community's decree is not sealed, or if sealed, can be torn
items.text_en: A community's decree is not sealed, or if sealed, can be torn
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Inya cites Rav that a community's decree is not sealed. The Gemara objects with a verse, and resolves that even if sealed, it can be torn. Another verse is cited, and the Gemara distinguishes between an individual and the community.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Inya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Inya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Inya cites Rav that a community's decree is not sealed.
The Gemara objects that a verse says 'your iniquity is recorded before Me,' implying the decree is sealed.
The Gemara resolves that even if the decree is sealed, it can be torn, as another verse indicates.
The Gemara objects with another verse that implies a limited time for seeking God.
The Gemara distinguishes: that verse applies to an individual, while here the discussion is about the community.

items.text: The ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur for an individual
items.text_en: The ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur for an individual
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for an individual, the time to seek God is the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, citing the story of Naval and the ten days of his punishment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: when is the time for an individual?
Rabbah bar Avuha answers: these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains that the ten days Nabal lived correspond to the ten gifts he gave to David's servants.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha reiterates that these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's answer in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's answer in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: The ten days correspond to the ten gifts Naval gave to David's servants.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's resolution in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman says in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha: These are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, concluding the section.

items.text: All pass before God on Rosh Hashanah like sheep
items.text_en: All pass before God on Rosh Hashanah like sheep
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Rosh Hashanah all pass before God like sheep. The Gemara explains the phrase, and Rabbi Yochanan says they are all inspected in a single glance, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Rosh Hashanah all pass before God like sheep.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'like sheep'.
The local sages translate the phrase as 'like sheep'.
Resh Lakish explains the phrase as 'like the ascent of Beit Maron'.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains the phrase as 'like the troops of the house of David'.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds that all are inspected in a single glance.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse to support Rabbi Yochanan's statement.
The Gemara questions the verse's meaning, rejecting a possible interpretation that God creates all hearts alike.
The Gemara resolves that the verse means God sees all hearts together and understands all their deeds.

items.text: Mishnah: Months for which messengers go out
items.text_en: Mishnah: Months for which messengers go out
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the six months for which messengers go out to announce the new moon: Nisan, Av, Elul, Tishrei, Kislev, and Adar, and adds Iyar when the Temple stood. The Gemara asks why messengers do not go out for Tammuz and Tevet.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the six months for which messengers go out to announce the new moon, each for a specific festival.
The Mishnah adds that when the Temple stood, messengers also went out for Iyar due to the minor Passover (Pesach Sheni).
The Gemara asks why messengers do not also go out for the months of Tammuz and Tevet.

items.text: Interpretation of the four fasts
items.text_en: Interpretation of the four fasts
items.desc_en: Rav Hana bar Bizna cites Rabbi Shimon HaChasid on the verse in Zechariah that calls the fasts both 'fast' and 'joy and gladness'. Rav Pappa clarifies: when there is peace they are for joy, when there is persecution they are fasts, and when there is neither, it is optional.

sub.text: Rav Hana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon HaChasid
sub.text_en: Rav Hana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon HaChasid
sub.desc_en: Rav Hana bar Bizna cites Rabbi Shimon HaChasid's question on the verse that calls the fasts both 'fast' and 'joy and gladness', and his answer that when there is peace they are for joy, when there is no peace they are fasts.
Rav Pappa clarifies the three scenarios: when there is peace they are for joy, when there is persecution they are fasts, and when there is neither, fasting is optional.

items.text: Exception of Tisha B'Av
items.text_en: Exception of Tisha B'Av
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if the same logic applies to Tisha B'Av, and Rav Pappa answers that Tisha B'Av is different because multiple calamities occurred on that day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the same logic applies to Tisha B'Av, implying it should also be optional.
Rav Pappa distinguishes Tisha B'Av because multiple calamities occurred on that day, citing the destruction of both Temples, the fall of Beitar, and the plowing of the city.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Shimon's dispute on identifying the fasts
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Shimon's dispute on identifying the fasts
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon's disagreement with Rabbi Akiva: Rabbi Akiva identifies the four fasts with specific historical events, while Rabbi Shimon argues that the tenth fast is the fifth of Tevet (when news of the city's fall reached the exile), and he claims his view is superior because he orders events chronologically.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Rabbi Shimon's disagreement with Rabbi Akiva regarding the identification of the four fasts.

Rabbi Akiva identifies the four fasts with specific historical events: the ninth of Tammuz (breach of the city), the ninth of Av (burning of the Temple), the third of Tishrei (murder of Gedaliah), and the tenth of Tevet (siege of Jerusalem).
Rabbi Shimon objects, arguing that the tenth fast is the fifth of Tevet, when news of the city's fall reached the exile, and the day of hearing is treated like the day of burning.
Rabbi Shimon claims his view is superior because he orders events chronologically (first calamity first, last calamity last), while Rabbi Akiva orders by months.

items.text: Dispute on nullification of Megillat Ta'anit
items.text_en: Dispute on nullification of Megillat Ta'anit
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Chanina say Megillat Ta'anit is nullified, citing the verse that fasts depend on peace. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say it is not nullified, arguing that only the four fasts are conditional on the Temple's rebuilding, but other fasts remain.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the dispute: Rav and Rabbi Chanina say Megillat Ta'anit is nullified; Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say it is not nullified.
Rav and Rabbi Chanina explain their view: the verse teaches that fasts depend on peace, so all fasts (including those of Megillat Ta'anit) are nullified when there is peace.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explain their view: only the four fasts mentioned in the verse are conditional on the Temple's rebuilding, but other fasts (of Megillat Ta'anit) remain as they were.

items.text: Challenge from Chanukah fast
items.text_en: Challenge from Chanukah fast
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges the view that Megillat Ta'anit is nullified with a story about a fast decreed on Chanukah, where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua did not fast. Rav Yosef initially says Chanukah is different because of a mitzvah, but Abaye objects, and Rav Yosef then says it is because the miracle is publicized.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges the view that Megillat Ta'anit is nullified by citing a story where a fast was decreed on Chanukah in Lod, and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua did not fast, and the sages told them to fast later.
Rav Yosef initially answers that Chanukah is different because there is a מצוה (commandment) involved.
Abaye objects that if the fast is nullified, the מצוה (commandment) itself would also be nullified.
Rav Yosef revises his answer, saying Chanukah is different because the miracle is publicized (מפרסם ניסא).

items.text: Challenge from the third of Tishrei
items.text_en: Challenge from the third of Tishrei
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna challenges with a tradition that the third of Tishrei was established as a holiday when the mention of God's name was restored to documents. If Megillat Ta'anit were nullified, how could they add new holidays? The Gemara answers that this was when the Temple still stood.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna challenges the view that Megillat Ta'anit was nullified, citing the historical establishment of the third of Tishrei as a holiday when the mention of God's name was restored to documents, and asks how a new holiday could be added if the scroll was nullified.
The Gemara sharpens the challenge: if Megillat Ta'anit were nullified, how could they add new holidays after earlier ones were already nullified?
The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that the case of the third of Tishrei occurred when the Temple still stood, so the rules of Megillat Ta'anit still applied at that time.

items.text: First question: Why not forbid the day of Gedaliah's murder?
items.text_en: First question: Why not forbid the day of Gedaliah's murder?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the day of Gedaliah's murder itself is not prohibited. Rav answers that the decree only forbids the day before it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the day of Gedaliah's murder itself is not forbidden.
Rav answers that the decree only forbids the day before Gedaliah's murder.

items.text: Clarification: Why not forbid the day after Rosh Chodesh?
items.text_en: Clarification: Why not forbid the day after Rosh Chodesh?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the day before Gedaliah's murder is also the day after Rosh Chodesh, which is a Torah holiday and does not need reinforcement. A baraita explains that Torah laws do not need reinforcement, but rabbinic laws do.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the day before Gedaliah's murder is also the day after Rosh Chodesh, which is a Torah holiday and does not need reinforcement.
The Gemara answers that Rosh Chodesh is a Torah law, and Torah laws do not need reinforcement.
A baraita is cited to support the distinction: Torah laws do not need reinforcement, but rabbinic laws do.

items.text: Second question: Why not forbid the day before Gedaliah's murder?
items.text_en: Second question: Why not forbid the day before Gedaliah's murder?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the day before Gedaliah's murder is not forbidden. Rav Ashi answers that Gedaliah's murder is a matter of prophetic tradition (divrei kabbalah), which is like Torah law and does not need reinforcement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the day before Gedaliah's murder is not forbidden, since Gedaliah's day is rabbinic.
Rav Ashi answers that Gedaliah's day is based on דברי קבלה (prophetic tradition), which is treated like Torah law and thus does not need reinforcement.

items.text: Challenge from Megillat Taanit: The 28th of Adar
items.text_en: Challenge from Megillat Taanit: The 28th of Adar
items.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Matna challenges the assumption that Megillat Taanit was annulled, citing the story of Yehuda ben Shamu'a who established a holiday on the 28th of Adar after the evil decree was nullified. If Megillat Taanit were annulled, how could they add new holidays?

sub.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Matna challenges the assumption that Megillat Taanit was annulled by citing the story of Yehuda ben Shamu'a, who, after the evil decree was nullified, established the 28th of Adar as a holiday.
Rav Tovi bar Matna objects: if Megillat Taanit were annulled, how could they add new holidays after the earlier ones were nullified?

items.text: Objection: Yehuda ben Shamu'a was after the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: Objection: Yehuda ben Shamu'a was after the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the story of Yehuda ben Shamu'a occurred after the Temple's destruction, so it does not prove that Megillat Taanit was still in effect during the Temple period. Yehuda ben Shamu'a was a student of Rabbi Meir, who lived later.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that Judah ben Shammua was a student of Rabbi Meir, who lived after the Temple's destruction, so the story does not prove that מגילת תענית was still in effect.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei about Megillat Ta'anit
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei about Megillat Ta'anit
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that the Sages permit the days is a Tannaic dispute. Rabbi Meir holds the days are always forbidden, while Rabbi Yosei says they are forbidden only when the Temple stands (due to joy) and permitted when it is destroyed (due to mourning).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that the Sages permit the days reflects a Tannaic dispute.
A baraita cites the dispute: Rabbi Meir forbids these days always, while Rabbi Yosei permits them when the Temple is destroyed due to mourning.

items.text: Contradiction about the nullification of Megillat Ta'anit
items.text_en: Contradiction about the nullification of Megillat Ta'anit
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one statement says the days were nullified, another says they were not. It resolves that Hanukkah and Purim remain forbidden, while other days are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one halachic statement says the days of Megillat Ta'anit were nullified, another says they were not.
The Gemara resolves: the prohibition remains for Hanukkah and Purim, but other days were nullified.

items.text: Why messengers go out for Elul and Tishrei
items.text_en: Why messengers go out for Elul and Tishrei
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why messengers go out for Elul (due to Rosh Hashanah) and Tishrei (due to fixing the festivals). It considers the possibility of intercalating Elul, but Rabbi Chinana bar Kahana says Elul has never been intercalated since Ezra. The Gemara concludes that if needed, Elul could be intercalated, and it is better to disrupt Rosh Hashanah than all the festivals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why messengers go out for both Elul (for Rosh Hashanah) and Tishrei (for fixing the festivals), since if they already go out for Elul, what need is there for Tishrei?

The Gemara considers the possibility that Elul might be intercalated (made a full month of 30 days), but Rabbi Chinana bar Kahana in the name of Rav states that since Ezra's time, Elul has never been found to be intercalated.
The Gemara resolves that 'we have not found' means it was never needed, but if needed, we would indeed intercalate Elul.
The Gemara objects that intercalating Elul would disrupt Rosh Hashanah, but answers that it is better to disrupt Rosh Hashanah than to disrupt all the festivals.
The Gemara provides supporting evidence from the Mishnah's wording 'for Tishrei due to fixing the festivals,' implying that the concern is for all festivals, not just Rosh Hashanah.

items.text: Missing clause about Adar Sheni in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Missing clause about Adar Sheni in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions going out for Kislev (Hanukkah) and Adar (Purim) but not for a second Adar in a leap year. The Gemara notes this excludes Rabbi's opinion, who holds that in a leap year messengers go out for Adar Sheni.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah lists going out for Kislev and Adar but does not include a clause for Adar Sheni in a leap year.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah follows the view of the Sages, not Rabbi, who holds that messengers do go out for Adar Sheni.

items.text: Dispute about the intercalation of Adar
items.text_en: Dispute about the intercalation of Adar
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests the dispute is about whether Purim practices apply to the first Adar. It then clarifies that all agree they do not, and the real dispute is about the length of the intercalated month: thirty days (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) or a full month (the first opinion). Rav Pappa explains that 'month' means either a full month or thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute in the Mishnah is about whether the Purim practices of the second Adar apply also to the first Adar.
The Gemara rejects this, stating that all agree the first Adar does not take on Purim practices, and the real dispute is about the intercalation of the year.
A baraita is cited: the intercalation period is thirty days, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says it is a full month.
The Gemara questions the distinction between thirty days and a month, since both are known quantities.
Rav Pappa explains that the one who says 'month' means either a full month or thirty days, as the term is flexible.

items.text: Testimony about sanctifying the two Adars
items.text_en: Testimony about sanctifying the two Adars
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi testifies that the two Adars are sanctified on their intercalation day, implying they are deficient. Rabbi Simai testifies that they can be both full, both deficient, or one full and one deficient, as practiced in the diaspora. Mar Ukva rules that the Adar adjacent to Nisan is always deficient. Rav Nachman challenges this from the Mishnah about sanctifying Nisan and Tishrei, which implies they vary.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi testifies that the two Adars are sanctified on their intercalation day, implying they are deficient.
The gemara questions whether this testimony means the Adars are always made deficient, never full.
The gemara explains that the testimony only excludes the view of Rav Nachman bar Chisda, not that full Adars are impossible.
Rabbi Simai testifies that the two Adars can be both full, both deficient, or one full and one deficient, as practiced in the diaspora.
Our rabbis rule that one Adar is always full and the other deficient, until the new moon is established in its proper time.
Mar Ukva rules that the Adar adjacent to Nisan is always deficient.
Rav Nachman challenges Mar Ukva from the Mishnah about sanctifying Nisan and Tishrei, which implies they vary between full and deficient.

items.text: Rav Nachman's proof and the Gemara's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's proof and the Gemara's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a mishnah that only Nisan and Tishrei are desecrated for the new month, implying that these months are always חָסֵר, so that the thirtieth day is the new moon and one must sanctify it on that day. The Gemara objects that if months could be either מָלֵא or חָסֵר, one could simply wait until the next day. It answers that the case is when the thirty-first day falls on Shabbat, so the mitzvah to sanctify on the day of sighting requires desecrating Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If Adar is always short, why desecrate Shabbat for Nisan's new moon?
The Gemara answers: Because it is a mitzva to sanctify based on actual sighting.
Rav Nachman cites a mishnah that only Nisan and Tishrei are desecrated, supporting that Adar is always short.
The Gemara objects: If Adar varies, why not just add a day and sanctify tomorrow?
The Gemara resolves: If the 30th falls on Shabbat, that works; but here the 31st falls on Shabbat, so desecration is needed.

items.text: Rav Kahana's objection and the refutation
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection and the refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges the assumption that Nisan and Tishrei are special because of the mitzvah to sanctify on sight, citing a baraita that when the Temple stood, all months were desecrated for the sake of the sacrifice. The Gemara concludes that this proves the months are sometimes מָלֵא and sometimes חָסֵר, and that the view that they are always חָסֵר is refuted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects by citing a baraita that when the Temple stood, witnesses desecrated Shabbat for all months due to the sacrifice, not because of the mitzvah to sanctify on sight.

sub.text: Gemara's inference from Rav Kahana's objection
sub.text_en: Gemara's inference from Rav Kahana's objection
sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that since for all other months the reason is not the mitzvah to sanctify on sight, the same must apply to Nisan and Tishrei.
The Gemara concludes that the view that Adar is always short is refuted, and the months must be sometimes full and sometimes short.

items.text: Ulla's report and the reasons for intercalating Elul
items.text_en: Ulla's report and the reasons for intercalating Elul
items.desc_en: Ulla reports that the court intercalated Elul (added a day to the month). He praises the Babylonian sages for understanding the benefit. Two reasons are given: Ulla says it was for the sake of vegetables (יַרְקַיָּא), and Rabbi Acha bar Chanina says it was for the sake of the dead (מִתַיָּא). The Gemara explores the practical difference between these reasons, discussing cases like Yom Kippur after Shabbat or a festival adjacent to Shabbat, and concludes that for us (Babylonians) the world is dear, so we intercalate, but for them (in Israel) it is not.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that the court intercalated Elul and asks if the Babylonian sages understand the benefit.
The Gemara asks what the benefit is; Ulla says it is for vegetables, and Rabbi Acha bar Chanina says it is for the dead.
The Gemara asks the practical difference between the two reasons and analyzes the case of Yom Kippur after Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that even according to the vegetable reason, one should intercalate for the dead, then refines the difference to a festival adjacent to Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that even according to the dead reason, one should intercalate for vegetables, and answers that soaking in hot water restores freshness.
The Gemara asks why the benefit is specific to Babylonia, and answers that for us the world is hot, but for them it is not.
The Gemara objects with a baraita from Rabba bar Shmuel that one might think a month can be intercalated for need, but the verse limits it.

items.text: The distinction between intercalating and sanctifying the month
items.text_en: The distinction between intercalating and sanctifying the month
items.desc_en: Rava resolves a contradiction between a baraita of Rabbah bar Shmuel, which says the month cannot be intercalated for need, and the practice of intercalating Elul. He explains that the baraita refers to sanctifying the month (קִדּוּשׁ), not intercalating (עִבּוּר). Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi supports this: witnesses are pressured to intercalate a month seen on time, but not to sanctify a month not seen on time.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between intercalating the month (עִבּוּר) and sanctifying it (קִדּוּשׁ), explaining that the baraita prohibits sanctifying early for need, not intercalating.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi supports Rava's distinction: witnesses may be pressured to intercalate a month seen on time, but not to sanctify a month not seen on time.

items.text: Contradiction from Rabbi Yochanan's teaching and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction from Rabbi Yochanan's teaching and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: A letter from Rabbi Yehudah Nesi'ah quotes Rabbi Yochanan as saying that witnesses are pressured to sanctify a month not seen on time, even to lie. Abaye resolves the contradiction with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi by distinguishing between Nisan/Tishrei (where pressure is applied to sanctify) and other months (where pressure is applied to intercalate).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that witnesses are pressured to sanctify a month not seen on time, even to falsely claim they saw it.
Abaye resolves that the dispute depends on the month: for Nisan and Tishrei one pressures to sanctify, for other months one pressures to intercalate.

items.text: Rava's alternative resolution and Rav Dimi's version
items.text_en: Rava's alternative resolution and Rav Dimi's version
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different resolution: the baraita of Rabbah bar Shmuel follows the opinion of Acheirim, who hold that the interval between festivals is fixed, implying no intercalation for need. Rav Dimi from Nehardea teaches the opposite version of the ruling about pressuring witnesses, and the Gemara begins to explain the reason.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by attributing the baraita of Rabbah bar Shmuel to the opinion of Acheirim, who hold that the interval between festivals is fixed, implying no intercalation for need.
Rava cites the baraita of Acheirim that the interval between festivals is fixed, supporting his attribution.
Rav Dimi from Nehardea teaches the opposite version of the ruling about pressuring witnesses.
The Gemara begins to ask for the reason behind Rav Dimi's version.

items.text: Opening distinction between two scenarios
items.text_en: Opening distinction between two scenarios
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts two cases: one where the new moon's appearance would appear false, and one where it would not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by contrasting two scenarios: one where the new moon's appearance would appear false, and one where it would not.

items.text: Shmuel's claim and Abba's challenge
items.text_en: Shmuel's claim and Abba's challenge
items.desc_en: Shmuel claims he can fix the calendar for the entire diaspora. Abba, father of Rabbi Simlai, questions him about a tradition from the secret of intercalation regarding whether the molad occurred before or after noon, and Shmuel admits ignorance.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel asserts that he can fix the calendar for the entire diaspora.
Abba, father of Rabbi Simlai, asks Shmuel whether he knows the tradition from the secret of intercalation about whether the molad occurred before or after noon.
Shmuel admits he does not know that tradition.
Abba challenges Shmuel that if he does not know this, there are other matters he does not know, undermining his claim to fix the calendar.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's ruling and the calculation of the molad
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's ruling and the calculation of the molad
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira sends a ruling that there must be a night and a day from the new moon. Abba's tradition is explained: one calculates the molad; if it occurred before noon, the moon is visible near sunset; if after noon, it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira sends a ruling that there must be a night and a day from the new moon before the month is sanctified.

sub.text: Abba the father of Rabbi Simlai's tradition
sub.text_en: Abba the father of Rabbi Simlai's tradition
sub.desc_en: Abba's tradition is explained: one calculates the molad; if it occurred before noon, the moon is visible near sunset; if after noon, it is not.

items.text: Practical application: discrediting witnesses
items.text_en: Practical application: discrediting witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the calculation of the molad is used to discredit witnesses who claim to have seen the new moon at a time when it was impossible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference emerges from the calculation of the molad (the moon's birth).
Rav Ashi answers that the calculation is used to discredit witnesses who claim to have seen the new moon at an impossible time.

items.text: Twenty-four hour period of moon concealment
items.text_en: Twenty-four hour period of moon concealment
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that the moon is concealed for twenty-four hours each month: for us (in Babylonia) six from the old moon and eighteen from the new; for them (in Israel) six from the new and eighteen from the old. Rav Ashi again applies this to discrediting witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that the moon is concealed for twenty-four hours each month, with the distribution differing between Babylonia and Israel.
Rav Ashi applies this rule to discredit witnesses who claim to have seen the new moon at a time when it was concealed.

items.text: Source for the requirement of a night and a day
items.text_en: Source for the requirement of a night and a day
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the biblical source for the requirement that the new moon be visible for a night and a day. Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish offer different verses. Abaye and Rava debate the practical difference between their views: whether it is a matter of interpreting the verses or whether midnight is the cutoff.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that a night and a day must pass from the new moon and asks for its biblical source.
Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'מֵעֶרֶב עַד עֶרֶב' (from evening to evening) as the source.
Resh Lakish cites the verse 'עַד יוֹם הָאֶחָד וְעֶשְׂרִים לַחֹדֶשׁ בָּעָרֶב' (until the twenty-first day of the month in the evening) as the source.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two verses.
Abaye says the difference lies in the method of interpreting the verses (משמעות דורשין).
Rava says the difference is whether midnight (חצות לילה) is the cutoff point.

items.text: Ruling for a doubtful case and the possibility of a deficient month
items.text_en: Ruling for a doubtful case and the possibility of a deficient month
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that in a case of doubt, we postpone the festival to the sixteenth, not the fifteenth. The Gemara questions why we do not also observe the fourteenth, due to the possibility that both Av and Elul were deficient months.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that in a doubtful case regarding the new moon, we postpone the festival to the sixteenth, not the fifteenth, and we do not observe the fourteenth.
The Gemara questions why we do not also observe the fourteenth, given the possibility that both Av and Elul were deficient months, which would shift the calendar.

items.text: Opening statement about months that are deficient
items.text_en: Opening statement about months that are deficient
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that two deficient months (Cheshvan and Kislev) have a 'voice' (i.e., their deficiency is known). This sets the stage for the discussion about the calendar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that two deficient months (Cheshvan and Kislev) have a 'voice' (their deficiency is known).

items.text: Levi's arrival in Babylonia on the eleventh of Tishrei
items.text_en: Levi's arrival in Babylonia on the eleventh of Tishrei
items.desc_en: Levi arrived in Babylonia on the eleventh of Tishrei and commented that the Babylonian stew was good on the 'great day' of the West (Yom Kippur). They asked him to testify, but he said he did not hear the court declare it sanctified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story: Levi arrived in Babylonia on the eleventh of Tishrei.
Levi remarks that the Babylonian stew is good on the 'great day' of the West (Yom Kippur).
The Babylonians challenge Levi to testify that the day is indeed Yom Kippur.
Levi responds that he did not hear the declaration 'Mekudash' (sanctified) from the court, so he cannot testify.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's decree to observe two days
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's decree to observe two days
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan proclaimed that wherever the messengers of Nisan arrived but those of Tishrei did not, they should observe two days, as a decree for Nisan due to Tishrei.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan proclaims that wherever the messengers of Nisan have arrived but those of Tishrei have not, they should observe two days.
Rabbi Yochanan explains the reason: a decree lest Nisan be confused with Tishrei.

items.text: Rabbi Aiyvu and Rabbi Chiyya's incident and Rabbi Yochanan's anger
items.text_en: Rabbi Aiyvu and Rabbi Chiyya's incident and Rabbi Yochanan's anger
items.desc_en: Rabbi Aiyvu bar Nagarei and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba came to a place where the messengers of Nisan arrived but not those of Tishrei, and they observed only one day. Rabbi Yochanan heard and was angry, reiterating his decree.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Ayvu bar Nagarei and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Ayvu bar Nagarei and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rabbi Ayvu bar Nagarei and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba arrived at a place where the Nisan messengers had come but the Tishrei messengers had not.
They observed only one day (of Rosh Hashanah), contrary to Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.
Rabbi Yochanan heard about this and became angry.
Rabbi Yochanan rebukes them, reiterating his ruling that they should have observed two days due to the decree.

items.text: Rava's custom of fasting two days
items.text_en: Rava's custom of fasting two days
items.desc_en: Rava was accustomed to fasting two days (for Yom Kippur), and once it happened that the fast coincided with the correct day.

sub.desc_en: Rava was accustomed to fasting for two days (for Yom Kippur due to uncertainty).
Once it happened that the correct day coincided with his second fast day.

items.text: Rav Nachman's fast and the traveler's news
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's fast and the traveler's news
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman fasted all of Yom Kippur. In the evening, a man came and told him that the next day was the 'great day' in the West. Rav Nachman asked where he was from, and upon hearing 'Dimharya', he cursed him, saying his end would be blood, and applied the verse 'Our pursuers were swifter'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman fasted all of Yom Kippur, and in the evening a man told him that the next day was the 'great day' in the West.
Rav Nachman asked the man's origin, cursed him upon hearing 'Dimharya', and applied the verse 'Our pursuers were swifter'.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Avin's instruction about intercalation
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Avin's instruction about intercalation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Avin sent to Rava: If you see that the Tevet solstice extends until the sixteenth of Nisan, intercalate that year and do not hesitate, as it is written 'Guard the month of spring' — guard that the spring of the solstice be in the month of Nisan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman said to those who go down to the sea (sailors).
He instructs: since you do not know the fixed calendar, when you see the moon completing its cycle during the day, burn the leaven (chametz).

items.text: Rav Nachman's advice to sailors about leavened bread
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's advice to sailors about leavened bread
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman told sailors who do not know the fixed calendar: When you see the moon completing on the day (i.e., the fifteenth), remove leavened bread. They questioned this, as they remove it from the fourteenth, but he explained that for them, who are at sea, the moon completes on the fourteenth.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman instructs sailors who do not know the fixed calendar that when they see the moon completing on the day (i.e., the fifteenth), they should remove leavened bread.
The sailors question Rav Nachman: the moon completes on the fifteenth, but they remove leavened bread from the fourteenth.
Rav Nachman explains that for them, who are at sea, the moon completes on the fourteenth, so their removal of leavened bread aligns with the correct date.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Shabbat is desecrated only for the months of Nisan and Tishrei, because messengers go out to Syria and the festivals are set. When the Temple stood, all months were desecrated due to the sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Shabbat is desecrated only for Nisan and Tishrei due to messengers and festivals, but when the Temple stood, all months were desecrated for the sacrifice.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's limitation to two months, citing a baraita that messengers go out for six months. Abaye resolves that messengers go out for all months in advance, but only for Nisan and Tishrei do they wait to hear the court's declaration of sanctification. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's limitation to two months, citing a contradictory baraita that messengers go out for six months.
Abaye resolves that messengers go out for all months in advance, but only for Nisan and Tishrei do they wait to hear the court's declaration of sanctification.
A baraita is cited in support of Abaye's resolution, repeating the same distinction.

items.text: Scriptural derivation for desecrating Shabbat
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation for desecrating Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'These are the appointed times of the Lord' that Shabbat is desecrated for sanctification. It limits this to the act of sanctification, not the subsequent confirmation, based on the phrase 'which you shall proclaim.'

sub.desc_en: The rabbis derive from the verse 'אלה מועדי ה (these are the festivals of the Lord)' that Shabbat is desecrated for sanctification but not for confirmation of the month.

The baraita opens by asking for the scriptural source permitting desecration of Shabbat for sanctifying the new month, and cites the verse 'אֵלֶּה מוֹעֲדֵי ה׳' (These are the appointed times of the Lord).
The baraita limits the desecration to the act of sanctification (קריאה), not to the subsequent confirmation (קיום), based on the phrase 'אשר תקראו אותם'.

The baraita limits the permission: one may desecrate Shabbat only for the act of sanctification (קְרִיאָתָם), not for the subsequent confirmation (קִיּוּמָן), based on the phrase 'אֲשֶׁר תִּקְרְאוּ אוֹתָם' (which you shall proclaim).

items.text: Enactment after Temple destruction
items.text_en: Enactment after Temple destruction
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that initially all months were desecrated, but after the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that only Nisan and Tishrei are desecrated, since there is no sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that originally all months were desecrated, but after the Temple's destruction Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai restricted it to Nisan and Tishrei since there was no sacrifice.
A baraita recounts that originally they desecrated for all months, but after the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai restricted it to Nisan and Tishrei only.

items.text: Dispute about visibility and a precedent
items.text_en: Dispute about visibility and a precedent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Shabbat is desecrated whether the moon was seen clearly or not, but Rabbi Yossi disagrees if it was clearly visible. A story is told of Rabbi Akiva delaying witnesses, and Rabban Gamliel warns him against causing future stumbling.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Shabbat is desecrated for the new moon whether it was clearly visible or not.
Rabbi Yossi objects that if the moon was clearly visible, Shabbat is not desecrated.
A story is told of Rabbi Akiva delaying witnesses in Lod, and Rabban Gamliel warns him that delaying the many will cause future stumbling.

items.text: Meaning of 'ba'alil'
items.text_en: Meaning of 'ba'alil'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that 'ba'alil' means 'clearly visible,' and Rabbi Abahu cites a verse from Psalms where 'ba'alil' refers to refined silver, implying clarity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that 'עליל (alil)' means 'clearly visible', and Rabbi Abahu cites a verse where 'בעליל (ba'alil)' means 'refined and revealed'.
Rabbi Avahu cites a verse (Psalms 12:7) where 'בעליל' means 'refined' or 'clearly', proving the meaning.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel on Solomon's wisdom
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel on Solomon's wisdom
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute: one says Moses lacked one of fifty gates of understanding, and Solomon sought to equal him but was told no prophet like Moses arose. The other says Solomon surpassed kings but not prophets, and sought to judge based on inner thoughts without witnesses, but was rebuked by a bat kol citing the requirement of two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that fifty gates of understanding were created, all given to Moses except one, as per the verse 'ותחסרהו מעט מאלהים' (You made him lack a little from God).
Rav explains that Solomon (Kohelet) sought to equal Moses, but a bat kol (heavenly voice) rebuked him, citing the verse 'ולא קם נביא עוד בישראל כמשה' (no prophet arose in Israel like Moses).

Shmuel argues that Solomon surpassed kings but not prophets, and sought to judge based on inner thoughts without witnesses or warning, but a bat kol rebuked him, citing the requirement of two witnesses (על פי שני עדים).

items.text: Opening story about Rabbi Akiva and the witnesses
items.text_en: Opening story about Rabbi Akiva and the witnesses
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Yehuda objects to the mishnah's claim that Rabbi Akiva held back more than forty pairs of witnesses, explaining that it was actually a certain person named Shazpar who was held back, and Rabban Gamliel had him removed from his position.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Yehuda objects to the mishnah's claim that Rabbi Akiva held back more than forty pairs of witnesses, explaining that it was actually Shazpar who was held back, and Rabban Gamliel had him removed from his position.

items.text: Mishnah: Relatives as witnesses for the new moon
items.text_en: Mishnah: Relatives as witnesses for the new moon
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that a father and son who saw the new moon may both go to testify, not to join together but in case one is disqualified. Rabbi Shimon permits all relatives. Rabbi Yosei brings a story about Toviya the doctor, his son, and his freed slave, where the priests accepted the father and son but rejected the slave, while the court accepted the father and slave but rejected the son.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that a father and son who saw the new moon may both go to testify, not to join together but in case one is disqualified.
Rabbi Shimon permits all relatives, including father and son, as witnesses for the new moon.

Rabbi Yosei brings a story about Toviya the doctor, his son, and his freed slave, where the priests accepted the father and son but rejected the slave, while the court accepted the father and slave but rejected the son.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's proof and the Sages' response
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's proof and the Sages' response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning from the verse 'This month shall be for you' – this testimony shall be valid among you, implying relatives are fit. The Sages interpret the verse differently: this testimony shall be entrusted to you, meaning only to those fit to judge.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi asks what is Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and answers by citing the verse 'הַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה לָכֶם' (This month shall be for you), interpreting it to mean that this testimony shall be valid among you, thus relatives are fit.
The Sages respond by interpreting the same verse differently: 'עֵדוּת זוֹ תְּהֵא מְסוּרָה לָכֶם' (this testimony shall be entrusted to you), meaning only to those fit to judge, excluding relatives.

items.text: Halakhic ruling in favor of Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling in favor of Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava rules the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon. Rav Huna challenges him based on Rabbi Yosei's story. Rav Chanan explains he had taught the mishnah in reverse order before Rav, and Rav Huna accepts this. Finally, Mar Ukva quotes Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava rules the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon; Rav Huna objects, citing Rabbi Yosei's precedent that seems to contradict this ruling.
Rav Chanan bar Rava rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Huna challenges Rav Chanan bar Rava, pointing out that Rabbi Yosei's story contradicts the ruling in favor of Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Chanan bar Rava explains that he had taught the mishnah in reverse order before Rav, and Rav Huna accepts this explanation.
Mar Ukva quotes Shmuel that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon, resolving the discussion.

items.text: Mishnah: Those disqualified from testifying
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those disqualified from testifying
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists those disqualified: dice players, lenders with interest, pigeon racers, traders in shemittah produce, and slaves. The general rule is that any testimony for which a woman is unfit, these are also unfit.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists those disqualified from testifying about the new moon: dice players, lenders on interest, pigeon racers, traders in shemittah produce, and slaves; the general rule is that any testimony for which a woman is unfit, these are also unfit.
The mishnah lists those disqualified from testifying about the new moon: dice players, lenders with interest, pigeon racers, traders in shemittah produce, and slaves.
The mishnah states the general rule: any testimony for which a woman is unfit, these disqualified individuals are also unfit.
The Mishnah states the general rule: wherever a woman is disqualified from testifying, these people likewise are disqualified.

items.text: Gemara: Inference about a rabbinic robber
items.text_en: Gemara: Inference about a rabbinic robber
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi infers from the mishnah's general rule that a robber by rabbinic law is fit to testify about a woman's status, since a woman is fit for that testimony.

sub.desc_en: The gemara infers from the mishnah's rule that if a woman is fit for a testimony, these disqualified individuals are also fit.
Rav Ashi concludes that this implies a robber by rabbinic decree (not Torah law) is fit to testify about a woman's status.

items.text: Mishnah: Transporting witnesses on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Transporting witnesses on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The mishnah discusses how to bring a witness who cannot walk: they carry him on a donkey or even a bed. If there is an ambush, they may take sticks. For a distant journey, they take provisions. They may desecrate Shabbat for a day and night's travel to testify about the new moon, based on the verse 'These are the appointed times of the Lord.'

sub.desc_en: The mishnah details how one who saw the new moon but cannot walk is transported on a donkey or bed; if ambushed, they may carry sticks; for a journey of a day and night, they may desecrate Shabbat to testify, based on the verse 'אֵלֶּה מוֹעֲדֵי ה׳'.
The mishnah adds that if there is an ambush, they may take sticks, and for a distant journey they take provisions.

The mishnah concludes that for a journey of a day and a night, they may desecrate Shabbat to testify about the new moon, citing the verse 'אלה מועדי ה׳ אשר תקראו אותם במועדם' (These are the appointed times of the Lord).

items.text: Mishnah: Sending an escort and the Boethusian decree
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sending an escort and the Boethusian decree
items.desc_en: If the court does not recognize the witness, they send another person to testify for him. Originally they accepted testimony from anyone, but after the Boethusians corrupted the process, they instituted that only those known to the court may testify.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the court does not recognize the witness, they send another person to testify for him.
The Mishnah explains that originally they accepted testimony from anyone, but after the Boethusians corrupted the process, they instituted that only those known to the court may testify.
The Gemara asks: what does 'another' mean? It means one additional person.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'another'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'another'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'another' means and answers: one person.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks what 'another' means in the mishnah, and answers: one additional person.
The Gemara answers that 'another' means one additional person.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'another' witness
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'another' witness
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a single witness is reliable, citing a case where a witness came with his fellow witnesses. Rav Pappa explains that 'another' refers to another pair, and the Gemara supports this by comparing to the Mishnah's phrase 'if they do not recognize him'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a single witness is reliable, citing a baraita where a witness came with his fellow witnesses.
Rav Pappa explains that 'another' in the Mishnah refers to another pair of witnesses, not a single individual.
The Gemara supports Rav Pappa by arguing that the Mishnah's phrase 'if they do not recognize him' must refer to a pair, not an individual, since a single witness is not reliable for testimony.

items.text: The case of Rabbi Nehorai and the single witness
items.text_en: The case of Rabbi Nehorai and the single witness
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another challenge: a story where Rabbi Nehorai went to testify alone on Shabbat. The answer is that another witness was with him, but not mentioned due to respect for Rabbi Nehorai, or that the other witness was already in Usha. The Gemara concludes that this teaches that we do not desecrate Shabbat for a doubtful case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a single witness is indeed unreliable, citing a baraita where Rabbi Nehorai went to a witness on Shabbat in Usha.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Nehorai had another witness with him, but the baraita omitted mention of the other witness out of respect for Rabbi Nehorai.
Rav Ashi explains that Rabbi Nehorai went to join another witness already in Usha, so he was not acting alone.
The Gemara asks why the baraita is necessary if Rabbi Nehorai was merely joining another witness.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita teaches that even a ספק (doubt) about the new moon justifies desecrating Shabbat, contrary to what one might think.

items.text: Ulla's statement and the principle of public knowledge
items.text_en: Ulla's statement and the principle of public knowledge
items.desc_en: Ulla reports that the new month was sanctified in the West. Rav Kahana says that not only Ulla, but any person is believed because anything destined to become public knowledge is not lied about. A baraita supports this: if one says the court sanctified the month, he is believed.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that in the West (Eretz Yisrael), they sanctified the new month based on a single witness.
Rav Kahana explains that Ulla is reliable because he is a great man, but even an ordinary person is believed because anything destined to be revealed is not lied about.
A baraita supports the principle that a single witness is believed for the new month because the matter will become known.

items.text: The Boethusian deception and the enactment
items.text_en: The Boethusian deception and the enactment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that originally testimony was accepted from anyone, but after the Boethusians corrupted it, they enacted to accept only from those who are known. The Gemara recounts how the Boethusians hired two witnesses to deceive the Sages, but the Jewish witness revealed the plot. Consequently, they instituted that only those who are familiar are accepted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the story of the Boethusians who hired two witnesses to deceive the Sages.
The Boethusian witness testified and left.
The Jewish witness describes in detail how he saw the new moon, including the bribe he was offered.

sub.text: Narrative: the Sages' question and the witness's explanation
sub.text_en: Narrative: the Sages' question and the witness's explanation
sub.desc_en: The Sages ask why he came, and the witness explains he feared unworthy people might deceive them.

sub.text: Narrative: the Sages' response and enactment
sub.text_en: Narrative: the Sages' response and enactment
sub.desc_en: The Sages reward the witness and enact that only those who are known (to the court) may testify about the new month.

items.text: Mishnah: Signal fires and their replacement
items.text_en: Mishnah: Signal fires and their replacement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that originally they would light signal fires to announce the new month, but after the Samaritans corrupted this, they instituted that messengers go out. It details the process of lighting fires from mount to mount, and the chain of mountains used.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that originally they would light signal fires, but after the Samaritans corrupted this, they instituted that messengers go out.
The Mishnah details the method of lighting signal fires using long cedar poles, reeds, olive wood, and flax tow, and the relay from mount to mount.
The Mishnah lists the chain of mountains from the Mount of Olives to Sartaba, Grofina, Hauran, Beit Biltin, and beyond, where the signal was visible to the entire diaspora.

items.text: Gemara on the meaning of 'mas'uin' and the timing of fires
items.text_en: Gemara on the meaning of 'mas'uin' and the timing of fires
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that 'mas'uin' means lighting, citing a verse and its Aramaic translation. A baraita states that fires are only lit for a month seen on time, and only on the night of its intercalation. Rabbi Zeira explains the reason: a decree lest a deficient month fall on Shabbat eve, causing people to mistakenly light fires on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that 'משיאין' (mas'uin) means lighting a fire.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וישאום דוד ואנשיו' (and David and his men carried them up) and its Aramaic translation 'ואוקדינון דוד' (and David burned them), proving that the root נש

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the potential for error in signaling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the potential for error in signaling
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether people might mistake a deficient month for a full one due to the timing of the bonfires, and whether they might think the lack of a fire was due to unavoidable circumstances rather than the month being deficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: people might mistake a deficient month for a full one, thinking the lack of a fire was due to impossibility, or they might think it was full and the fire was lit on time.

The Gemara proposes a solution: light fires for both a full and deficient month, but not on Shabbat eve; since they don't light on Saturday night but do for a full month, people will know it is deficient.
The Gemara objects that even so, people might err, thinking the month is full and the lack of fire was due to unavoidable circumstances.
The Gemara asks: why not simply light for a full month and never for a deficient one?
Abaye answers that this would cause a loss of work for the people for two days (if the month is deficient, they would have to refrain from work on both the thirtieth and thirty-first).

items.text: Abaye's explanation for not signaling only for a full month
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation for not signaling only for a full month
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that if they only signaled for a full month, people would refrain from work for two days, causing a loss of labor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah describing how they would signal with bonfires, bringing long poles.
Rav Yehuda lists four types of cedar used for the poles, with further identifications by Rav and the school of Rabbi Sheila.

items.text: Discussion of the types of cedars used for bonfires
items.text_en: Discussion of the types of cedars used for bonfires
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the four types of cedars according to Rav Yehuda, and then expands to ten types according to the school of Rav, with identifications of each tree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's description of how bonfires were lit.
Rav Yehuda lists four types of cedars used for the bonfires.

sub.text: Rav and School of Rabbi Sheila
sub.text_en: Rav and School of Rabbi Sheila
sub.desc_en: Rav identifies קתרום as אדרא, while the school of Rabbi Sheila identifies it as מבליגא, also called גולמיש.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing the school of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing the school of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna cites the school of Rav, which lists ten types of cedars from a verse and identifies each tree.
The Gemara notes that the verse lists only seven types, not ten.
Rav Dimi explains that three additional types were added: אלונים, אלמונים, and אלמוגין, and identifies each.
An alternative tradition lists the three additional types as ארונים, ערמונים, and אלמוגין, with different identifications.

items.text: Description of the transport of the ship and the types of wood
items.text_en: Description of the transport of the ship and the types of wood
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how a large ship was transported using thousands of men and ropes made of flax, and then lists the three types of wood (parvota) used for the ship.

sub.desc_en: Rav interprets the verse 'וְצִי אַדִּיר לֹא יַעַבְרֶנּוּ' as referring to a large ship (בורני גדולה).

sub.text: Gemara's description of the ship's transport
sub.text_en: Gemara's description of the ship's transport
sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes how the large ship was transported: thousands of men over months, using ropes of flax and a system of pulling and moving.

sub.text: Gemara's description of the types of wood
sub.text_en: Gemara's description of the types of wood
sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists the three types of wood (פַּרְווֹתָא) used for the ship: two from Rome and one from Persia, with their respective cargoes.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's homilies on the restoration of Jerusalem and the fate of the nations
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's homilies on the restoration of Jerusalem and the fate of the nations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will restore every tree taken from Jerusalem, and compares a Torah scholar who does not teach to a myrtle in the desert. He also laments that the nations have no remedy for their persecution of the righteous.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that God will restore every tree taken from Jerusalem, citing a verse that equates 'midbar' (desert) with Jerusalem.
Rabbi Yochanan compares a Torah scholar who does not teach to a myrtle in the desert, with an alternative version praising one who teaches where there are no scholars.
Rabbi Yochanan laments that the nations have no remedy for their persecution of the righteous, citing a verse that implies their blood will not be cleansed.

items.text: Question about the location Beit Biltin
items.text_en: Question about the location Beit Biltin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the meaning of Beit Biltin, a place mentioned in the Mishnah, and begins to provide an answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the meaning of the place name 'Beit Biltin' mentioned in the Mishnah.
Rav begins to provide an answer regarding the identity of Beit Biltin.

items.text: Explanation of the beacons' locations
items.text_en: Explanation of the beacons' locations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the names of the beacon locations mentioned in the Mishnah. Rav Yosef identifies 'Golah' as Pumbedita, and a Tanna describes how each person would take a torch and go up to their roof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the place name 'Golah' refers to.
Rav Yosef identifies 'Golah' as Pumbedita.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'like a bonfire' means.
A Tanna explains that each person would take a torch and go up to his roof.

items.text: Dispute about additional locations
items.text_en: Dispute about additional locations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds other locations to the list. There is a dispute about whether these locations were between the beacons or on the other side of Eretz Yisrael, with each authority counting a different side.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds the locations Charim, Kiyar, Gador, and their companions to the list of beacon sites.
The gemara presents a dispute: some say these locations were situated between the beacons.
