items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita that explicitly states that both the listener and the blower must intend, and the blower is analogous to the listener—just as the listener intends for himself, so too the blower must intend for himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: if the listener intended but the blower did not, or vice versa, one does not fulfill the obligation, requiring both to intend, which contradicts Rav's position.

items.text: Resolution: it is a dispute among Tannaim
items.text_en: Resolution: it is a dispute among Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute among Tannaim, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between a public emissary and an individual, and the first baraita follows the lenient opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that it is a dispute among Tannaim: one baraita permits the blower to blow for himself without intention, while Rabbi Yosei requires both to intend for an individual but not for a community emissary.

items.text: Mishnah: looking upward in battle and healing
items.text_en: Mishnah: looking upward in battle and healing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites verses about Moses raising his hands and the copper serpent, teaching that when Israel looks upward and subjugates their hearts to their Father in heaven, they prevail or are healed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites two biblical examples (Moses' hands in battle and the copper serpent) to teach that Israel's victory or healing depends on directing their hearts to their Father in Heaven.
The Mishnah provides a parallel example of the copper serpent, teaching that healing likewise depends on looking upward and subjugating the heart to God.

items.text: Mishnah: deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor cannot exempt the public
items.text_en: Mishnah: deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor cannot exempt the public
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor cannot fulfill the obligation for the public, and gives the general rule: one who is not obligated in a matter cannot exempt the public.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor cannot fulfill the obligation for the public, establishing the principle that one not obligated cannot exempt others.

items.text: Baraita: who is obligated and who can exempt others
items.text_en: Baraita: who is obligated and who can exempt others
items.desc_en: A baraita lists all who are obligated in shofar blowing, including priests, Levites, Israelites, converts, freed slaves, a tumtum, an androgynos, and a half-slave half-free person, and then details who can exempt whom.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing all who are obligated in shofar blowing: priests, Levites, Israelites, converts, freed slaves, a tumtum, an androgynos, and a half-slave half-free person.
The baraita specifies the exemption rules: a tumtum cannot exempt anyone, an androgynos can exempt its own kind but not others, and a half-slave half-free person cannot exempt anyone.

items.text: Gemara: why mention priests?
items.text_en: Gemara: why mention priests?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to mention priests, Levites, and Israelites, as they are obviously obligated, and explains that it was necessary to counter a possible assumption that priests might be exempt due to their involvement in trumpeting throughout the year or because they are not obligated in the Jubilee year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to list priests, Levites, and Israelites, since their obligation is obvious.
The Gemara answers that the baraita needed to include priests, lest one think they are exempt because they are already involved in trumpeting throughout the year.

items.text: Dispute about a half-slave half-free person exempting himself
items.text_en: Dispute about a half-slave half-free person exempting himself
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says a half-slave half-free person can exempt himself, but Rav Nachman objects that the slave side cannot exempt the free side, and a baraita supports Rav Nachman that he cannot even exempt himself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a half-slave half-free person can exempt himself from the shofar obligation.
Rav Nachman objects that just as the slave side cannot exempt others, it cannot exempt the free side of the same person.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and baraita support
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and baraita support
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the half-slave half-free person cannot even exempt himself, and a baraita supports this position.

items.text: Baraita: general rule for blessings
items.text_en: Baraita: general rule for blessings
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by Ahavah son of Rabbi Zeira states that for all blessings, one who has already fulfilled the obligation can still exempt others, except for the blessing over bread and wine, where only one who has not fulfilled can exempt others.

sub.desc_en: Ahavah son of Rabbi Zeira teaches a baraita: for all blessings, one who already fulfilled the obligation can still exempt others, except for the blessing over bread and wine, where one who already fulfilled cannot exempt others.

items.text: Rava's question
items.text_en: Rava's question
items.desc_en: Rava raises a question, which is left unresolved at the end of the amud.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a question (the content is cut off in the source).

items.text: Question about blessing for matzah and wine
items.text_en: Question about blessing for matzah and wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if one has already eaten matzah or recited kiddush, can he recite the blessing for others? The issue is whether the blessing is a mandatory obligation (חובה) or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the blessing for matzah and the wine of kiddush is a mandatory obligation (חובה) such that one who has already fulfilled it can still discharge others, or whether it is not an obligation.

items.text: Proof from Rav Ashi and Baraita
items.text_en: Proof from Rav Ashi and Baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi testifies that Rav Pappi would recite kiddush for his sharecropper, implying one can bless for others. A baraita states that while one should not break bread for guests unless eating with them, he may do so for his children to train them, and for Hallel and Megillah even if he already fulfilled the obligation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi testifies that Rav Pappi would recite kiddush for them and for his sharecropper, implying one can bless for others even after fulfilling one's own obligation.

A baraita rules that while one should not break bread for guests unless eating with them, one may do so for his children to train them, and for Hallel and Megillah even if he already fulfilled the obligation, supporting the principle that one can bless for others.

items.text: Conclusion of chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing formula for the chapter is stated: 'We return to you, [chapter] 'They saw it, the court...'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the conclusion of the previous chapter with the formula 'we return to you, 'They saw the court'.'

items.text: Mishnah: Shofar on Shabbat and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shofar on Shabbat and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, shofar was blown only in the Temple. After the destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that it be blown wherever there is a court. Rabbi Elazar limits this to Yavneh, but the Sages disagree. Jerusalem had an additional privilege: any city that could see, hear, and reach Jerusalem would blow, whereas in Yavneh only the court blew.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule that when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, shofar was blown only in the Temple, not in the rest of the country.
The Mishnah reports that after the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that shofar be blown wherever there is a court.
Rabbi Elazar objects that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment applied only to Yavneh, not to all places with a court.
The Sages reject Rabbi Elazar's limitation, asserting that the enactment applies equally to Yavneh and any place with a court.
The Mishnah adds that Jerusalem had an additional privilege: any city that could see, hear, and reach Jerusalem would blow shofar, whereas in Yavneh only the court blew.

items.text: Biblical source for shofar on Shabbat
items.text_en: Biblical source for shofar on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis. Rabbi Levi bar Lachma cites two verses: one says 'Shabbaton, remembrance of teruah' and another says 'a day of teruah'. The resolution: one applies when the holiday falls on Shabbat, the other on a weekday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the distinction between Shabbat and weekday) derived?

sub.text: Rabbi Levi bar Lachma in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Levi bar Lachma in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Lachma in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Chanina resolves the apparent contradiction between verses: 'Shabbaton, remembrance of teruah' applies when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, while 'a day of teruah' applies on a weekday.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one verse applies when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, the other when it falls on a weekday.

items.text: Rava's explanation: shofar is permitted by Torah, rabbinic decree due to carrying
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: shofar is permitted by Torah, rabbinic decree due to carrying
items.desc_en: Rava argues that shofar blowing is not a Torah-prohibited labor, as a baraita excludes it from 'melacha'. The real reason for the Shabbat prohibition is a rabbinic decree, as per Rabbah: lest one carry the shofar four cubits in the public domain to learn from an expert. The same reasoning applies to lulav and Megillah.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions how shofar could be blown in the Temple on Shabbat if it were a Torah-prohibited labor, and notes that it is not a labor at all, requiring a verse to exclude it.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Shmuel cites the verse 'כל מלאכת עבודה לא תעשו' (no work of labor shall be done) to exclude shofar blowing and bread baking as wisdom, not labor.

Rava resolves that shofar is permitted by Torah law, but the rabbis decreed against it on Shabbat due to Rabbah's concern: lest one carry the shofar four cubits in the public domain to learn from an expert.
The gemara notes that the same reasoning (rabbinic decree due to carrying) applies to lulav and Megillah as well.

items.text: Story of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment and dispute
items.text_en: Story of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment and dispute
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that when Rosh Hashanah fell on Shabbat, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai told the Bnei Beteira to blow the shofar. They wanted to deliberate first, but he insisted on blowing first, then after the fact said 'the horn has already been heard in Yavneh, and we do not respond after the deed.' The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar's limitation to Yavneh is disputed by the Sages, and the difference between them is a court that is fixed (קבע) versus occasional (אקראי).

sub.desc_en: A baraita opens with a story: once Rosh Hashanah fell on Shabbat and all the cities gathered.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai commands the Bnei Beteira to blow the shofar.
The Bnei Beteira object, wanting to deliberate first.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai insists on blowing first, then after the fact declares that the horn has already been heard and one does not respond after the deed.
Rabbi Elazar limits Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment to Yavneh alone.
The Sages object, saying the enactment applies both in Yavneh and any place with a court.
The Gemara objects that the Sages' statement is identical to the first Tanna's position.
The Gemara resolves the difference: the dispute is about a court that is fixed (קבע) versus occasional (אקראי).
Rav Huna begins a new statement, shifting the discussion.

items.text: Interpretation of 'with the court'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'with the court'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'with the court' in Rav Huna's statement, explaining that it means 'in the presence of the court', excluding blowing not in the presence of the court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'with the court' in Rav Huna's statement means.
The Gemara answers that it means 'in the presence of the court', excluding blowing not in the presence of the court.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution regarding Jerusalem and Yavneh
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution regarding Jerusalem and Yavneh
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a baraita about Jerusalem being greater than Yavneh, initially suggesting that in Jerusalem individuals blow the shofar, but not in Yavneh. The Gemara resolves that the difference is about blowing during the court's session or not, but Rava's proof is rejected by reinterpreting the baraita as referring to blowing in the presence of the court.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a baraita that distinguishes Jerusalem as greater than Yavneh, interpreting it to mean that in Jerusalem individuals blow the shofar but in Yavneh they do not.
The Gemara objects that in Yavneh individuals did blow the shofar, as evidenced by Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef's report that the sound of the individual blowers drowned out the communal blower.

The Gemara reinterprets the baraita: the difference is that in Jerusalem they blow both during and outside the court's session, while in Yavneh only during the session, implying that even outside the court's presence they blow during the session.

The Gemara rejects Rava's proof by reinterpreting the baraita as referring to blowing in the presence of the court: in Jerusalem they blow both in and out of the court's presence, but in Yavneh only in the court's presence.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Huna's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Huna's statement
items.desc_en: An alternative version of Rav Huna's statement is presented, where 'with the court' means 'during the court's session', excluding times when the court is not in session.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version of Rav Huna's statement is presented, interpreting 'with the court' as 'during the court's session', excluding times when the court is not in session.

items.text: Rava's objection from the Mishnah about Rosh Hashanah and Yovel
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the Mishnah about Rosh Hashanah and Yovel
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a Mishnah that states the shofar blowing for Rosh Hashanah and Yovel overrides Shabbat, with 'each man and his house' implying even not during the court's session. The Gemara rejects this, insisting it means during the court's session.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a Mishnah that states the shofar blowing for Rosh Hashanah and Yovel overrides Shabbat, with 'each man and his house' implying even not during the court's session, and he rejects the interpretation that it means 'a man and his wife' because women are exempt from positive time-bound commandments.
The Gemara rejects Rava's objection, insisting that 'each man and his house' means during the court's session, not without it.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection and resolution regarding Yovel and Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection and resolution regarding Yovel and Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita comparing Yovel and Rosh Hashanah, which seems to show that on Yovel they blow even not during the court's session. The Gemara resolves that both require the court's session, but Yovel allows blowing even not in the court's presence, while Rosh Hashanah requires both the court's session and presence.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects by citing a baraita that compares Yovel and Rosh Hashanah regarding shofar blowing and blessings, noting that on Yovel they blow even in a court that did not sanctify the month, while on Rosh Hashanah only in a court that sanctified the month.

The Gemara questions the meaning of 'no individual is obligated to blow' and rejects the interpretation that on Rosh Hashanah individuals do not blow at all, citing a report that in Yavneh the sound of the ram's horn was drowned out by individual blowers.

The Gemara proposes that the baraita means Yovel allows blowing both during and not during the court session, while Rosh Hashanah only during the court session, and challenges that the baraita explicitly states Yovel allows blowing even not during the court session.

The Gemara resolves that both Yovel and Rosh Hashanah require the court session, but Yovel allows blowing even not in the court's presence, while Rosh Hashanah requires both the court's session and presence, and supports this with a statement from Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul and Rabbi.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about the court rising
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about the court rising
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether if the court members stirred to stand but did not actually stand, it is still considered 'the court is sitting' or not. The question remains unresolved (Teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether if the court members stirred to stand but did not actually stand, it is still considered 'the court is sitting' or not; the question remains unresolved (Teiku).

items.text: Interpretation of the baraita about Jerusalem
items.text_en: Interpretation of the baraita about Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the baraita's terms: 'seeing' excludes one sitting in a valley, 'hearing' excludes one on a mountain, 'near' excludes one outside the boundary, and 'able to come' excludes one blocked by a river.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita listing Jerusalem's superiority over Yavneh, and begins explaining the first term: 'seeing' excludes one sitting in a valley.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the baraita's terms
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the baraita's terms
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the remaining terms: 'hearing' excludes one on a mountain, 'near' excludes one outside the boundary, and 'able to come' excludes one blocked by a river.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactments
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that originally the lulav was taken for seven days in the Temple and one day in the provinces. After the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that the lulav be taken for seven days in the provinces as a memorial to the Temple, and that the entire day of waving (the Omer) be forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the original practice of taking the lulav for seven days in the Temple and one day in the provinces, and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment after the Temple's destruction to take the lulav for seven days in the provinces as a memorial to the Temple, and to forbid the entire day of waving (the Omer).

items.text: Gemara: Source for enacting memorials and reason for the day of waving
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for enacting memorials and reason for the day of waving
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that we make memorials for the Temple. It then explains the reason for forbidding the entire day of waving: to prevent confusion if the Temple is rebuilt, as people might mistakenly think they can eat after dawn, not realizing the Omer permits it. The Gemara discusses scenarios of when the Temple might be rebuilt and concludes that the enactment is necessary only if built on the 15th close to sunset or at night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for enacting memorials for the Temple, and answers with a verse indicating that Zion requires seeking.
The Gemara asks why the entire day of waving was forbidden, and explains the concern that if the Temple is rebuilt, people might mistakenly think they can eat after dawn without the Omer.
The Gemara clarifies that people would not know that previously there was no Omer, but now the Omer permits eating.
The Gemara asks when the Temple might be rebuilt, and considers the case of building on the 16th, where dawn already permits eating.
The Gemara answers that the concern is if the Temple is built on the 15th, but notes that from midday onward it should be permitted because distant people are allowed from midday.
The Gemara resolves that the enactment is necessary only if the Temple is rebuilt on the 15th close to sunset or at night.

items.text: Beginning of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement
items.text_en: Beginning of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins to say something about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak begins a statement about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Defending Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment against Rabbi Yehuda's objection
items.text_en: Defending Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment against Rabbi Yehuda's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda misread Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment as a biblical prohibition; in truth, the enactment was rabbinic. The term 'ha-tkin' (established) means he taught and then enacted, so the objection is defused.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the objection is stated according to Rabbi Yehuda's view, who interprets 'עַד עֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה' (until the selfsame day) to include the entire day.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda actually disputes Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment, citing the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda argues that the prohibition is from the Torah.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda mistakenly thought Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment was biblical, but in truth it was rabbinic.
The Gemara explains that the term 'הִתְקִין' (established) in the Mishnah means he first taught (דָּרַשׁ) and then enacted (הִתְקִין), so the enactment was rabbinic.

items.text: Mishnah: Changes in accepting testimony for the new moon
items.text_en: Mishnah: Changes in accepting testimony for the new moon
items.desc_en: The mishnah describes the original practice of accepting testimony all day, the disruption when witnesses were delayed and Levites became confused in the song, and the enactment to accept testimony only until mincha. After the Temple was destroyed, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai restored the original practice of acceptance all day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that originally they would accept testimony about the new moon all day.
The mishnah opens by stating the original practice of accepting testimony for the new moon all day.
The mishnah recounts the incident when witnesses were delayed, causing the Levites to err in the song, leading to the enactment that testimony be accepted only until mincha.
The Mishnah recounts that once the witnesses were delayed, causing the Levites to err in the song, so they enacted that testimony would only be accepted until the afternoon (מִנְחָה).
The mishnah states the rule for when witnesses arrive after mincha: the day is treated as sacred and the next day also as sacred.
The Mishnah adds that if witnesses came after the afternoon, they would treat that day as sacred and the next day as sacred.
The mishnah concludes that after the Temple's destruction, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted the restoration of accepting testimony all day.
The Mishnah concludes that after the Temple was destroyed, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that testimony about the new moon would be accepted all day.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute over the nature of the Levites' error
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute over the nature of the Levites' error
items.desc_en: The Gemara first identifies the Levites' error: either they did not recite any song at all (local tradition) or they recited a weekday song along with the afternoon Tamid (Rabbi Zeira). Rabbi Zeira then asserts that the enactment was to ensure enough daylight for sacrifices and an uninterrupted song, and he demonstrates that even saying no song is a great disruption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what error the Levites made in the song, and the local scholars answer that they did not recite the song at all.
The Gemara asks what specific error the Levites made in the song, and the local tradition answers that they did not recite any song at all.
Rabbi Zeira answers that they recited a weekday song with the afternoon daily offering.
Rabbi Zeira offers an alternative answer: the Levites recited a weekday song along with the afternoon Tamid offering.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection to his own son
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection to his own son
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira tells his son Ahavah to teach that the enactment was to ensure time for offerings and song without error, and then objects that if the Levites said no song at all, there is no error.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira to his son Ahava
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira to his son Ahava
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira instructs his son Ahava to teach that the enactment ensured enough daylight for sacrifices and an uninterrupted song, and he argues that saying a weekday song constitutes a disruption, whereas saying no song at all would be an even greater disruption.
The Gemara resolves that since they said no song at all, there is no greater error than that.
The Gemara concludes that since the Levites said no song at all, there is no greater disruption than that.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Huna's objection: proof from Rosh Hashanah Temple song protocols
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Huna's objection: proof from Rosh Hashanah Temple song protocols
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna challenges the explanation that the Levites sang a weekday song: the mishnah about Rosh Hashanah songs shows that when uncertain, the Levites repeat a festal psalm rather than sing a weekday song. This supports the view that they sang no song at all, contradicted by the possibility of repeating a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna objects by citing a baraita about the daily offerings on Rosh Hashanah and the songs recited at each time.
The baraita continues that when Rosh Hashanah falls on Thursday, the song 'הַרְנִינוּ' is not said in the morning because it would repeat the chapter.
The baraita concludes that instead they say 'הֲסִירוֹתִי', and if witnesses come after the morning offering, they say 'הַרְנִינוּ' even though it repeats the chapter.

Rav Acha bar Huna objects that if the Levites said a weekday song when uncertain, the baraita's mention of repeating the chapter makes sense, but if they said nothing, what does 'saying and repeating' mean?

items.text: Transition from previous daf: reason for the daily Psalm
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf: reason for the daily Psalm
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Levites recited a different Psalm each day because it was the song of that day, not because of the additional sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes the daily Psalm from the additional sacrifices, explaining that the Levites recited the song of that day.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva on the daily Psalms
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva on the daily Psalms
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's teaching in the name of Rabbi Akiva, listing the Psalm for each day of the week and its thematic reason based on the creation narrative.

sub.text: Baraita citation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.text_en: Baraita citation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva, stating that on the first day the Levites recited Psalm 24 because God acquired, granted, and rules the world.

sub.text: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.text_en: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.desc_en: On the second day they recited Psalm 48 because God divided His works and reigned over them.

sub.text: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.text_en: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.desc_en: On the third day they recited Psalm 82 because God revealed the earth in His wisdom and prepared the world for His congregation.

sub.text: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.text_en: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.desc_en: On the fourth day they recited Psalm 94 because God created the sun and moon and will punish their worshippers.

sub.text: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.text_en: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.desc_en: On the fifth day they recited Psalm 81 because God created birds and fish to praise His name.

sub.text: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.text_en: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.desc_en: On the sixth day they recited Psalm 93 because God completed His work and reigned over them.

sub.text: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.text_en: Baraita continuation (Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva)
sub.desc_en: On the seventh day they recited Psalm 92 for the day that is entirely Shabbat.

items.text: Rabbi Nechemya's alternative rationale
items.text_en: Rabbi Nechemya's alternative rationale
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemya objects to the division of Psalms by days, arguing instead that each Psalm corresponds to a specific act of creation on that day, ending with the seventh day as a day of rest.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemya objects to the division of Psalms by days, arguing instead that each Psalm corresponds to a specific act of creation on that day, ending with the seventh day as a day of rest.

items.text: Dispute rooted in Rav Katina's teaching
items.text_en: Dispute rooted in Rav Katina's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya hinges on Rav Katina's statement about the world lasting six thousand years and one thousand years of desolation, with Abaye adding a second thousand based on a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya hinges on Rav Katina's teaching.
Rav Katina teaches that the world lasts six thousand years and one thousand years of desolation, citing the verse 'ונשגב ה' לבדו ביום ההוא'.
Abaye adds a second thousand years of desolation, citing the verse 'יחיינו מיומים'.

items.text: Psalm for Musaf of Shabbat and synagogue practice
items.text_en: Psalm for Musaf of Shabbat and synagogue practice
items.desc_en: Rav Anan bar Rava quotes Rav that the Psalm for the Musaf offering on Shabbat was 'Haziv lakh', and Rav Chanan bar Rava adds that the same dispute about daily Psalms applies in the synagogue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Psalm was recited for the Musaf offering on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Anan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Anan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Anan bar Rava quotes Rav that the Psalm was 'Haziv lakh'.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava adds in Rav's name that the same dispute about daily Psalms applies in the synagogue.

items.text: Psalm for Mincha of Shabbat and the pattern of recitation
items.text_en: Psalm for Mincha of Shabbat and the pattern of recitation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states the Psalm for Mincha on Shabbat is 'Az Yashir', 'Mi Chamocha', and 'Az Yashir'. A query arises whether all are said on one Shabbat or one per Shabbat, resolved by a baraita of Rabbi Yosei showing each Shabbat has one Psalm.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Psalm was recited at the Mincha (afternoon) service on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that they recited 'Az Yashir', 'Mi Chamocha', and 'Az Yashir'.
The Gemara queries whether all three Psalms are said on one Shabbat or one per Shabbat.
The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yosei describes a pattern of recitation that implies one Psalm per Shabbat.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that each Shabbat they recited one Psalm, not all three.

items.text: Ten journeys of the Shekhinah from Scripture
items.text_en: Ten journeys of the Shekhinah from Scripture
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Idi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the Shekhinah made ten journeys, listed from the Kaporet to the desert and back, each supported by a biblical verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Idi quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Idi quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Idi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the Shekhinah made ten journeys from Scripture, and correspondingly the Sanhedrin was exiled, from tradition.
The Gemara lists the ten journeys of the Shekhinah from the Kaporet to the desert and back, citing the verse 'I will go and return to My place'.

sub.text: Supporting verses for first three journeys
sub.text_en: Supporting verses for first three journeys
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses for the journeys from the Kaporet to the cherub, from cherub to cherub, and from cherub to the threshold.

sub.text: Supporting verses for journeys from threshold to city
sub.text_en: Supporting verses for journeys from threshold to city
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses for the journeys from the threshold to the courtyard, to the altar, to the roof, to the wall, and to the city.

sub.text: Supporting verses for journeys from city to desert and return
sub.text_en: Supporting verses for journeys from city to desert and return
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses for the journeys from the city to the mountain, to the desert, and the return to the original place.

items.text: Shekhinah's delay in the desert and the Sanhedrin's exile
items.text_en: Shekhinah's delay in the desert and the Sanhedrin's exile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan adds that the Shekhinah waited six months in the desert for Israel to repent, and when they did not, it departed. The Gemara then begins listing the corresponding exiles of the Sanhedrin from the Chamber of Hewn Stone.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Shekhinah (שכינה) delayed six months in the desert hoping Israel would repent, and when they did not, it departed, citing the verse 'ותקותם מפח נפש' (and their hope is a breath of despair).

items.text: Beginning of the Sanhedrin's exiles
items.text_en: Beginning of the Sanhedrin's exiles
items.desc_en: The Gemara starts listing the ten exiles of the Sanhedrin corresponding to the Shekhinah's journeys, beginning from the Chamber of Hewn Stone to the shops, to Jerusalem, and to Yavneh.

sub.desc_en: The gemara begins listing the ten exiles of the Sanhedrin corresponding to the Shekhinah's journeys, starting from the Chamber of Hewn Stone to the shops, to Jerusalem, and to Yavneh.

items.text: The relocations of the Sanhedrin and the promise of redemption
items.text_en: The relocations of the Sanhedrin and the promise of redemption
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the places the Sanhedrin moved from Yavne to Usha and back, then to Shfar'am, Beit She'arim, Tzipori, and Teveria. Rabbi Elazar counts six exiles, and Rabbi Yochanan adds that from the lowest place (Teveria) they will be redeemed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the successive relocations of the Sanhedrin from Yavne to Usha and back, then to Shfar'am, Beit She'arim, Tzipori, and Teveria, noting that Teveria is the lowest of all, as per the verse.
Rabbi Elazar counts six exiles of the Sanhedrin, citing a verse that describes a progressive descent.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that from the lowest place (Teveria) they will be redeemed, citing a verse that calls them to rise from the dust.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment about witnesses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's enactment about witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that even if the head of the court is elsewhere, witnesses need only go to the place of the assembly (the court's meeting place).

sub.text: Mishnah via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Mishnah via Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted that witnesses need only go to the place of the assembly, even if the head of the court is elsewhere.

items.text: Gemara: Amemar's case and the limitation of the enactment
items.text_en: Gemara: Amemar's case and the limitation of the enactment
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Amemar summoned a woman to court in Neharde'a but went to Machoza; when she didn't follow, he wrote a ban against her. Rav Ashi objected based on the Mishnah, but Amemar replied that the enactment only applies to testimony about the new moon, not to monetary cases, citing the principle that a borrower is a slave to the lender.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Amemar summoned a woman to court in Neharde'a, went to Machoza, and when she did not follow, he wrote a ban against her.
Rav Ashi objects to Amemar's action, citing the Mishnah's enactment that even the head of the court must not compel witnesses to travel except to the place of assembly.
Amemar answers that the Mishnah's enactment applies only to testimony about the new moon, not to monetary cases, citing the principle that a borrower is a slave to the lender.

items.text: The nine enactments of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: first two
items.text_en: The nine enactments of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: first two
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai made nine enactments: six in this chapter, one in the first chapter, and two others. The first additional one is that priests may not go up to the platform in sandals. The second is that a convert nowadays must set aside a quarter-log for a bird-offering, but Rabban Yochanan later nullified it due to potential stumbling.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that priests may not go up to the platform in sandals, listing this as one of nine enactments of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.

A second baraita adds that a convert nowadays must set aside a quarter-log for a bird-offering, but Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai later nullified this enactment due to the potential for stumbling.

items.text: Debate: the ninth enactment – Kerem Revai or the tongue of crimson
items.text_en: Debate: the ninth enactment – Kerem Revai or the tongue of crimson
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak about the identity of the ninth enactment. Rav Pappa says it is about Kerem Revai (fourth-year vineyard), while Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is about the tongue of crimson (the scarlet thread of the Yom Kippur scapegoat).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak about the identity of the ninth enactment.

Rav Pappa states that the ninth enactment is about Kerem Revai (fourth-year vineyard), citing a baraita about its boundaries and Ulla's explanation that it was to adorn Jerusalem's markets with fruits.

A baraita recounts that Rabbi Eliezer had a Kerem Revai and sought to declare it ownerless for the poor, but his students told him that his colleagues, including Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, had already permitted it.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that the ninth enactment is about the tongue of crimson (the scarlet thread of the Yom Kippur scapegoat), citing a baraita about its placement and the subsequent changes to prevent sadness.

sub.text: Gemara's question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Gemara's question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak does not accept Rav Pappa's view, and he answers that the baraita about Rabbi Eliezer refers to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai as 'your colleagues,' but since they were students, it would be disrespectful to call him 'your rabbi'.

The Gemara asks why Rav Pappa does not accept Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's view, and he answers that the tongue of crimson ceased to turn white forty years before the Temple's destruction, so it could not have been enacted by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai after the destruction; the other view responds that those forty years were when he was a student, and he stated a teaching whose reasoning was accepted.

items.text: Support for Rav Pappa: Kerem Revai and Rabbi Eliezer's vineyard
items.text_en: Support for Rav Pappa: Kerem Revai and Rabbi Eliezer's vineyard
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa supports his view with a baraita about Kerem Revai's boundaries and Ulla's explanation that the enactment was to adorn Jerusalem's markets with fruit. The Gemara then recounts that Rabbi Eliezer had a Kerem Revai near Lod and wanted to declare it ownerless for the poor, but his students told him that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and his colleagues had already permitted it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a baraita defining the boundaries of Kerem Revai (fourth-year vineyard fruit) that must be brought to Jerusalem.

sub.text: Ulla / Rabbah bar Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ulla / Rabbah bar Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ulla (or Rabbah bar Ulla) explains in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the enactment was to adorn Jerusalem's markets with fruit.
A baraita recounts that Rabbi Eliezer had a Kerem Revai near Lod and wanted to declare it ownerless for the poor.
Rabbi Eliezer's students inform him that his colleagues, led by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, had already permitted the Kerem Revai to be redeemed with money rather than brought to Jerusalem.

items.text: Support for Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: the tongue of crimson
items.text_en: Support for Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: the tongue of crimson
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports his view with a baraita describing the practice of tying a crimson tongue on the Temple entrance. Initially it was tied outside, then inside, and finally half on the rock and half between the horns of the scapegoat, to prevent people from being distressed when it didn't turn white.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asserts that the ninth enactment was about the crimson tongue, citing a baraita that describes how it was initially tied outside the Temple entrance, then moved inside to avoid public distress.
The baraita continues that even after moving the tongue inside, people still peeked and were distressed, so the enactment was made to tie half on the rock and half between the scapegoat's horns.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: why each sage rejects the other's view
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: why each sage rejects the other's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects Rav Pappa's view: if the enactment were about Kerem Revai, the students would not have called Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai 'your colleagues' to Rabbi Eliezer, since he was their teacher. Rav Pappa rejects Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's view because the crimson tongue stopped turning white 40 years before the Temple's destruction, yet Rabban Yochanan enacted after the destruction; the Gemara resolves that during his 40 years of study he was a student and proposed the idea, and his reasoning was accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects Rav Pappa's view that the enactment was about Kerem Revai, and answers that calling Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai 'your colleagues' would be disrespectful since he was Rabbi Eliezer's teacher.

The Gemara asks why Rav Pappa rejects Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's view that the enactment was about the crimson tongue, citing that the tongue stopped turning white 40 years before the Temple's destruction, yet Rabban Yochanan enacted after the destruction.
The Gemara resolves that during those 40 years of study, Rabban Yochanan was a student who proposed the idea, and his reasoning was accepted.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute over the order of blessings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute over the order of blessings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva regarding the order of blessings for the Musaf prayer on Rosh Hashanah. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that Malchiyot is recited with the first three blessings, while Rabbi Akiva argues that Malchiyot should be included with Kedushat Hayom, followed by tekiot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the order of blessings for Musaf on Rosh Hashanah: one recites Avot, Gevurot, and Kedushat Hashem, and includes Malchuyot with them without blowing the shofar.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri presents his view: after Kedushat Hayom one blows the shofar, then Zichronot with shofar, then Shofarot with shofar, and concludes with Avodah, Hoda'ah, and Birkat Kohanim.

Rabbi Akiva objects: if one does not blow the shofar for Malchuyot, why mention it? He argues that Malchuyot should be included with Kedushat Hayom and then blow the shofar, followed by Zichronot and Shofarot with shofar.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's statement, asking why he says 'why mention Malchiyot if not for tekiot,' since the Torah commands mentioning them. It reinterprets his question as asking why there are ten verses, rather than nine, since the structure changes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Akiva's statement, noting that the Torah itself commands mentioning Malchiyot, so his question 'why mention them' seems absurd.
The Gemara quotes Rabbi Akiva's objection from the Mishnah and then questions the phrasing: why does he say 'why mention it'?
The Gemara objects: the Merciful One commanded to mention Malchuyot, so why question the mention? Rather, the question should be: why ten verses? Let him say nine, since the structure changed.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting Rabbi Akiva's question: he asks why there are ten Malchiyot verses rather than nine, since the structure changes.

items.text: Sources for the blessings and the placement of Malchiyot
items.text_en: Sources for the blessings and the placement of Malchiyot
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita providing scriptural sources for Avot, Gevurot, and Kedushot. It then presents a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva on deriving Zichronot and Shofarot from the verse 'Shabbaton Zichron Teruah.' Finally, it brings Rabbi's and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's opinions on the source for Malchiyot, with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda arguing that Malchiyot is implied wherever Zichronot is mentioned.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites scriptural verses for Avot, Gevurot, and Kedushot from Psalms.
Rabbi Eliezer derives Zichronot and Shofarot from the verse 'Shabbaton Zichron Teruah', interpreting each word.
Rabbi Akiva objects to Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation, arguing that 'Shabbaton' should refer to the prohibition of work, and reassigns the words to different elements.
Rabbi derives the source for Malchiyot from the verse 'Ani Hashem Eloheichem' and 'Bachodesh Hashevi'i'.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda argues that Malchiyot is not derived separately but is implied wherever Zichronot is mentioned, based on the verse 'VeHayu Lachem LeZikaron'.

items.text: Dispute on where to recite Kedushat Hayom
items.text_en: Dispute on where to recite Kedushat Hayom
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses where Kedushat Hayom is recited: Rabbi says with Malchiyot (in the fourth blessing), while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says with Zichronot (in the middle). A story from Usha shows that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka followed Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, and Rabbi Chanina followed Rabbi Akiva, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel approving the latter as the practice in Yavne.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Kedushat Hayom is recited in the Amidah.
Rabbi rules that Kedushat Hayom is recited with Malchiyot (in the fourth blessing), based on the pattern that it is always placed in the fourth blessing.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that Kedushat Hayom is recited with Zichronot (in the middle blessing), based on the pattern that it is always placed in the middle.

A baraita recounts a story from Usha where Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka followed Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's practice, and Rabbi Chanina followed Rabbi Akiva's practice, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel approving the latter as the custom in Yavne.

items.text: Reconciling Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel can agree with Rabbi Akiva's practice if he holds Kedushat Hayom is with Zichronot. Rabbi Zeira explains that the agreement is only that tekiot are blown for Malchiyot. The Gemara then clarifies that 'second day' refers to the second day of the following year, not the second day of the festival, due to the rule that Elul is never intercalated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agrees with Rabbi Akiva's position, given the apparent contradiction between his practice and his stated view.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Akiva places Malchiyot with Kedushat Hayom, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel places Kedushat Hayom with Zichronot, showing a clear disagreement.
Rabbi Zeira answers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's agreement is only that tekiot are blown for Malchiyot, not about the placement of Kedushat Hayom.
The Gemara asks what 'second day' means in the story of Rabbi Chanina descending before the ark.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that 'second day' refers to the second day of the festival, as that would require intercalating Elul.
Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana provides evidence that Elul has never been intercalated since the days of Ezra.
Rav Chisda resolves that 'second day' refers to the second day of the following year, not the second day of the festival.

items.text: Minimum number of verses for Malchiyot, Zichronot, Shofarot
items.text_en: Minimum number of verses for Malchiyot, Zichronot, Shofarot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one must recite at least ten verses each for Malchiyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot, with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri allowing three of each. The Gemara provides reasons for ten (corresponding to ten praises, ten commandments, or ten utterances of creation). It then clarifies Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's opinion: a baraita shows he requires seven, but three suffice, corresponding to Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim or Kohanim, Levi'im, Yisraelim. Rav Huna rules in accordance with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the minimum of ten verses each for Malchiyot, Zichronot, and Shofarot, with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri allowing three of each.
The Gemara asks what the ten Malchiyot correspond to.
Rabbi answers that the ten Malchiyot correspond to ten praises (הלולים) in Psalms that mention the shofar.
Rav Yosef answers that the ten Malchiyot correspond to the Ten Commandments given at Sinai.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the ten Malchiyot correspond to the ten utterances (מאמרות) by which the world was created, including 'בראשית' as a speech act.

The Gemara raises a question about the interpretation of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's statement: whether he meant three from each section (Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim) totaling nine plus one, or one from each section totaling three.
The Gemara cites a baraita that states one may recite seven verses from all sections, corresponding to seven firmaments, to clarify the minimum.

The baraita clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri requires a minimum of seven verses but three suffice, corresponding to Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim or Kohanim, Levi'im, Yisraelim, and Rav Huna rules in accordance with him.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition of verses of punishment and order of verses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition of verses of punishment and order of verses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one should not mention verses of punishment for Malchiyot, Zichronot, or Shofarot. One begins with Torah verses and concludes with a prophet, though Rabbi Yosei allows concluding with Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one does not mention verses of remembrance, kingship, or shofar that are of punishment; one begins with Torah verses and concludes with a prophet; Rabbi Yosei says if one concludes with Torah, he fulfills his obligation.
Rabbi Yosei offers a lenient opinion that if one concluded with Torah verses, he has fulfilled his obligation.

items.text: Opening Gemara: Examples of verses for Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofar
items.text_en: Opening Gemara: Examples of verses for Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofar
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides examples of verses for the three sections of the Rosh Hashanah prayer: Malchuyot (Kingship), Zichronot (Remembrance), and Shofar. It notes that a verse expressing God's anger is not suitable for Malchuyot on Rosh Hashanah, citing Rav Nachman's statement.

items.text: Permissible verses of punishment for the nations
items.text_en: Permissible verses of punishment for the nations
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one wishes to recite verses of punishment for the nations for Malchuyot, Zichronot, and Shofar, they may do so, providing examples from Psalms and other prophets.

items.text: No individual remembrance verses; dispute on Pikdonot
items.text_en: No individual remembrance verses; dispute on Pikdonot
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules that one does not recite verses of remembrance for an individual, even for good. It then discusses whether verses of 'visitation' (Pikdonot) are considered like remembrance verses, with a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Resolution of the difficulty regarding Pikdonot of an individual
items.text_en: Resolution of the difficulty regarding Pikdonot of an individual
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a difficulty: the verse 'And the Lord visited Sarah' is a Pikdon of an individual, yet Rabbi Yosei considers it valid. The answer is that since many came from her, it is considered like a public matter.

items.text: Dispute on the number of verses in Psalm 24 and Psalm 47
items.text_en: Dispute on the number of verses in Psalm 24 and Psalm 47
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the number of 'Kingship' verses in Psalm 24 and Psalm 47. Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda dispute whether the first section of Psalm 24 contains two or one verses, and similarly for Psalm 47. They agree on one verse in another section.

items.text: Disputes on verses with Teruah: Zichron, Malchut, and plain Teruah
items.text_en: Disputes on verses with Teruah: Zichron, Malchut, and plain Teruah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents disputes between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda regarding verses that contain the word 'Teruah' along with Zichron or Malchut, and a verse with only 'Teruah'. Rabbi Yosei allows them to be recited with both sections, while Rabbi Yehuda restricts them.

items.text: Dispute on beginning with Torah and completing with Prophet
items.text_en: Dispute on beginning with Torah and completing with Prophet
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether one begins the verses with Torah and completes with a Prophet. It clarifies Rabbi Yosei's statement: he says one should complete with Torah, and if one completed with a Prophet, they have fulfilled their obligation. A baraita supports this with the practice of the pious.

items.text: Finding ten Malchuyot verses: dispute on Shema and other verses
items.text_en: Finding ten Malchuyot verses: dispute on Shema and other verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how to find ten Malchuyot verses, as only three are obvious. Rav Huna suggests that verses like 'Shema Yisrael' and others are considered Malchuyot by Rabbi Yosei, but Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the order of shofar blowing and Hallel
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the order of shofar blowing and Hallel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Rosh Hashanah, the second person to lead the prayer blows the shofar, and the first leads Hallel. The Gemara questions this, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that this was instituted during a time of persecution. The Gemara also explains why Hallel is not recited on Rosh Hashanah.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on restrictions of shofar on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on restrictions of shofar on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists restrictions on handling the shofar on Rosh Hashanah, such as not carrying it beyond the techum, not climbing a tree, etc. The Gemara explains the rationale: shofar is a positive commandment, and Yom Tov involves both positive and negative commandments, and a positive commandment does not override them. It also clarifies the Mishnah's listing of prohibitions.

items.text: Cutting the shofar: prohibition and its gradation
items.text_en: Cutting the shofar: prohibition and its gradation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not cut the shofar, whether the cutting is prohibited by rabbinic decree (shevut) or by Torah law (lo ta'aseh). The Gemara questions why both categories are mentioned, explaining that the Mishnah uses the style 'this and needless to say that' to include both.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not cut the shofar, whether the cutting is prohibited by rabbinic decree (שבות) or by Torah law (לא תעשה), specifying the tools involved.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions both categories, arguing that if a lesser prohibition (שבות) is forbidden, the greater one (לא תעשה) is obvious.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah uses the style 'this and needless to say that' to include both gradations.

items.text: Liquids for cleaning the shofar
items.text_en: Liquids for cleaning the shofar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits putting water or wine into the shofar to clean it, but not urine. The Gemara identifies this as the view of Abba Shaul, who explicitly permits water or wine for polishing but forbids urine due to respect.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may put water or wine into the shofar to clean it, but not urine.
The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as the view of Abba Shaul, who explicitly permits water or wine for polishing but forbids urine due to respect.

items.text: Women and children blowing the shofar
items.text_en: Women and children blowing the shofar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says children are not prevented from blowing, implying women are prevented. A baraita contradicts this by saying neither women nor children are prevented. Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita to Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon, citing a dispute about women performing semikhah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that children are not prevented from blowing the shofar, implying that women are prevented.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says neither women nor children are prevented from blowing.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita to Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon.
A baraita is cited showing the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei/Rabbi Shimon regarding women performing semikhah (laying of hands), which parallels the shofar dispute.

items.text: Engaging children in learning and the contradiction about initial permission
items.text_en: Engaging children in learning and the contradiction about initial permission
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says we engage children until they learn, and Rabbi Elazar adds even on Shabbat. A baraita supports this. However, the Gemara notes a contradiction: the baraita says 'we engage' (implying initial encouragement) but also says 'we do not prevent' (implying only passive allowance). The Gemara resolves that the two clauses refer to different situations: one for learning and one for already knowing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that we engage children in learning to blow the shofar until they learn.
Rabbi Elazar adds that this engagement is permitted even on Shabbat.
A baraita supports Rabbi Elazar's ruling, stating that we engage children even on Shabbat and do not prevent them from blowing on Shabbat, certainly on Yom Tov.

The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: the first clause says 'we engage' (לכתחילה (the ideal standard) encouragement), but the second clause says 'we do not prevent' (implying only passive allowance, not active encouragement).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between two situations: one clause refers to engaging children who are learning, the other to not preventing those who already know.

items.text: Distinction regarding a minor who blows the shofar
items.text_en: Distinction regarding a minor who blows the shofar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's ruling about a minor who blows the shofar is explained: the case of a minor who has reached the age of training is different from one who has not. This sets up the discussion of intent in performing the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between a minor who has reached the age of training (חינוך) and one who has not, regarding the validity of shofar blowing.

items.text: The case of one who blows for music
items.text_en: The case of one who blows for music
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that one who blows the shofar for music has fulfilled his obligation, supporting Rava's statement. However, it suggests that even one who blows for music might be considered merely engaged in activity (mit'asek) and not fulfill the mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says one who is merely occupied (מתעסק) does not fulfill the obligation, and asks whether this supports Rava's view that one who blows for music (תוקע לשיר) is exempt.
The Gemara rejects the support, suggesting that even one who blows for music is still called a מתעסק (one who is occupied without intent).
The Gemara suggests that this inference supports Rava's statement that one who blows for music has fulfilled the obligation.
The Gemara rejects the support, suggesting that even one who blows for music might be considered merely engaged in activity (mit'asek) and thus not fulfill the obligation.

items.text: One who hears from one who blows for himself
items.text_en: One who hears from one who blows for himself
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who hears from one who is merely engaged (mit'asek) does not fulfill the obligation. The Gemara infers that one who hears from one who blows for himself does fulfill the obligation, which seems to contradict Rabbi Zeira's instruction to his attendant to intend to blow for him. The Gemara resolves this by suggesting that the Mishnah's wording is due to the context of the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who hears the shofar from one who is merely engaged (mit'asek) does not fulfill the obligation.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that one who hears from one who blows for himself does fulfill the obligation.
The Gemara raises a challenge against Rabbi Zeira, who instructed his attendant to intend to blow for him, implying that without intent the listener does not fulfill the obligation.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's wording is merely due to the context of the first clause, not to exclude the case of one who blows for himself.

items.text: Mishnah: Order of blasts and related laws
items.text_en: Mishnah: Order of blasts and related laws
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the order of shofar blasts: three sets of three each. It defines the duration of a tekiah as three teruot, and a teruah as three yevavot (sobs). It also discusses a case where one prolonged the second blast, and the rule for one who was appointed a shofar after the blessing. Finally, it notes that the shaliach tzibbur is obligated, and Rabban Gamliel says he fulfills the obligation for the many.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the order of shofar blasts: three sets of three each, defines the duration of a tekiah as three teruot and a teruah as three yevavot, and rules on a case where one prolonged the second blast.
The Mishnah rules that one who blessed and then obtained a shofar must blow three sets of tekiah-teruah-tekiah.
The Mishnah states that the shaliach tzibbur is obligated, and Rabban Gamliel says he fulfills the obligation for the many.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute on the duration of tekiah
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute on the duration of tekiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that states the duration of a tekiah is like a teruah, contradicting the Mishnah. Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah counts the tekiah of all sets and the teruot of all sets, while the baraita counts only one set.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction: a baraita states that the length of a תרועה is three broken sounds (שברים), not three wails (יבבות) as in our Mishnah.
Abaye explains that the Tannaim genuinely disagree: one interprets תרועה as groaning (גנוחי) and the other as wailing (ילולי), based on the verse about Sisera's mother.

items.text: Dispute on the nature of teruah: groaning or wailing
items.text_en: Dispute on the nature of teruah: groaning or wailing
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that says the duration of a teruah is like three shevarim (broken sounds), contradicting the Mishnah's definition of three yevavot. Abaye explains that this is a genuine dispute: one opinion holds that teruah is a groaning (genuha), and the other holds it is a wailing (yelula), each derived from verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's statement that the duration of a teruah is like three yevavot (wails) by citing a baraita that says it is like three shevarim (broken sounds).

Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the two sources reflect a genuine dispute: one opinion holds that teruah is a groaning (גנוחי גנח), derived from the verse about Sisera's mother, and the other holds it is a wailing (ילולי יליל), derived from the Aramaic translation of the verse.

items.text: Derivation of the shofar blasts from the Torah
items.text_en: Derivation of the shofar blasts from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the requirement of a shofar for teruah from the verse "veha'avarta shofar teruah." It then derives that the same applies to Rosh Hashanah from the phrase "bachodesh hashevi'i." Finally, it derives the requirement of a plain blast (tekiah) before and after the teruah from the verses "veha'avarta shofar teruah" and "ta'aviru shofar."

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse "veha'avarta shofar teruah" to derive that the teruah blast must be performed with a shofar.
The baraita asks: the verse applies only to Yovel (Jubilee), but how do we derive the same requirement for Rosh Hashanah?
The baraita answers by citing the verse "bachodesh hashevi'i" (in the seventh month), which is superfluous and teaches that all teruah blasts of the seventh month are equivalent to those of Yovel.

items.text: Derivation of the nine blasts from verses
items.text_en: Derivation of the nine blasts from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how the Torah verses teach that all teruah blasts of the seventh month are alike, that there are three sets of three blasts each, and that the verses are linked by a gezerah shavah. It concludes that the shiur of a tekiah is like a teruah, and the shiur of a teruah is like three broken sounds.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna derives from the superfluous phrase 'בחדש השביעי' (in the seventh month) that all teruah blasts of the seventh month are alike.
The Tanna derives three sets of three blasts each from three verses mentioning 'teruah' in the context of the seventh month.
The Tanna links the verses through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) using the repeated word 'שביעי' (seventh) to apply the teaching of each verse to the others.
The Tanna concludes that the three verses yield nine blasts total, with the length of a תקיעה (tekiah) equal to a תרועה (teruah) and the length of a תרועה equal to three broken sounds.

items.text: Question on the Tanna's method
items.text_en: Question on the Tanna's method
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna first used a hekesh and then a gezerah shavah, and explains that without the gezerah shavah he would have used the hekesh, but now that the gezerah shavah is available, the hekesh is unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna first derived the law through a היקש (analogy) and now derives it through a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy).
The Gemara explains that the Tanna meant: had there been no גזירה שוה (verbal analogy), he would have used the היקש (analogy), but now that the גזירה שוה is available, the היקש is unnecessary.

items.text: Derivation from the wilderness (midbar)
items.text_en: Derivation from the wilderness (midbar)
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the wilderness that tekiah and teruah are separate, and that a simple blast (peshutah) precedes and follows the teruah, based on the verses 'וּתְקַעְתֶּם תְּרוּעָה' and 'תְּרוּעָה יִתְקְעוּ'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'וּתְקַעְתֶּם תְּרוּעָה' to prove that tekiah and teruah are separate blasts, not one combined sound.
The baraita derives from the verses that a simple blast (peshutah) precedes and follows the teruah.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's alternative derivation and the three teruah verses
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's alternative derivation and the three teruah verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka argues that the requirement for a simple blast after the teruah is derived from the word 'שֵׁנִית' in the wilderness, and then applies to Rosh Hashanah via a gezerah shavah. The Gemara then lists the three teruah verses in Rosh Hashanah and notes that two are from the Torah and one from the Scribes.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael argues that the requirement for a simple blast after the teruah is derived from the word 'שֵׁנִית' in the wilderness, and then applies to Rosh Hashanah via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).
The Gemara lists the three teruah verses in Rosh Hashanah and notes that each requires two simple blasts.
The Gemara concludes that there are three teruah blasts and six simple blasts in Rosh Hashanah, two from the Torah and one from the Scribes.

items.text: Dispute over which verses are Torah and which are rabbinic
items.text_en: Dispute over which verses are Torah and which are rabbinic
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan argues that only one verse is from the Torah and two from the Scribes. The Gemara explains that the extra verse comes to teach that the shofar is blown during the day and not at night, and the other opinion derives this from the verse 'בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan states that only one verse ('וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ שׁוֹפַר תְּרוּעָה') is from the Torah, while the other two ('שַׁבָּתוֹן זִכְרוֹן תְּרוּעָה' and 'יוֹם תְּרוּעָה יִהְיֶה לָכֶם') are from the Scribes.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'לְתַלְמוּדוֹ הוּא בָּא' (it comes for its teaching) means, and explains that it teaches that the shofar is blown during the day and not at night.

The Gemara explains that the other opinion (which counts two verses as Torah) derives the requirement that shofar be blown during the day and not at night from the verse 'בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים' (on the Day of Atonement).

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the derivation from Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the derivation from Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one learns from Yom Kippur, one should also learn the requirement for simple blasts, but the verses 'וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ' and 'תַּעֲבִירוּ' do not imply that. It then explains that these verses are used for other teachings, such as Rav Mattana's derivation about passing the shofar over the mouth, and a gezerah shavah from Moshe that it is with voice. Finally, it addresses the concern that the wilderness derivation might imply trumpets, but the verse 'תִּקְעוּ בַחֹדֶשׁ שׁוֹפָר' specifies a shofar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one learns from Yom Kippur, one should also derive the requirement for simple blasts (פשוטה לפניה ופשוטה לאחריה), but the verses 'וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ' and 'תַּעֲבִירוּ' do not imply that.

The Gemara answers that the verses are used for Rav Mattana's teaching: 'וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ' teaches the manner of passing the shofar over the mouth, and 'תַּעֲבִירוּ' teaches that one should pass it by hand.

sub.text: Gemara's answer — alternative derivation for the other Tanna
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer — alternative derivation for the other Tanna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the other Tanna (who does not use the verses for Rav Mattana's teaching) derives Rav Mattana's point from the fact that the Torah changed its phrasing from 'וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ' to 'תַּעֲבִירוּ'.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution — gezerah shavah from Moshe
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution — gezerah shavah from Moshe
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that 'תַּעֲבִירוּ' cannot mean by hand, because a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'עֲבָרָה' used by Moshe teaches that it is with voice, not by hand.

sub.text: Gemara's objection — wilderness derivation might imply trumpets
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection — wilderness derivation might imply trumpets
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that for the Tanna who derives the blasts from the wilderness, one might think the instrument should be trumpets (חצוצרות) like in the wilderness.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'תִּקְעוּ בַחֹדֶשׁ שׁוֹפָר' specifies a shofar, not trumpets, for Rosh Hashanah.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's enactment in Caesarea
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's enactment in Caesarea
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu enacted a sequence of tekiah, shevarim, teruah, tekiah to cover both possible sounds of the teruah (groaning or wailing). The Gemara questions why he didn't do the reverse, and explains that when a person is stricken, they first groan and then wail.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu enacted in Caesarea a sequence of tekiah, shevarim, teruah, tekiah to cover both possible sounds of the teruah.
Rav Avira objects that if the teruah is wailing, the shevarim inserted between teruah and tekiah would be an invalid interruption.
Ravina objects that if the teruah is groaning, the teruah inserted between shevarim and tekiah would be an invalid interruption.

The Gemara questions what Rabbi Avahu's enactment actually accomplishes, since he already covers both possibilities, and answers that he was uncertain whether the teruah might be a combination of groaning and wailing.
The Gemara resolves that the order is not reversed because when a person is stricken, they first groan and then wail.

items.text: Case of a prolonged blast
items.text_en: Case of a prolonged blast
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion about a case where one blew a tekiah in the first blast and drew out the second blast to the length of two, and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one blew the first blast (tekiah) and drew out the second blast to the length of two, and introduces Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that he has fulfilled his obligation.

items.text: Opening baraita on hearing shofar blasts
items.text_en: Opening baraita on hearing shofar blasts
items.desc_en: The baraita states that hearing nine blasts over nine hours fulfills the obligation, but hearing them from nine people simultaneously does not. However, hearing a tekiah from one person and a teruah from another is valid, even if interrupted or spread over the entire day.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that hearing nine shofar blasts over nine hours fulfills the obligation, but hearing them from nine people simultaneously does not; a tekiah from one person and a teruah from another is valid even if interrupted or spread over the entire day.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yochanan's consistency
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yochanan's consistency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan holds that interruptions invalidate the sequence, citing his ruling on Hallel and Megillah. It resolves that the baraita reflects his teacher's view, not his own, and a story with Rabbi Avahu confirms that Rabbi Yochanan personally holds that a pause long enough to complete the entire reading requires starting over.

sub.desc_en: The gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing his own statement in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak that in Hallel and Megillah, if one paused long enough to finish the entire text, he must return to the beginning.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's consistency, citing his ruling that a pause long enough to complete the entire Hallel or Megillah requires starting over.
The gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Rabbi Yochanan's own view and that of his teacher.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita reflects Rabbi Yochanan's teacher's view, not his own.

The gemara objects by recounting an incident where Rabbi Avahu followed Rabbi Yochanan and was told that if he paused during Shema long enough to finish the entire text, he must return to the beginning.
The Gemara objects with a story where Rabbi Yochanan told Rabbi Avahu that a pause long enough to complete the entire Shema requires starting over, implying his own view.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was stating the rule according to Rabbi Avahu's own assumption, not his own view.
The gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan was telling Rabbi Avahu that he himself does not hold that view, but since Rabbi Avahu does, he must follow it.

items.text: Baraita on blasts and blessings not impeding each other
items.text_en: Baraita on blasts and blessings not impeding each other
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that blasts do not impede each other, nor do blessings, but for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, blasts and blessings are interdependent. Rabbah explains the reason: God wants us to recite Kingships, Remembrances, and Shofarot, with the shofar as the medium.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that shofar blasts do not invalidate each other, blessings do not invalidate each other, but the blasts and blessings of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur do invalidate each other.
A baraita states that blasts do not impede each other, nor do blessings, but for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, blasts and blessings are interdependent.

Rabbah explains the reason: The Holy One said to recite before Him on Rosh Hashanah verses of Kingship, Remembrance, and Shofar — Kingship to coronate Him, Remembrance for a favorable memory, and through what? Through the shofar.
Rabbah explains the reason: God wants us to recite Kingships, Remembrances, and Shofarot, with the shofar as the medium.

items.text: Case of one who blessed before obtaining a shofar
items.text_en: Case of one who blessed before obtaining a shofar
items.desc_en: If one recited the blessings and then obtained a shofar, he blows tekiah, teruah, tekiah. The Gemara infers that if he had a shofar from the outset, he must hear the blasts in the order of the blessings.
