sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that if one blessed and then obtained a shofar, he blows tekiah-teruah-tekiah; implying that if he had a shofar from the outset, he would hear the blasts in the order of the blessings.
The Gemara infers that the baraita's ruling applies only because he lacked a shofar initially, implying that if he had one from the outset, the rule would differ.
The Gemara concludes that if he had a shofar from the outset, he must hear the blasts in the order of the blessings.

items.text: Rav Pappa's case and the rule of a city congregation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's case and the rule of a city congregation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa instructed his attendant to blow for him when he signaled, but Rava said this is only permitted in a city congregation. A baraita supports this: in a city congregation, one hears blasts in order of blessings; otherwise, not. The Gemara explains why going to the place of blasts is preferable to blessings, even considering certainty versus uncertainty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa stood to pray and instructed his attendant to blow the shofar for him when he signaled.
Rava objected that this leniency was only stated for a city congregation, not for an individual.
A baraita supports Rava: in a city congregation one hears blasts in order of blessings; otherwise not; an individual who did not blow has a friend blow for him, but not for blessings.
The baraita adds that it is a greater מצוה (commandment) to go to the place of blasts than to the place of blessings.
The Gemara questions why this is obvious: one is a Torah commandment and the other is rabbinic.
The Gemara answers that the ruling is necessary even though one is certain (Torah) and the other is uncertain (rabbinic), because the preference for the certain over the uncertain is not obvious.

items.text: Debate between Rabban Gamliel and the Sages on prayer
items.text_en: Debate between Rabban Gamliel and the Sages on prayer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that as the shaliach tzibbur is obligated, so is every individual. The Sages ask Rabban Gamliel why the congregation prays if the shaliach exempts them; he answers to arrange his prayer. Rabban Gamliel retorts why the shaliach descends before the ark; they answer to exempt the unlearned. He argues he exempts the learned as well. Rabbi Yochanan holds the Sages agree with Rabban Gamliel, but Rav says the dispute remains, with Resh Lakish supporting Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that just as the shaliach tzibbur (prayer leader) is obligated, so is every individual.
The Sages ask Rabban Gamliel: according to your view, why does the congregation pray at all?
Rabban Gamliel answers: so that the shaliach tzibbur can arrange his prayer.
Rabban Gamliel retorts: according to your view, why does the shaliach tzibbur descend before the ark?
The Sages answer: to exempt the unlearned who cannot pray on their own.
Rabban Gamliel argues: just as the shaliach tzibbur exempts the unlearned, so too he exempts the learned.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports that Rabbi Yochanan holds the Sages agree with Rabban Gamliel.
Rav states that the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and the Sages still stands.
Rabbi Chiyya hears the tradition and reports it to Rav Dimi bar Chinana, who confirms that Rav said the dispute remains, and that Rabbah bar bar Chanah also said so.
Resh Lakish disputes Rabbi Yochanan's statement, asserting that the dispute remains.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan really holds that view, citing a contradictory statement.
Rabbi Chanah Tzipora'ah reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabban Gamliel, implying that the Sages originally disagreed.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba explains that the Sages agree with Rabban Gamliel only regarding the blessings of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, implying they disagree regarding the blessings of the rest of the year.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba explains that the Sages agree with Rabban Gamliel only regarding the blessings of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, implying they disagree regarding the blessings of the rest of the year.

items.text: Challenge and resolution by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanah of Tzippori quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, contradicting Rabbi Abba's implication. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that 'the Sages agree' refers to Rabbi Meir, and the dispute is with the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Chanah of Tzippori quoted Rabbi Yochanan stating the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabban Gamliel for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, contradicting Rabbi Abba's implication that the Sages only agree on those days.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that 'the Sages agree' refers to Rabbi Meir, and the dispute is with the Rabbis, so Rabbi Abba's statement is consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Meir vs. Sages on the prayer leader's role
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Meir vs. Sages on the prayer leader's role
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir says the prayer leader fulfills the obligation for the public on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, while the Sages say each individual is obligated like the leader.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir says the prayer leader fulfills the obligation for the public on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, while the Sages say each individual is obligated.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why these days?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why these days?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why these days are special, rejecting the reason of many verses (citing Rav Chananel quoting Rav) and suggesting it is due to the length of the blessings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What distinguishes these days from others? It rejects the possibility that it is due to the many verses, citing Rav Chananel's statement, and concludes it is because the blessings are lengthy.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection via Rav Chananel citing Rav
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection via Rav Chananel citing Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the first proposal, citing Rav Chananel in the name of Rav that once one says 'וּבְתוֹרָתְךָ כָּתוּב לֵאמֹר' (and in Your Torah it is written, saying), one need not recite additional verses.
The Gemara concludes that the reason is because the blessings are lengthy (אָוְושִׁי בְּרָכוֹת).

items.text: Rav Chananel's statement and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Chananel's statement and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies Rav Chananel's statement that after saying 'and in Your Torah it is written saying' one need not continue, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules this applies to both an individual and a congregation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananel reports in the name of Rav: Once one says 'וּבְתוֹרָתְךָ כָּתוּב לֵאמֹר' (and in Your Torah it is written to say), one no longer needs to recite additional verses.
The Gemara initially assumes this applies only to an individual, but not to a congregation.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that both an individual and a congregation, once they say 'וּבְתוֹרָתְךָ כָּתוּב לֵאמֹר', need no further verses.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar on arranging prayer and Rabbi Abba's qualification
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar on arranging prayer and Rabbi Abba's qualification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says one should always arrange his prayer before praying. Rabbi Abba limits this to Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and festival prayers. The Gemara challenges with Rav Yehuda, who arranged his prayer regularly, and answers that Rav Yehuda's practice was like festivals due to infrequency.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one should always arrange his prayer (יַסְדִּיר) before praying.
Rabbi Abba limits Rabbi Elazar's ruling to the prayers of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and festivals (פְּרָקִים), but not for the rest of the year.
The Gemara objects: Rav Yehuda regularly arranged his prayer before praying, contradicting Rabbi Abba's limitation.
The Gemara resolves: Rav Yehuda's case is different because he prayed only once every thirty days, so his prayers were like festivals (כִּפְרָקִים דָּמֵי).

items.text: Rabban Gamliel's exemption of field workers and final resolution
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's exemption of field workers and final resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avira quotes Rabbi Shimon the Pious that Rabban Gamliel exempted even field workers. The Gemara questions this, citing a baraita that those behind the priests are not included in the blessing. Ravin resolves that Rabban Gamliel only exempted field workers due to their preoccupation with work, not city dwellers.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Avira quoting Rabbi Shimon the Pious
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avira quoting Rabbi Shimon the Pious
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avira reports in the name of Rabbi Shimon the Pious that Rabban Gamliel exempted even field workers from the repetition, and certainly those standing in the synagogue.
The Gemara objects: on the contrary, field workers are preoccupied (אונסי) and thus exempt, while those in the synagogue are not preoccupied and should not be exempt.

sub.text: Supporting baraita cited by Abba the son of Rav Binyamin bar Chiya
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita cited by Abba the son of Rav Binyamin bar Chiya
sub.desc_en: A baraita taught by Abba the son of Rav Binyamin bar Chiya states that people standing behind the priests are not included in the priestly blessing, supporting the objection that those present are not automatically exempt.

sub.text: Ravin quoting Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi quoting Rabbi Shimon the Pious
sub.text_en: Ravin quoting Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi quoting Rabbi Shimon the Pious
sub.desc_en: Ravin resolves the difficulty by clarifying that Rabban Gamliel exempted only field workers because they are preoccupied with their work, but not city dwellers.
